title: Information Theory and Inference
text:
0.1 Scope
These are lecture notes for Information Theory and Inference (third-semester elective, Master in Physics of Data, University of Padova, instructor Prof. Michele Allegra). The course starts from Shannon’s operational definition of information and ends with modern Markov-Chain Monte Carlo methods for high-dimensional Bayesian inference.
The two halves of the course share a single organising object: the probability distribution. In Part I we ask how much information such a distribution contains, and how many bits are needed to communicate outcomes over a noisy channel. In Part II we ask, given a small amount of data, how to sample from a posterior distribution we can evaluate only up to an unknown normalisation constant.

title: Information Theory and Inference
text:
0.2 Reading the notes
Chapters 1–5 build up Shannon’s toolbox: surprisal, entropy, KL divergence, mutual information, the two coding theorems (source and noisy-channel), and their continuous counterparts. Chapter 6 extends information to time series and introduces the Markov-chain theory that powers Part II. Chapters 7–8 develop Monte Carlo sampling: Metropolis, convergence and autocorrelation, Gibbs sampling with latent variables. Chapter 9 applies them to a real high-dimensional problem (the origin of grey-seal founders). Chapters 10–12 cover the alternatives and extensions: variational Bayes (and the variational autoencoder), Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and approximate Bayesian computation for models whose likelihood can only be simulated.
Every chapter uses the styled callout environments (definition, theorem, proposition, lemma, corollary, example, remark, note, exercise, solution) so that key results can be scanned without reading the surrounding prose.

title: Information Theory and Inference
text:
0.3 Notation

\(X, Y, Z\): random variables; \(x, y, z\) realisations; \(\mathcal X\) their alphabet.
\(p_X(x) = P(X = x)\), \(p(x, y)\): probability mass or density; \(p(x \mid y)\) conditional.
\(H(X)\), \(H(X, Y)\), \(H(X \mid Y)\): entropy, joint entropy, conditional entropy.
\(I(X; Y)\): mutual information; \(D(p \| q)\): Kullback–Leibler divergence.
\(C\): channel capacity; \(R\): code rate.
\(\pi(\mathbf x)\): target distribution in MCMC; \(T(\mathbf x \to \mathbf x')\): transition kernel; \(q(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x)\): proposal.

0.4 Sources
These notes are a re-organised version of Notes on Information Theory and Inference by Prof. Michele Allegra (University of Padova, 2025), with additional material from the two standard textbooks:

Thomas M. Cover & Joy A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006.
David J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, Cambridge, 2003.

Chapters 7–8 also draw on Steve Brooks, Andrew Gelman, Galin Jones & Xiao-Li Meng (eds.), Handbook of Markov Chain Monte Carlo, CRC Press, 2011.
Every chapter closes with its own Sources section naming the specific sections used.

title: 2  Defining information
text:
2.1 Events and probability spaces
Information theory begins with a puzzle: what does it mean, quantitatively, that one message is more informative than another? The outcome of a random variable \(X\) is, by definition, uncertain — when we toss a coin we do not know whether it will land heads or tails. We can think of the information associated with \(X\) either as the uncertainty we have before the outcome is known, or, equivalently, as the knowledge we gain once the outcome is revealed.
In this chapter we derive a measure of information from first principles, by requiring it to satisfy a few intuitively appealing properties. Shannon’s answer — the information content of an event is the logarithm of the reciprocal of its probability — turns out to be the only answer compatible with those properties. Averaging it over all outcomes gives the first central quantity of the course, the entropy of a probability space.
We start in the most abstract setting.
For most of what follows we work with a finite alphabet \(\mathcal X\) and take \(\Omega = \mathcal X\), \(\mathcal F = 2^{\mathcal X}\) (the power set). The atomic events are singletons \(\{x\}\) with probabilities \(p_X(x) = P(\{X = x\})\).

title: 2  Defining information
text:
A probability space is a triple \(S = (\Omega, \mathcal F, P)\) where

\(\Omega\) is the sample space, the set of elementary outcomes;
\(\mathcal F \subseteq \mathcal P(\Omega)\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra of events. An event \(E\) is a set of outcomes, \(E \subseteq \Omega\); the family \(\mathcal F\) must be closed under union, intersection and complement;
\(P : \mathcal F \to [0, 1]\) is a probability, with (i) \(P(\Omega) = 1\) and (ii) \(\sigma\)-additivity: for any countable family of pairwise disjoint events \(\{E_i\}_{i \in I}\), \(E_i \cap E_j = \emptyset\) for \(i \neq j\), \[P\Bigl(\bigcup_{i \in I} E_i\Bigr) = \sum_{i \in I} P(E_i).\]




Toss two independent fair coins. The sample space is \[\Omega = \{hh, ht, th, tt\},\] where \(hh\) means “heads in the first toss and heads in the second toss”. The set of events is the whole power set, \(2^4 = 16\) events: \[\begin{aligned}
\mathcal F = \bigl\{&\emptyset,\ \{hh\}, \{ht\}, \{th\}, \{tt\},\ \{hh,ht\}, \{hh,th\}, \{hh,tt\}, \{ht,th\}, \{ht,tt\}, \{th,tt\},\\
&\{hh,ht,th\}, \{hh,ht,tt\}, \{hh,th,tt\}, \{ht,th,tt\},\ \{hh,ht,th,tt\}\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}\] Since all outcomes are equiprobable, \(P(E) = |E|/4\): one-outcome events have probability \(1/4\), two-outcome events \(1/2\), three-outcome events \(3/4\), and \(P(\Omega) = 1\).


2.1.1 Events as answers
A useful way to think about events — and the one that leads naturally to information — is the following: every event is a possible answer to the question “What was the outcome?”. Answers can be more or less specific depending on how many outcomes they include.

The four singletons \(\{hh\}, \{ht\}, \{th\}, \{tt\}\) fully specify the outcome (“the outcome was \(hh\)”).
The six two-outcome events are less detailed: \(\{hh, ht\}\) means “the outcome was \(hh\) or \(ht\)” — equivalently, “the first coin gave heads”.
The four three-outcome events are even vaguer: \(\{hh, ht, th\}\) means “the outcome was not \(tt\)”; it only excludes one possibility.
The event \(\Omega = \{hh, ht, th, tt\}\) is the trivial answer — we already knew that one of these happened.

So \(\mathcal F\) contains every possible answer, from the most detailed to the least detailed, and each answer has its own probability.


2.1.2 Conditional probability and independence
Disjoint events (\(E_1 \cap E_2 = \emptyset\)) are mutually exclusive answers; non-disjoint events are possibly compatible answers. Any event \(E_2\) splits into a part compatible with \(E_1\) and a part incompatible with it, \[E_2 = (E_1 \cap E_2) \cup (\bar E_1 \cap E_2).\] If we know that \(E_2\) occurred, then either \(E_1\) occurred too, or it did not. The relative weight of the first case defines the conditional probability.

For \(P(E_2) > 0\), the conditional probability of \(E_1\) given \(E_2\) is \[P(E_1 \mid E_2) \equiv \frac{P(E_1 \cap E_2)}{P(E_2)} = \frac{P(E_1 \cap E_2)}{P(E_1 \cap E_2) + P(\bar E_1 \cap E_2)}.\] Two events are independent if the probability of the joint event factorises, \[P(E_1 \cap E_2) = P(E_1)\,P(E_2),\] or equivalently \(P(E_1 \mid E_2) = P(E_1)\) and \(P(E_2 \mid E_1) = P(E_2)\).

In the “answers” language: independent events are complementary answers — knowing one does not make the other more or less likely.

In the two-coin space:

\(E_1 = \{hh, ht\}\) (“first toss gave \(h\)”) and \(E_2 = \{th, tt\}\) (“first toss gave \(t\)”) are mutually exclusive: \(E_1 \cap E_2 = \emptyset\).
\(E_1 = \{hh, ht, th\}\) (“not \(tt\)”) and \(E_2 = \{hh, ht, tt\}\) (“not \(th\)”) intersect in \(\{hh, ht\}\). Then \[P(E_1 \mid E_2) = \frac{P(\{hh, ht\})}{P(\{hh, ht, tt\})} = \frac{1/2}{3/4} = \frac23 < P(E_1) = \frac34 .\] Learning \(E_2\) decreases the likelihood of \(E_1\).
\(E_1 = \{hh\}\) and \(E_2 = \{hh, ht, tt\}\): \[P(E_1 \mid E_2) = \frac{1/4}{3/4} = \frac13 > P(E_1) = \frac14 .\] Learning \(E_2\) increases the likelihood of \(E_1\).
The pairs \[(\{hh,ht\}, \{hh,th\}),\quad (\{hh,ht\}, \{hh,tt\}),\quad (\{hh,ht\}, \{ht,th\})\] are all independent: e.g. for the second pair, “first toss gave \(h\)” and “the two tosses agree”, \(P(E_1 \cap E_2) = P(\{hh\}) = 1/4 = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12\). Knowing that the coins agree tells us nothing about the first coin. (In fact nearly all pairs of two-outcome events in this space are independent.)



Remark (When does conditioning increase a probability?). Write \(\Delta \equiv P(E_1 \cap \bar E_2)\) and \(\bar\Delta \equiv P(\bar E_1 \cap \bar E_2)\) for the probability that is “removed” from \(E_1\) and from its complement when we learn \(E_2\). Then \[P(E_1) = \frac{P(E_1)}{P(E_1) + P(\bar E_1)}, \qquad P(E_1 \mid E_2) = \frac{P(E_1) - \Delta}{P(E_1) - \Delta + P(\bar E_1) - \bar\Delta}.\] The two expressions have the same structure; conditioning simply subtracts the excluded probability. One checks that \[P(E_1 \mid E_2) > P(E_1) \iff \frac{\Delta}{\bar \Delta} < \frac{P(E_1)}{P(\bar E_1)},\] i.e. \(E_1\) becomes more likely exactly when it loses proportionally less probability than its complement.

title: 2  Defining information
text:
2.2 The surprisal
Each event specifies the outcome to a larger or lesser degree, i.e. provides more or less information about it. Let us make this quantitative by constructing a function \[I : \mathcal F \to \mathbb R_+\] that assigns to each event the information it provides about the outcome.

2.2.1 Requirements
Intuitively we should agree that:

Events with the same probability provide the same amount of information. Hence \(I\) depends on \(E\) only through its probability: \(I(E) = f(P(E))\) for some unknown \(f : [0,1] \to \mathbb R_+\).
More probable events (more outcomes, vaguer answers) provide less information: \(f\) is monotonically decreasing. In particular \(I(\Omega) = f(1)\) should be zero — the trivial answer tells us nothing.
Additivity for independent events. Independent events are complementary answers, so the information of the combined answer \(E = E_1 \cap E_2\) should be the sum of the two pieces: \(I(E_1 \cap E_2) = I(E_1) + I(E_2)\). Since \(P(E_1 \cap E_2) = P(E_1)P(E_2)\), this means \[f(x_1 x_2) = f(x_1) + f(x_2).\]


We could first say “the first coin gave \(h\)” (\(E_1 = \{hh, ht\}\)) and then “the second coin gave \(h\)” (\(E_2 = \{hh, th\}\)). These events are independent, and together they say exactly “the outcome was \(hh\)” (\(E_1 \cap E_2 = \{hh\}\)). It is natural to demand that the information in the single answer \(\{hh\}\) equal the sum of the information in the two partial answers.



2.2.2 The logarithm is forced

A monotonically decreasing function \(f : (0, 1] \to \mathbb R_+\) satisfying \(f(x_1 x_2) = f(x_1) + f(x_2)\) must be of the form \[f(x) = -\alpha \log x, \qquad \alpha > 0 .\]


Proof. Set \(x = e^y\) and \(g(y) = f(e^y)\). The functional equation becomes \[f(e^{y_1} e^{y_2}) = f(e^{y_1 + y_2}) = f(e^{y_1}) + f(e^{y_2}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g(y_1 + y_2) = g(y_1) + g(y_2).\] This is Cauchy’s functional equation; its only monotone solutions are linear, \(g(y) = \alpha' y\). Hence \(f(e^y) = \alpha' y\), i.e. \(f(x) = \alpha' \log x\). Monotonic decrease requires \(\alpha' < 0\); write \(\alpha' = -\alpha\) with \(\alpha > 0\).


The surprisal (or self-information) of an event \(E\) is \[I(E) = -\log_2 P(E) \quad \text{bits}.\] For a random variable \(X\) taking value \(x\) we write \(I(x) = -\log_2 p_X(x)\).

The name reflects that low-probability events are more “surprising”. It is worth stressing what the surprisal measures: the amount of information we obtain when we learn that the outcome of a random process lies in a given subset \(E\) of all possible outcomes.

Remark (Units). The constant \(\alpha\) is arbitrary and only fixes the unit. Choosing \(\alpha\) is the same as choosing a base \(\beta = e^{1/\alpha}\) for the logarithm: \[-\alpha \log P = -\frac{\log P}{\log \beta} = -\log_\beta P .\] With \(\beta = 2\) we measure information in bits (binary digits); with \(\beta = e\) in nats; with \(\beta = 10\) in hartleys. Since \(\ln 2 \approx 0.693\), \(1\ \text{bit} \approx 0.693\ \text{nat}\). From now on \(\log \equiv \log_2\) unless stated otherwise.
The bit has a simple interpretation: it is the information revealed when we learn the outcome of a process with two equiprobable outcomes, such as the toss of a fair coin.


For a fair coin each outcome carries \(\log_2 2 = 1\) bit. For a biased coin with \(p(H) = 0.99\), seeing heads carries only \(-\log_2 0.99 \approx 0.014\) bits — the outcome was almost certain. Seeing tails carries \(-\log_2 0.01 \approx 6.6\) bits — a much more informative event.


\(I(\{hh\}) = -\log_2(1/4) = 2\) bits; \(I(\{hh, ht\}) = 1\) bit; \(I(\{hh, ht, th\}) = -\log_2(3/4) \approx 0.415\) bits; \(I(\Omega) = 0\). The more specific the answer, the more bits it carries; full specification of two coins costs two bits, one per coin.



2.2.3 Conditional surprisal: redundant and synergistic answers
What if we specify the outcome through answers that are not independent? If we already know that the outcome is in \(E_1\), the natural information carried by \(E_2\) is
\[I(E_2 \mid E_1) = -\log P(E_2 \mid E_1).\]
Since \(P(E_1 \cap E_2) = P(E_1) P(E_2 \mid E_1)\), taking logarithms gives the chain rule for surprisal \[I(E_1 \cap E_2) = I(E_1) + I(E_2 \mid E_1).\]
In general \(I(E_2 \mid E_1)\) can be larger or smaller than \(I(E_2)\). Correspondingly the information provided jointly by two non-independent events can be less (redundancy) or more (synergy) than the sum of their separate informations.

The event \(E = \{hh\}\) can be obtained as the intersection of the non-independent events \(E_1 = \{hh, ht, th\}\) (“at least one \(h\)”), \(E_2 = \{hh, th\}\) (“heads in the second toss”), \(E_3 = \{hh\}\). There is redundancy among these answers: \[P(E_2 \mid E_1) = \tfrac23 > P(E_2) = \tfrac12, \qquad P(E_3 \mid E_2) = \tfrac12 > P(E_3) = \tfrac14 .\] The separate surprisals are \[I(E_1) = -\log\tfrac34 \approx 0.42, \quad I(E_2) = 1, \quad I(E_3) = 2,\] so naïvely summing gives \(3.42 > I(E) = 2\) bits: we have “overcounted” the information. Using conditional surprisals instead, \[I(E) = I(E_1) + I(E_2 \mid E_1) + I(E_3 \mid E_2) = -\log\Bigl(\tfrac34 \cdot \tfrac23 \cdot \tfrac12\Bigr) = -\log\tfrac14 = 2 \text{ bits}. \checkmark\]


Take \(E = \{hh, ht\}\) as the intersection of \(E_1 = \{hh, ht, th\}\) and \(E_2 = \{hh, ht, tt\}\). Then \[P(E) = \tfrac12 = \tfrac{8}{16} < P(E_1)P(E_2) = \tfrac{9}{16},\] and therefore \[I(E) = 1 > I(E_1) + I(E_2) = 2 \times 0.415 = 0.83 \text{ bits}.\] Each answer alone only excludes one outcome, but together they exclude two: the combination is worth more than the parts.


For any sequence of random variables \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\), \[I(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} I(x_i \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}),\] where \(I(x_i \mid \cdot) = -\log_2 p(x_i \mid \cdot)\) is the conditional surprisal.

This follows from the chain rule of probability \(p(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \prod_i p(x_i \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1})\) and the additivity of the logarithm.

title: 2  Defining information
2  Defining information
text:
2.4 Information for a probability space
The surprisal \(I(E)\) measures how much information event \(E\) gives about the outcome. We now ask: how much information is needed, on average, to completely specify the outcome? This will be the information content of the probability space as a whole.

An urn contains red, blue and green balls in proportions \(50\%, 25\%, 25\%\). We draw one ball. To identify its colour we may first ask “is it red?” (\(E_1 = \{r\}\) vs \(\bar E_1 = \{b, g\}\), each answer worth 1 bit). If not red, we ask “is it blue?” — a second bit. Thus red is identified with 1 bit, blue and green with 2 bits. On average \[\tfrac12 \cdot 1 + \tfrac14 \cdot 2 + \tfrac14 \cdot 2 = 1.5 \text{ bits},\] which is the average number of yes/no questions needed to identify the outcome.


Now red, blue, green, yellow, purple in proportions \(50\%, 12.5\%, 12.5\%, 12.5\%, 12.5\%\). Ask “red?” (1 bit); if not, “blue or green?” (2nd bit); then “blue?” or “yellow?” (3rd bit). Red costs 1 question, every other colour 3. On average \[\tfrac12 \cdot 1 + 4 \cdot \tfrac18 \cdot 3 = 2 \text{ bits}.\] Note that each question was designed to split the remaining probability in half, so every answer was worth exactly one bit.

Formalising the argument: for each outcome \(a \in \Omega\) of a discrete space there is an elementary event \(\{a\}\) with information \(-\log P(\{a\})\). The average information needed to specify the outcome is \[H(S) = \langle I \rangle = -\sum_{a \in \Omega} P(\{a\}) \log P(\{a\}),\] a single number for the whole space \(S = (\Omega, \mathcal F, P)\). Introducing a random variable \(X : \Omega \to \{x_1, \ldots, x_N\}\) with \(p_X(x_i) = P(\{a\})\) when \(X(a) = x_i\) (in the urn, \(r \mapsto x_1\), \(b \mapsto x_2\), \(g \mapsto x_3\)):

The Shannon entropy of a discrete random variable \(X\) with distribution \(p_X\) is \[H(X) = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal X} p_X(x)\,\log_2 p_X(x) = \mathbb E[I(X)] .\] By convention \(0\log 0 = 0\).

The entropy is the expected number of bits carried by a random outcome — the average information needed to specify it. This operational reading will be made rigorous by the source-coding theorem in Chapter 3.

For \(X \sim \text{Bern}(p)\), \(H(X) = -p\log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p) \equiv h_2(p)\). The binary entropy function \(h_2\) is symmetric around \(p = 1/2\), where it takes its maximum value \(h_2(1/2) = 1\) bit. It vanishes at \(p = 0\) or \(p = 1\) — no information from a certain outcome. A few values worth remembering: \(h_2(0.1) \approx 0.469\), \(h_2(0.11) \approx 0.5\), \(h_2(0.25) \approx 0.811\).


Let \(X\) take values \(a, b, c, d\) with probabilities \(\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18\). Then \[H(X) = \tfrac12 \cdot 1 + \tfrac14 \cdot 2 + \tfrac18 \cdot 3 + \tfrac18 \cdot 3 = 1.75 \text{ bits}.\] An efficient questioning strategy is “Is \(X = a\)?”, then “Is \(X = b\)?”, then “Is \(X = c\)?”; the expected number of questions is exactly \(1.75\). We will see in Chapter 3 that no strategy can use fewer than \(H(X)\) questions on average.


An integer \(x\) is chosen uniformly in \(\{0, 1, \ldots, 63\}\). Ask: “is \(x \geq 32\)?”, “is \(x \bmod 32 \geq 16\)?”, “is \(x \bmod 16 \geq 8\)?”, “is \(x \bmod 8 \geq 4\)?”, “is \(x \bmod 4 \geq 2\)?”, “is \(x \bmod 2 = 1\)?”. Each question halves the set of candidates and therefore yields exactly one bit; after six questions \(x\) is known, consistent with \(H = \log_2 64 = 6\) bits. Writing the answers as \(1\) = yes, \(0\) = no gives precisely the binary expansion of \(x\) — the bits of information are the binary digits.


For a variable \(X\) taking \(M\) values, the entropy is maximised when \(p_X\) is uniform, in which case \(H(X) = \log_2 M\). Non-uniform distributions give strictly less entropy — a preview of the general result proved in Chapter 2.

title: 2  Defining information
text:
2.5 An axiomatic derivation of entropy
Had we not derived the surprisal first, we could have obtained Shannon’s formula directly from requirements on \(H\) itself, following an argument reported by Bialek. We look for a functional \(H[X]\) measuring the information content of the distribution of \(X\).
Step 1: equiprobable outcomes. If \(p_X(x_i) = 1/N\) for all \(i\), then \(H\) should be a monotonically increasing function of the number of outcomes: \(H[X] = g(N)\).
Step 2: composition. Let \(N = k^m\). We can draw a tree with \(m\) levels and \(k\) equiprobable branches at each level, and map \(X \mapsto (X_1, \ldots, X_m)\) where each \(X_j\) is an independent variable with \(k\) equally likely outcomes — each outcome of \(X\) is identified by answering \(m\) independent sub-questions. (Two coins: \(k = 2\), \(m = 2\).) The total information must be the sum of the parts: \[g(k^m) = \sum_{j=1}^m H[X_j] = m\, g(k).\]

The only monotonic function satisfying \(g(k^m) = m\, g(k)\) for all integers \(k, m\) is \(g(x) = \alpha \log x\).


Proof. Fix integers \(k, \ell \geq 2\) and \(n \geq 1\), and choose \(m\) such that \(k^m \leq \ell^n < k^{m+1}\), i.e. \(m = \lfloor n \log \ell / \log k \rfloor\). (E.g. \(k = 4\), \(\ell = 3\), \(n = 3\): \(m = \lfloor 2.37 \rfloor = 2\).) Taking logarithms and dividing by \(n \log k\): \[\frac mn \leq \frac{\log \ell}{\log k} < \frac mn + \frac1n \quad\Rightarrow\quad \Bigl|\frac{\log \ell}{\log k} - \frac mn\Bigr| \leq \frac1n .\] By monotonicity \(g(k^m) \leq g(\ell^n) < g(k^{m+1})\), i.e. \(m\, g(k) \leq n\, g(\ell) < (m+1) g(k)\); dividing by \(n\, g(k)\), \[\Bigl|\frac{g(\ell)}{g(k)} - \frac mn\Bigr| \leq \frac1n .\] By the triangle inequality, \(|g(\ell)/g(k) - \log \ell/\log k| \leq 2/n\) for every \(n\). Letting \(n \to \infty\) gives \(g(\ell)/g(k) = \log \ell / \log k\) for all \(k, \ell\), i.e. \(g(x) = \alpha \log x\).

Thus for \(N\) equiprobable outcomes \(H[X] = \log N\) (choosing \(\alpha\) so that we work in bits).
Step 3: non-uniform probabilities. Suppose the probabilities \(p_i\) are rational (any real can be approximated arbitrarily well). Write \(p_i = r_i / s_i\) and let \(M = \prod_l s_l\); then \(p_i = k_i / M\) with \(k_i = r_i \prod_{l \neq i} s_l \in \mathbb N\) and \(\sum_i k_i = M\).
Imagine a variable \(Y\) with \(M\) equiprobable outcomes arranged into \(N\) groups, group \(i\) containing \(k_i\) outcomes. Let \(X\) be the group label (so \(P(X = i) = k_i / M = p_i\)) and \(Z_i\) the position within group \(i\) (uniform on \(k_i\) values). Identifying \(Y\) takes two sub-questions — first the group, then the element — so \[H[Y] = H[X] + \sum_i p_i\, H[Z_i],\] where the second term is averaged because the different branches are reached with different probabilities. Since \(H[Y] = \log M\) and \(H[Z_i] = \log k_i\), \[\log M = H[X] + \sum_i p_i \log k_i \quad\Longrightarrow\quad H[X] = -\sum_i p_i \log\frac{k_i}{M} = -\sum_i p_i \log p_i . \qquad\blacksquare\]

Take \(p = (\tfrac12, \tfrac13, \tfrac16)\). With \(M = 6\): \(k = (3, 2, 1)\). Then \(H[Y] = \log 6 \approx 2.585\), and the within-group terms give \(\tfrac12 \log 3 + \tfrac13 \log 2 + \tfrac16 \log 1 \approx 0.792 + 0.333 = 1.126\). Hence \(H[X] \approx 2.585 - 1.126 = 1.459\) bits, which agrees with \(-\tfrac12\log\tfrac12 - \tfrac13\log\tfrac13 - \tfrac16\log\tfrac16 \approx 0.5 + 0.528 + 0.431 = 1.459\). \(\checkmark\)

The composition rule used in Step 3 is the grouping property of entropy, which we state in general below.

title: 2  Defining information
text:
2.6 Elementary properties
The entropy is well-behaved as a function of the distribution (proofs in Chapter 2).

For any discrete random variable \(X\) with distribution on \(\mathcal X\):

\(H(X) \geq 0\), with equality iff \(X\) is deterministic.
\(H(X) \leq \log_2 |\mathcal X|\), with equality iff \(X\) is uniform.
\(H\) is a concave function of \(p_X\).
Grouping property. If two outcomes \(x_1, x_2\) are merged into one with probability \(p_1 + p_2\), then \[H(X) = H(X_{merged}) + (p_1 + p_2)\,h_2\bigl(p_1/(p_1 + p_2)\bigr).\]



For a pair \((X, Y)\) with joint distribution \(p(x, y)\), \[H(X, Y) = -\sum_{x, y} p(x, y)\log_2 p(x, y) \leq H(X) + H(Y),\] with equality iff \(X, Y\) are independent (sub-additivity, proved in Chapter 2).

title: 2  Defining information
text:
2.7 Exercises

A fair die is rolled. Compute (i) the surprisal of the event “the outcome is 6”, (ii) the entropy of the rolling process, (iii) the surprisal of the event “the outcome is even”.


Solution. 

\(I(\{6\}) = -\log_2(1/6) = \log_2 6 \approx 2.585\) bits.
\(H(X) = \log_2 6 \approx 2.585\) bits (uniform on 6 outcomes).
\(I(\{2, 4, 6\}) = -\log_2(3/6) = 1\) bit — exactly one bit of information (equivalent to a coin toss).



Show that for a Bernoulli\((p)\) variable the entropy is maximised at \(p = 1/2\) by direct differentiation. What is the second derivative at the maximum?


Solution. \(H'(p) = -\log_2 p + \log_2(1 - p) = \log_2\bigl((1-p)/p\bigr)\). Setting \(H' = 0\) gives \(p = 1/2\). The second derivative is \(H''(p) = -[1/(p\ln 2) + 1/((1 - p)\ln 2)]\), which at \(p = 1/2\) equals \(-4/\ln 2 \approx -5.77\). Negative \(H''\) confirms concavity — a global maximum.


Verify the grouping property for a three-outcome variable with probabilities \((1/2, 1/4, 1/4)\).


Solution. Direct: \(H = -\tfrac12\log_2\tfrac12 - \tfrac14\log_2\tfrac14 - \tfrac14\log_2\tfrac14 = 1.5\) bits. Grouping the last two into a merged outcome of probability \(1/2\): \(H_{merged} = h_2(1/2) = 1\) bit, plus \(1/2 \cdot h_2(1/2) = 0.5\) bits, total \(1.5\) bits. \(\checkmark\)


In the two-coin space, check that \(E_1 = \{hh, ht\}\) (“first coin \(h\)”) and \(E_2 = \{ht, th\}\) (“coins differ”) are independent, and compute \(I(E_1)\), \(I(E_2)\) and \(I(E_1 \cap E_2)\).


Solution. \(E_1 \cap E_2 = \{ht\}\), \(P = 1/4 = P(E_1)P(E_2) = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12\): independent. \(I(E_1) = I(E_2) = 1\) bit and \(I(\{ht\}) = 2 = I(E_1) + I(E_2)\) bits, as additivity requires.


Twelve balls look identical, but one is either heavier or lighter than the others. How much information is needed to identify the odd ball and whether it is heavy or light? A balance has three outcomes (left heavy, right heavy, balanced). What is the minimum number of weighings needed in principle?


Solution. There are \(12 \times 2 = 24\) equiprobable hypotheses, so \(\log_2 24 \approx 4.58\) bits are needed. A weighing has three outcomes and can deliver at most \(\log_2 3 \approx 1.58\) bits. Hence at least \(\lceil 4.58 / 1.58 \rceil = 3\) weighings are needed — and three indeed suffice if each weighing is designed so that its three outcomes are as close to equiprobable as possible (MacKay §4.1). The lesson: good experiments maximise the entropy of their outcome.

title: 2  Defining information
text:
2.8 Callouts






Shannon’s definition is operational — it derives its meaning from the coding theorems of Chapter 3. Purely axiomatic derivations (like the one above) show that the formula is unique, but do not tell you why it is useful.









When computing entropies by hand, remember the identity \(\log_2 n = \log_2 e \cdot \ln n \approx 1.4427 \ln n\): it lets you convert between nats and bits without a calculator.









The convention \(0\log 0 = 0\) is genuine, not a hack: \(p \log(1/p) \to 0\) as \(p \to 0^+\). But if you compute \(I(x)\) for an event that has empirical probability zero from a finite sample, the value is \(+\infty\), and downstream computations will be nonsense. Always regularise.

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
text:
3.1 Properties of Shannon entropy
Entropy is only the first in a family of information measures. This chapter first proves the basic properties of the entropy, then introduces the three other quantities we will use constantly — the Kullback–Leibler divergence, the conditional entropy and the mutual information — and develops the identities and inequalities that connect them. Every result here will be used in the coding theorems of Chapters 3–4 and, later, in variational inference (Chapter 10).

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
text:
3.1.1 Range

Let \(X\) take values in an alphabet \(\mathcal A_X\) with \(|\mathcal A_X| = N\). Then \[0 \leq H[X] \leq \log N .\] The minimum is attained iff one outcome has probability one (\(\exists i: p_i = 1\)); the maximum is attained iff all outcomes are equiprobable (\(p_i = 1/N\) for all \(i\)).


Proof. Lower bound. \(0 \leq p_i \leq 1\) implies \(-p_i \log p_i \geq 0\), with equality only for \(p_i \in \{0, 1\}\); so \(H = 0\) iff a single outcome has probability one.
Upper bound. Maximise \(H\) under the constraint \(\sum_i p_i = 1\) with a Lagrange multiplier (natural logs for convenience): \[\mathcal L[\{p_i\}, \lambda] = -\sum_i p_i \ln p_i + \lambda\Bigl(\sum_i p_i - 1\Bigr).\] Stationarity gives \[\frac{\partial \mathcal L}{\partial p_i} = -1 - \ln p_i + \lambda = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; p_i = e^{\lambda - 1} \equiv \mu \;\;\forall i, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal L}{\partial \lambda} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \sum_i p_i = 1 .\] All \(p_i\) are equal, and normalisation gives \(\mu = 1/N\). Because \(H\) is concave (below), this stationary point is the global maximum, \(H = \log N\). A second proof, via the KL divergence, is given below.



3.1.2 Concavity
Recall that \(f\) is concave if \(f(\lambda x_1 + (1 - \lambda) x_2) \geq \lambda f(x_1) + (1 - \lambda) f(x_2)\) for all \(\lambda \in [0, 1]\) (the chord lies below the graph), and convex if the inequality is reversed (the chord lies above).

The Shannon entropy is a concave function of the distribution: for any two distributions \(p, q\) on the same alphabet and \(\lambda \in [0, 1]\), \[H(\lambda p + (1 - \lambda)q) \geq \lambda H(p) + (1 - \lambda)H(q),\] with equality (for \(0 < \lambda < 1\)) iff \(p = q\).

The mixture \(\lambda p + (1 - \lambda) q\) has a concrete meaning. Let \(X_1 \sim p\) and \(X_2 \sim q\), and let \(Z = X_1\) with probability \(\lambda\) and \(Z = X_2\) with probability \(1 - \lambda\). Then \(p_Z = \lambda p + (1 - \lambda) q\), and concavity states that mixing two distributions increases entropy: not knowing which source produced the symbol adds uncertainty. The proof is given after we introduce the KL divergence.

Let \(p = (1, 0)\) and \(q = (0, 1)\): both \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are deterministic, \(H(p) = H(q) = 0\). Their mixture is \((\lambda, 1 - \lambda)\), with entropy \(h_2(\lambda) > 0\) for every \(0 < \lambda < 1\). All the uncertainty of \(Z\) comes from the coin that selects the source.

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
text:
3.2 Kullback–Leibler divergence
The KL divergence (or relative entropy) measures how different a distribution \(p\) is from another distribution \(q\).

For distributions \(p, q\) on a discrete alphabet \(\mathcal X\) (write \(p_i = p(x_i)\), \(q_i = q(x_i)\)), \[D_{KL}(p \| q) = \sum_i p_i \log \frac{p_i}{q_i}.\] By convention \(0\log(0/q) = 0\) and \(p\log(p/0) = +\infty\) for \(p > 0\).


For any two distributions \(p, q\) on the same alphabet, \(D_{KL}(p \| q) \geq 0\), with equality iff \(p = q\).

The proof (below) uses Jensen’s inequality. Because of Gibbs’ inequality, \(D_{KL}\) can be read as a measure of discriminability between two distributions — a kind of “distance” on the space of distributions.

Remark. The KL divergence is not a metric: it is not symmetric (\(D(p \| q) \neq D(q \| p)\) in general) and it does not satisfy the triangle inequality. It does, however, satisfy \(D(p \| q) = 0 \iff p = q\), and it is jointly convex (below).


3.2.1 Interpretation: the cost of a wrong model
Suppose \(X\) takes value \(x_i\) with probability \(p_i\), but an observer (mistakenly) believes the probabilities are \(q_i\). When the outcome \(x_i\) is revealed, the observer assigns it surprisal \(-\log q_i\) — they think they have received \(-\log q_i\) bits. Since \(x_i\) occurs with probability \(p_i\), the average perceived information is the cross entropy \[H(p, q) = -\sum_i p_i \log q_i .\] The cross entropy is always at least the true entropy, and the excess is exactly the KL divergence: \[D_{KL}(p \| q) = H(p, q) - H(p) = -\sum_i p_i \log q_i + \sum_i p_i \log p_i = \sum_i p_i (\log p_i - \log q_i) \geq 0 .\] The observer always overestimates the information obtained; the overestimate is \(D_{KL}(p \| q)\). In Chapter 3 this becomes concrete: \(D(p\|q)\) is the number of extra bits per symbol paid by a code designed for \(q\) when the source is really \(p\).

Let \(p = (1 - \epsilon, \epsilon)\) with \(\epsilon \ll 1\). The entropy is tiny, \[H(p) = -\epsilon\log\epsilon - (1 - \epsilon)\log(1 - \epsilon) \approx \epsilon\,(\log(1/\epsilon) + \log e) ,\] because the outcome is nearly always \(x_1\), which carries almost no information (\(-\log(1 - \epsilon) \approx \epsilon \log e\)). An observer who assumes \(q = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)\) will nearly always see \(x_1\) and believe they received one full bit: \[H(p, q) = -(1 - \epsilon)\log\tfrac12 - \epsilon\log\tfrac12 = 1 \gg H(p).\]


Conversely, let \(p = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)\), so \(H(p) = 1\), but the observer believes \(q = (1 - \epsilon, \epsilon)\). Half of the time they see the “rare” outcome \(x_2\) and think they received \(-\log\epsilon \gg 1\) bits: \[H(p, q) = -\tfrac12 \log\bigl(\epsilon(1 - \epsilon)\bigr) \approx \tfrac12 \log\frac1\epsilon \gg 1 .\] Here \(D(p\|q) \approx \tfrac12\log(1/\epsilon) - 1\) diverges as \(\epsilon \to 0\), whereas in the previous example the divergence \(D(p\|q) = 1 - H(p) \to 1\) stays bounded: a vivid illustration of the asymmetry of KL. Assigning near-zero probability to something that actually happens is punished very severely.


For \(\text{Bern}(a)\) vs \(\text{Bern}(b)\), \[D(a \| b) = a \log \frac{a}{b} + (1 - a)\log\frac{1 - a}{1 - b}.\] When \(b = 1/2\) this reduces to \(1 - h_2(a)\), the “distance from uniform” of a biased coin. Numerically, \(D(0.5 \| 0.25) \approx 0.208\) bits but \(D(0.25 \| 0.5) \approx 0.189\) bits.



3.2.2 Entropy as distance from uniform
Let \(u_i = 1/N\) be the uniform distribution on the same alphabet. Then \[H(p) = -\sum_i p_i \log\Bigl(\frac{p_i}{u_i} \cdot u_i\Bigr) = -D_{KL}(p \| u) - \sum_i p_i \log\frac1N = \log N - D_{KL}(p \| u).\] Combined with Gibbs’ inequality this gives a one-line proof of \(H(p) \leq \log N\), with equality iff \(p = u\). The entropy is the maximal entropy minus how far the distribution is from uniform.


3.2.3 Proofs

If \(f\) is convex and \(X\) is a random variable, \(\mathbb E[f(X)] \geq f(\mathbb E[X])\). If \(f\) is strictly convex, equality holds iff \(X\) is constant (almost surely). For concave \(f\) the inequality is reversed.


Proof. For a discrete \(X\) with values \(x_i\) and probabilities \(p_i\), peel off one term at a time. Define \(p_i^{(1)} = p_i/(1 - p_1)\) for \(i \neq 1\) (a normalised distribution). By convexity, \[f\Bigl(\sum_i p_i x_i\Bigr) = f\Bigl(p_1 x_1 + (1 - p_1)\sum_{i\neq 1} p_i^{(1)} x_i\Bigr) \leq p_1 f(x_1) + (1 - p_1)\, f\Bigl(\sum_{i \neq 1} p_i^{(1)} x_i\Bigr).\] Repeating the step on the last term with \(p_i^{(2)} = p_i/(1 - p_1 - p_2)\), and so on, after \(N - 1\) steps we arrive at \(f(\sum_i p_i x_i) \leq \sum_i p_i f(x_i)\). (Equivalently, a short induction on \(N\).)


Proof (Proof of Gibbs’ inequality). Let \(Z = q(X)/p(X)\) with \(X \sim p\), and apply Jensen to the convex function \(-\log\): \[D_{KL}(p\|q) = \sum_i p_i \Bigl(-\log\frac{q_i}{p_i}\Bigr) = \mathbb E[-\log Z] \geq -\log \mathbb E[Z] = -\log \sum_i p_i \frac{q_i}{p_i} = -\log \sum_i q_i = 0 .\] Since \(-\log\) is strictly convex, equality requires \(q_i/p_i\) constant, i.e. \(p = q\).


For non-negative \(a_i\) and positive \(b_i\), \[\sum_i a_i \log \frac{a_i}{b_i} \geq \Bigl(\sum_i a_i\Bigr)\log \frac{\sum_i a_i}{\sum_i b_i},\] with equality iff \(a_i / b_i\) is constant across \(i\).


Proof. \(t \mapsto t\log t\) is strictly convex. Let \(A = \sum a_i\), \(B = \sum b_i\), weights \(w_i = b_i/B\) and points \(t_i = a_i/b_i\). Jensen gives \(\sum_i w_i t_i \log t_i \geq (\sum_i w_i t_i)\log(\sum_i w_i t_i)\), i.e. \(\frac1B\sum_i a_i\log\frac{a_i}{b_i} \geq \frac AB\log\frac AB\). Multiply by \(B\).

The log-sum inequality is the workhorse behind almost every information-theoretic inequality that follows.

\(D(p \| q)\) is convex in the pair \((p, q)\): for \(\lambda \in [0, 1]\), \[D(\lambda p_1 + (1 - \lambda)p_2 \,\|\, \lambda q_1 + (1 - \lambda)q_2) \leq \lambda D(p_1 \| q_1) + (1 - \lambda)D(p_2 \| q_2).\] In words, mixing decreases discriminability.


Proof. For each \(i\), apply the log-sum inequality to the two-term sums \(a = (\lambda p_{1i}, (1-\lambda)p_{2i})\), \(b = (\lambda q_{1i}, (1 - \lambda) q_{2i})\): \[(\lambda p_{1i} + (1-\lambda)p_{2i})\log\frac{\lambda p_{1i} + (1-\lambda)p_{2i}}{\lambda q_{1i} + (1-\lambda)q_{2i}} \leq \lambda p_{1i}\log\frac{\lambda p_{1i}}{\lambda q_{1i}} + (1-\lambda)p_{2i}\log\frac{(1-\lambda)p_{2i}}{(1-\lambda)q_{2i}} .\] The factors \(\lambda\) and \(1 - \lambda\) cancel inside the logarithms; summing over \(i\) gives the claim.


Proof (Proof of concavity of entropy). Using \(H(p) = \log N - D(p\|u)\) and convexity of \(D\) in its first argument (take \(q_1 = q_2 = u\)): \[H(\lambda p + (1-\lambda) q) = \log N - D(\lambda p + (1-\lambda)q \,\|\, u) \geq \log N - \lambda D(p\|u) - (1-\lambda) D(q\|u) = \lambda H(p) + (1 - \lambda) H(q).\]

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
section: 3.3 Joint entropy, conditional entropy, mutual information
text:
3.3 Joint entropy, conditional entropy, mutual information
Let \(X, Y\) take values \(\{x_i\}\), \(\{y_j\}\), with joint probabilities \(p_{ij} \equiv p_{X,Y}(x_i, y_j)\) and marginals \(p_i = \sum_j p_{ij}\), \(q_j = \sum_i p_{ij}\).

The joint entropy is the entropy of the joint distribution, \[H[X, Y] = -\sum_{i,j} p_{ij} \log p_{ij}.\]

If we learn that \(X = x_i\), then \(Y\) has the conditional distribution \(p_{Y|X}(y_j \mid x_i) = p_{ij}/p_i\), with entropy \[H[Y \mid x_i] = -\sum_j \frac{p_{ij}}{p_i}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{p_i} .\]

The conditional entropy of \(Y\) given \(X\) is the average of \(H[Y \mid x_i]\) over the outcomes of \(X\): \[H[Y \mid X] = \sum_i p_i\, H[Y \mid x_i] = -\sum_{i,j} p_{ij}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{p_i}.\] It is the average uncertainty remaining in \(Y\) once \(X\) is known. Since each \(H[Y \mid x_i]\) is a genuine entropy, \(H[Y \mid X] \geq 0\).


\[H[X, Y] = H[X] + H[Y \mid X] = H[Y] + H[X \mid Y].\] More generally, \(H(X_1, \ldots, X_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} H(X_i \mid X_1, \ldots, X_{i-1})\).


Proof. Write \(p_{ij} = p_i \cdot (p_{ij}/p_i)\) inside the logarithm: \[-\sum_{i,j} p_{ij}\log p_{ij} = -\sum_{i,j} p_{ij}\log p_i - \sum_{i,j} p_{ij}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{p_i} = -\sum_i p_i \log p_i + H[Y \mid X].\] The second form follows by symmetry; the \(n\)-variable version by induction.

The interpretation is simple: the uncertainty about the pair is the uncertainty about \(X\) plus the uncertainty about \(Y\) once \(X\) is known. This generalises the chain rule for surprisal of Chapter 1 (take expectations of \(I(x, y) = I(x) + I(y \mid x)\)).

The mutual information between \(X\) and \(Y\) is \[I[X : Y] = H[X] + H[Y] - H[X, Y] = H[Y] - H[Y \mid X] = H[X] - H[X \mid Y].\]

Rearranging, \[H[X] = H[X \mid Y] + I[X : Y], \qquad H[Y] = H[Y \mid X] + I[X : Y].\] So \(I[X:Y]\) is the information that \(X\) provides about \(Y\), and vice versa: the information needed to specify \(X\) splits into the part supplied by knowing \(Y\) plus the residual \(H[X \mid Y]\).

\[I[X : Y] = D_{KL}(p_{ij} \,\|\, p_i q_j) = \sum_{i,j} p_{ij} \log \frac{p_{ij}}{p_i q_j} \geq 0,\] with equality iff \(p_{ij} = p_i q_j\), i.e. iff \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.

Independent variables carry no information about each other; and mutual information measures how far the joint distribution is from the independent one. Similarly, the conditional entropy is itself a KL divergence: with \(u_j = 1/N_Y\), \[H[Y \mid X] = -\sum_{ij} p_{ij} \log\frac{p_{ij}}{p_i} = \log N_Y - D_{KL}(p_{ij} \,\|\, p_i\, u_j).\]


Conditioning reduces entropy (on average): \(H[X \mid Y] \leq H[X]\), with equality iff \(X \perp Y\).
Sub-additivity: \(H[X, Y] \leq H[X] + H[Y]\), with equality iff \(X \perp Y\).
Independence bound: \(H(X_1, \ldots, X_n) \leq \sum_i H(X_i)\).

Conditioning on each row, \[H(X \mid Y) = \tfrac14\bigl[H(\tfrac12,\tfrac14,\tfrac18,\tfrac18) + H(\tfrac14,\tfrac12,\tfrac18,\tfrac18) + H(\tfrac14,\tfrac14,\tfrac14,\tfrac14) + H(1,0,0,0)\bigr] = \tfrac14\bigl[\tfrac74 + \tfrac74 + 2 + 0\bigr] = \tfrac{11}{8}.\] Then \(H(X, Y) = H(Y) + H(X \mid Y) = 27/8\), \(H(Y \mid X) = 27/8 - 7/4 = 13/8\), and \(I(X;Y) = 7/4 - 11/8 = 3/8\) bits. Note also that observing \(y = 3\) increases the uncertainty about \(X\) (\(H(X \mid Y = 3) = 2 > H(X)\)); only the average over \(y\) is guaranteed to decrease it.

Let \(X \in \{1^+, 1^-, 2^+, 2^-, 3^+, 3^-\}\), where \(n^\pm\) means “ball \(n\) is odd and heavier/lighter”, all equiprobable: \(H[X] = \log 6 = 1 + \log 3\) bits. Each weighing has three outcomes (\(g, l, e\) = left greater, lighter, equal) and yields at most \(\log 3\) bits, so at least two weighings are needed.

Given \(Y_1\), only two values of \(Y_2\) remain possible, each with probability \(1/2\) (e.g. \(P(Y_2 = e \mid Y_1 = e) = 0\)), hence \(H[Y_2 \mid Y_1] = 1\) and \(H[Y_1, Y_2] = 1 + \log 3 = H[X]\). Since \((Y_1, Y_2)\) determines \(X\), \(I[X : Y_1, Y_2] = H[X]\). Individually \(I[X : Y_1] = I[X : Y_2] = \log 3\), so \[I[X : Y_1, Y_2] = 1 + \log 3 < I[X : Y_1] + I[X : Y_2] = 2\log 3 :\] the two measurements are not independent and their information about \(X\) is partly redundant.


A binary symmetric channel with crossover probability \(f\) and uniform input has \(H(Y) = 1\) and \(H(Y \mid X) = h_2(f)\), so it carries \(I(X; Y) = 1 - h_2(f)\) bits per symbol. At \(f = 0\) (noise-free) it carries the full 1 bit; at \(f = 1/2\) (pure noise) zero. Chapter 4 shows this is the channel’s capacity.

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
3  Information-theoretic measures
section: 3.5 Conditional mutual information and the data-processing inequality
text:
3.5 Conditional mutual information and the data-processing inequality

\(I(X; Y \mid Z) = H(X \mid Z) - H(X \mid Y, Z)\) — the information \(Y\) provides about \(X\) when \(Z\) is already known. It satisfies the chain rule \[I(X; Y, Z) = I(X; Z) + I(X; Y \mid Z).\]

An operational classic: post-processing cannot increase information.

If \(X \to Y \to Z\) is a Markov chain (i.e. \(Z \perp\!\!\!\perp X \mid Y\)), then \[I(X; Y) \geq I(X; Z).\] Equality holds iff \(I(X; Y \mid Z) = 0\), i.e. \(Z\) preserves all the information \(Y\) had about \(X\).


Proof. Expand \(I(X; Y, Z)\) in two ways with the chain rule: \(I(X; Y, Z) = I(X; Y) + I(X; Z \mid Y) = I(X; Z) + I(X; Y \mid Z)\). The Markov property makes \(I(X; Z \mid Y) = 0\), so \(I(X; Y) = I(X; Z) + I(X; Y \mid Z) \geq I(X; Z)\).

In particular, for any function \(g\), \(I(X; g(Y)) \leq I(X; Y)\): no processing of data can create information about the source that was not already there. This is the theoretical basis of “sufficient statistics”: \(T(Y)\) is sufficient for \(X\) exactly when equality holds.

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
text:
3.6 Concavity of mutual information

For fixed conditional \(p(y \mid x)\), \(I(X; Y)\) is a concave function of \(p(x)\). For fixed marginal \(p(x)\), \(I(X; Y)\) is a convex function of \(p(y \mid x)\).

The first statement guarantees that maximising \(I(X;Y)\) over input distributions — the definition of channel capacity in Chapter 4 — is a concave maximisation problem with no spurious local maxima. The second underlies rate-distortion theory.

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
text:
3.7 Exercises

Show that \(H(X, Y) \leq H(X) + H(Y)\) with equality iff \(X, Y\) are independent, using the log-sum inequality directly (not via mutual information).


Solution. Write \(H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y) = \sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log[p(x,y)/(p(x)p(y))]\). By the log-sum inequality with \(a_{xy} = p(x,y)\) and \(b_{xy} = p(x)p(y)\) (both summing to 1), \[\sum_{x,y} p(x,y)\log \tfrac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)} \geq 1 \cdot \log \tfrac{1}{1} = 0.\] So the difference is \(\geq 0\), with equality iff \(p(x,y)/[p(x)p(y)]\) is constant — necessarily equal to 1 — iff independence.


Compute \(I(X; Y)\) for a binary symmetric channel with error probability \(f\) when the input is not uniform, \(P(X = 1) = \pi\).


Solution. \(P(Y = 1) = \pi(1 - f) + (1 - \pi) f \equiv \rho\). \(H(Y) = h_2(\rho)\) and \(H(Y \mid X) = h_2(f)\) regardless of \(\pi\). So \(I(X; Y) = h_2(\pi(1-f) + (1-\pi)f) - h_2(f)\), which is maximal (\(= 1 - h_2(f)\)) at \(\pi = 1/2\) where \(\rho = 1/2\).


Prove the data-processing inequality for the specific case \(Z = g(Y)\) with \(g\) a deterministic function.


Solution. \(X \to Y \to g(Y)\) is automatically a Markov chain, since given \(Y\) the value of \(Z\) is fixed. Then \(I(X;Z) = H(X) - H(X \mid Z) \leq H(X) - H(X \mid Y, Z)\) (conditioning reduces entropy), and \(H(X \mid Y, Z) = H(X \mid Y)\) because \(Z\) is a function of \(Y\). Hence \(I(X;Z) \leq H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = I(X;Y)\).


Let \(p = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac14)\) and \(q = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)\). Compute \(H(p)\), \(H(p, q)\), \(D(p\|q)\) and \(D(q\|p)\), and verify \(H(p) = \log 3 - D(p \| q)\).


Solution. \(H(p) = 1.5\) bits. \(H(p, q) = \log 3 \approx 1.585\). \(D(p\|q) = H(p,q) - H(p) \approx 0.085\) bits, and indeed \(\log 3 - 0.085 = 1.5\) since \(q\) is uniform. \(D(q\|p) = \tfrac13[\log\tfrac{1/3}{1/2} + 2\log\tfrac{1/3}{1/4}] = \tfrac13[-0.585 + 2(0.415)] \approx 0.082\) bits \(\neq D(p\|q)\).

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
text:
3.8 Callouts






The three interpretations of mutual information — as a KL divergence, as a reduction of entropy, and as an inclusion–exclusion of joint and marginal entropies — are all useful. Which one you invoke depends on what you want to prove.









When bounding an information quantity, try (i) Jensen’s inequality applied to \(-\log\); (ii) the log-sum inequality; (iii) the data-processing inequality. These three moves cover most of the proofs in Cover & Thomas.









The KL divergence \(D(p \| q)\) is asymmetric. In machine learning the direction matters: minimising \(D(p_{\text{data}} \| q_\theta)\) is maximum likelihood (“mass-covering”), whereas minimising \(D(q_\theta \| p)\) is what variational inference does (“mode-seeking”, Chapter 10).

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.1 Raw bit content
Information theory was born to solve telecommunication problems. A sender must transmit a message to a distant receiver through a channel — any physical means that carries signals. The sender first converts the message into a form suitable for the channel (encoding); the receiver reconstructs the message from what arrives (decoding). In a digital phone call, for instance, a sound is converted into a string of numbers and back.
A good encoding must satisfy two competing requirements:
Whatever the message (sound, image, text), the encoding converts it into the common currency of communication: a string of binary digits. Shannon’s motivation for defining entropy was to answer the question: what is the minimum number of binary digits per symbol needed to encode a source? This chapter proves that the answer is \(H(X)\), in two different settings:
Both rely on the same idea — exploiting the non-uniformity of \(p\) — and both give \(H(X)\) as the fundamental limit.
Let the message \(x\) be drawn from a finite set \(\mathcal A_X = \{x_1, \ldots, x_N\}\) with probability \(p_X(x)\). A fixed-length binary code is a map \[E : \mathcal A_X \to \mathcal B^K, \qquad \mathcal B^K = \{0, 1\}^K,\] and decoding is \(D = E^{-1}\). For \(E\) to be invertible it must be injective; since \(|\mathcal B^K| = 2^K\), we need \(2^K \geq |\mathcal A_X|\): \[K \geq H_0(X) \equiv \log_2 |\mathcal A_X| .\]
The intuition is correct, but the gain can only be realised for sequences of messages \(x^{(n)} = (x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \mathcal A_X^n\), each drawn independently from the same source. There are then two ways to compress:

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
\(H_0(X) = \log_2|\mathcal A_X|\) is the raw bit content of \(X\). By a simple counting argument, no invertible fixed-length code can use fewer than \(\lceil H_0 \rceil\) binary digits.


Toss a coin with \(P(h) = 0.9\), \(P(t) = 0.1\). Then \(H_0(X) = 1\) but \[H(X) = -0.9\log 0.9 - 0.1\log 0.1 \approx 0.47 \text{ bits}.\] To communicate one toss we must still use one binary digit (\(E: h \mapsto 0,\ t \mapsto 1\)). The information content of the outcome is less than half of the raw bit content, which suggests that one digit per toss is wasteful.



lossy coding: two different sequences may be mapped to the same codeword (or some sequences are discarded), but this happens with small probability;
lossless coding: use variable-length codewords of lengths \(\ell_x\). We cannot have \(\ell_x < H_0\) for all \(x\) (counting argument), but we can make the average \(\langle \ell \rangle = \sum_x p(x)\ell_x\) smaller than \(H_0\) by giving probable \(x\) short codewords.

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.2 Lossy coding
Consider sequences \(X^{(n)} = (X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) of i.i.d. symbols, i.e. a random vector in \(\mathcal A_X^n\), and a fixed-length code \(E^{(n)} : \mathcal A_X^n \to \mathcal B^K\). A perfectly faithful code needs \(K \geq H_0(X^{(n)}) = n H_0(X)\).
We now relax faithfulness. Choose a subset \(S \subset \mathcal A_X^n\) and assign codewords only to sequences in \(S\); sequences in \(\bar S\) are either discarded (\(E(x^{(n)}) = \emptyset\)) or mapped onto codewords already in use. The decoder makes an error exactly when \(x^{(n)} \in \bar S\), so the error probability is \[P_e = P\bigl(D(E(X^{(n)})) \neq X^{(n)}\bigr) = P(X^{(n)} \in \bar S).\]

For \(n = 3\) tosses with \(P(h) = 0.9\):

\(H(X^{(3)}) = 3H(X) \approx 1.41\) bits while \(H_0(X^{(3)}) = 3\). The invertible code \[hhh \mapsto 000,\ hht \mapsto 001,\ hth \mapsto 010,\ thh \mapsto 100,\ htt \mapsto 011,\ tht \mapsto 101,\ tth \mapsto 110,\ ttt \mapsto 111\] uses \(K = 3\) and has \(P_e = 0\). But the outcomes with two or more tails have total probability \(3(0.009) + 0.001 = 0.028\). If we keep only \[S = \{hhh, hht, hth, thh\}, \qquad \tilde E : hhh \mapsto 00,\ hht \mapsto 01,\ hth \mapsto 10,\ thh \mapsto 11,\] and send nothing for the other outcomes, we use only 2 digits at the price of \(P_e = 2.8\%\).

To keep the error below a tolerance \(\delta\), \(S\) must be \(\delta\)-sufficient: \(P(X^{(n)} \in S) \geq 1 - \delta\).

The smallest \(\delta\)-sufficient subset is \[S_\delta(X^{(n)}) = \arg\min_{S} \bigl\{ |S| \;:\; S \subseteq \mathcal A_X^n,\ P(X^{(n)} \in S) \geq 1 - \delta \bigr\}.\] It is obtained by sorting the outcomes by decreasing probability and keeping the first \(k\) of them, stopping as soon as their cumulative probability reaches \(1 - \delta\). The essential bit content is \[H_\delta(X^{(n)}) = \log_2 |S_\delta(X^{(n)})| ,\] the number of binary digits needed if we tolerate error probability \(\delta\).

\(H_\delta\) is a decreasing staircase function of \(\delta\); at \(n = 3\) it depends strongly on \(\delta\).


4.2.1 What happens as \(n\) grows
Plot \(H_\delta(X^{(n)})/n\) against \(\delta\) for increasing \(n\) (MacKay, Fig. 4.9; Allegra, Fig. 3.1). As \(n\) grows the curves become flatter and flatter and collapse onto the horizontal line \(H_\delta/n = H(X)\). This has two consequences:

Achievability. Fix a small tolerance \(\delta_1\). For large \(n\), \(H_{\delta_1}(X^{(n)})/n = H(X) + \beta\) with \(\beta \ll 1\): the smallest \(\delta_1\)-sufficient subset has about \(2^{n(H + \beta)}\) elements, and a code with that many codewords — about \(H(X)\) digits per symbol — has error at most \(\delta_1\). For the \(p = 0.9\) coin with \(n = 1000\), \(\delta_1 = 0.05\) gives \(\beta \approx 0.05\), i.e. about \(0.51\) digits per toss instead of 1.
Converse. Fix a small \(\beta\). For large \(n\), \(H_\delta/n < H(X) - \beta\) only when \(\delta \to 1\): using fewer than \(2^{n(H - \beta)}\) codewords means losing almost every message.

One can code with vanishing error using \(H(X)\) digits per symbol, but not fewer. The mechanism behind this is typicality.

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.3 Typicality and the AEP
In a long sequence each symbol \(x_i\) appears, with high probability, roughly \(m_i \approx n p_i\) times. For the biased coin, sequences of length \(n\) have about \(0.9n\) heads and \(0.1n\) tails. The probability of such a sequence is \[P(x^{(n)}) \approx p_1^{np_1}\, p_2^{np_2} \cdots p_N^{np_N} = 2^{n\sum_i p_i \log p_i} = 2^{-nH(X)},\] so its information content is \(-\log P(x^{(n)}) \approx nH(X)\). These are the typical sequences.

For \(\beta > 0\), the set of \((n, \beta)\)-typical sequences is \[T_{n\beta} = \Bigl\{ x^{(n)} \in \mathcal A_X^n \;:\; \Bigl|\,{-\tfrac{1}{n}\log_2 P(x^{(n)}) - H(X)}\Bigr| < \beta \Bigr\}.\] Equivalently, \(2^{-n(H + \beta)} < P(x^{(n)}) < 2^{-n(H - \beta)}\).


For \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) i.i.d. \(\sim p\):

\(-\tfrac{1}{n}\log_2 P(X_1, \ldots, X_n) \to H(X)\) in probability as \(n \to \infty\).
\(P(X^{(n)} \in T_{n\beta}) \to 1\) as \(n \to \infty\), for any \(\beta > 0\).
\(|T_{n\beta}| < 2^{n(H + \beta)}\), and \(|T_{n\beta}| > (1 - \epsilon)2^{n(H - \beta)}\) for \(n\) large enough.


So almost all probability concentrates on roughly \(2^{nH}\) sequences, which are (to exponential accuracy) equiprobable — hence equipartition. Since there are \(2^{nH_0} = |\mathcal A_X|^n\) sequences in total, the typical set is an exponentially small fraction \(2^{-n(H_0 - H)}\) of all sequences, yet it carries almost all the probability.

Take \(n = 100\), \(p(h) = 0.9\). Typical sequences have about 10 tails; their number is \(\binom{100}{10} \approx 1.7 \times 10^{13} \approx 2^{44}\), close to \(2^{nH} = 2^{46.9}\) (the agreement improves with \(n\)). There are \(2^{100}\) sequences in total. Each typical sequence has probability \(\approx 2^{-47}\).
Note that the single most probable sequence, \(hh\cdots h\), with \(P = 0.9^{100} \approx 2.7 \times 10^{-5}\), is not typical: \(-\tfrac1n \log P = 0.152 \ll H = 0.469\). It is very likely compared to any single typical sequence, but there is only one of it, while typical sequences are astronomically many. The histogram of the number of tails \(m\) concentrates around \(m = 10\) with width \(\sqrt{np(1-p)} = 3\); relative to \(n\), the width shrinks as \(1/\sqrt n\).


Remark (Physical meaning). The AEP is the information-theoretic analogue of the equivalence of ensembles in statistical mechanics: a system with fixed temperature (canonical) has, with overwhelming probability, an energy close to its mean, so it behaves like a microcanonical ensemble of \(\approx e^{S}\) equiprobable microstates. Here \(nH\) plays the role of the entropy \(S\).

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.4 Shannon’s source coding theorem

4.4.1 Intuitive argument

We have sequences \(X^{(n)}\) of i.i.d. messages from the same source.
We want a lossy fixed-length code with error at most \(\delta\): we must identify \(S_\delta(X^{(n)})\); codewords have length \(H_\delta = \log|S_\delta|\).
For large \(n\), a random sequence is almost surely typical, and each typical sequence has \(P \approx 2^{-nH}\). Since their probabilities add up to nearly 1, there are \(\approx 2^{nH}\) of them.
Hence a \(\delta\)-sufficient subset made of typical sequences has size \(\approx 2^{nH}\), and the smallest one can be no larger: codewords of length \(\approx nH\) suffice.
Codewords cannot be much shorter. With length \(n(H - \Delta)\) there are at most \(2^{n(H - \Delta)}\) codewords; since nearly all the probability sits on typical sequences of probability \(\approx 2^{-nH}\) each, the covered probability is at most \(2^{n(H - \Delta)} 2^{-nH} = 2^{-n\Delta} \to 0\). The error tends to 1.



4.4.2 Rigorous statement and proof

Let \(X\) have entropy \(H = H(X)\). For every \(\delta \in (0, 1)\) and every \(\beta > 0\) there exists \(n_0\) such that for all \(n > n_0\), \[\Bigl|\frac{H_\delta(X^{(n)})}{n} - H\Bigr| < \beta .\]

In words: for long enough sequences, lossy compression with arbitrarily small error is possible with \(n(H + \beta)\) bits, i.e. \(2^{n(H + \beta)}\) codewords; compression with \(n(H - \beta)\) bits is impossible unless we accept an error probability arbitrarily close to 1. Consequently:

the information in \(n\) i.i.d. realisations of \(X\) can be transmitted with \(\approx H(X)\) binary digits per realisation, with asymptotically vanishing loss;
it cannot be compressed further.

The proof has three parts.
Part I — typical sequences are typical. \[P(X^{(n)} \in T_{n\beta}) \geq 1 - \frac{\sigma^2}{n\beta^2}, \qquad \sigma^2 = \operatorname{Var}[-\log p(X_i)] .\]

Proof. Recall Chebyshev’s inequality \(P((Z - \mathbb E Z)^2 \geq \alpha) \leq \operatorname{Var}(Z)/\alpha\). For the mean \(M_n = \tfrac1n \sum_i Z_i\) of i.i.d. variables, \(\mathbb E M_n = \mathbb E Z\) and \(\operatorname{Var} M_n = \operatorname{Var}Z/n\), so \[P\bigl((M_n - \mathbb E Z)^2 < \alpha\bigr) \geq 1 - \frac{\operatorname{Var} Z}{n\alpha}.\] Let \(I_i = -\log p(X_i)\), the information content of the \(i\)-th symbol: these are i.i.d. with mean \(H\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). Because the symbols are independent, \[\bar I^{(n)} \equiv -\tfrac1n\log P(X^{(n)}) = -\tfrac1n\sum_i \log p(X_i) = \tfrac1n\sum_i I_i ,\] a mean of i.i.d. variables. Since \(X^{(n)} \in T_{n\beta} \iff (\bar I^{(n)} - H)^2 < \beta^2\), Chebyshev with \(\alpha = \beta^2\) gives the claim. (This is the weak law of large numbers for \(\bar I^{(n)}\), i.e. part 1 of the AEP.)

Part II — achievability: for all \(\delta, \beta\) there is \(n_1\) such that \(H_\delta(X^{(n)}) < n(H + \beta)\) for all \(n > n_1\).

Proof. Take \(n_1 > \sigma^2/(\beta^2\delta)\). By Part I, for \(n > n_1\), \(P(X^{(n)} \in T_{n\beta}) > 1 - \delta\): the typical set is \(\delta\)-sufficient, so \(|S_\delta| \leq |T_{n\beta}|\). Every typical sequence has \(P(x^{(n)}) > 2^{-n(H + \beta)}\), hence \[1 \geq P(T_{n\beta}) > |T_{n\beta}|\,2^{-n(H + \beta)} \quad\Rightarrow\quad |T_{n\beta}| < 2^{n(H + \beta)} .\] Therefore \(H_\delta = \log|S_\delta| \leq \log|T_{n\beta}| < n(H + \beta)\).

Part III — converse: for all \(\delta, \beta\) there is \(n_2\) such that \(H_\delta(X^{(n)}) > n(H - \beta)\) for all \(n > n_2\).

Proof. Suppose, for contradiction, that some set \(S\) with \(|S| \leq 2^{n(H - \beta)}\) is \(\delta\)-sufficient. Split it into its typical and atypical parts with respect to the narrower set \(T_{n,\beta/2}\): \[P(X^{(n)} \in S) = P(X^{(n)} \in S \cap T_{n,\beta/2}) + P(X^{(n)} \in S \cap \bar T_{n,\beta/2}).\] Every sequence in \(T_{n,\beta/2}\) has \(P(x^{(n)}) < 2^{-n(H - \beta/2)}\), so the first term is at most \[|S|\,2^{-n(H - \beta/2)} \leq 2^{n(H - \beta)}\,2^{-n(H - \beta/2)} = 2^{-n\beta/2}.\] The second term is at most \(P(X^{(n)} \notin T_{n,\beta/2}) \leq 4\sigma^2/(n\beta^2)\) by Part I. Hence \[P(X^{(n)} \in S) \leq 2^{-n\beta/2} + \frac{4\sigma^2}{n\beta^2},\] which decreases to zero; for \(n\) large enough it is below \(1 - \delta\), contradicting \(\delta\)-sufficiency. So \(|S_\delta| > 2^{n(H - \beta)}\).

Combining Parts II and III with \(n_0 = \max(n_1, n_2)\) proves the theorem. \(\blacksquare\)

Remark (How large must \(n\) be?). Part II requires \(n \gtrsim \sigma^2/(\beta^2\delta)\): lossy fixed-length coding is efficient only for very long blocks. For the \(p = 0.9\) coin, \(\sigma^2 = p(1-p)\bigl(\log\tfrac{p}{1-p}\bigr)^2 = 0.09 \times (\log_2 9)^2 \approx 0.90\), so \(\beta = 0.1\) and \(\delta = 0.01\) require \(n \approx 10^4\). (Chebyshev is pessimistic; sharper Chernoff bounds give exponential convergence, but the message stands.) This motivates lossless variable-length codes, which work symbol by symbol.


Remark (Rate–distortion theory). The lossy coding above is “lossy” only in that a vanishing fraction of messages is lost. In engineering, “lossy compression” (JPEG, MP3) usually means something different: every message is reconstructed approximately, with an average distortion \(D\). The optimal trade-off is the rate–distortion function \(R(D) = \min_{p(\hat x | x) : \mathbb E d(X, \hat X) \leq D} I(X; \hat X)\) (Cover & Thomas, Ch. 10). For a Gaussian source with variance \(\sigma^2\) and squared error, \(R(D) = \tfrac12\log_2(\sigma^2/D)\) for \(D \leq \sigma^2\). We will not develop this theory further.

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.5 Lossless coding: symbol codes
A symbol code maps each symbol to a binary string of variable length: \[E : \mathcal A_X \to \mathcal B^+, \qquad \mathcal B^+ = \mathcal B \cup \mathcal B^2 \cup \mathcal B^3 \cup \cdots,\] \(x_i \mapsto y_i \in \mathcal B^{\ell_i}\); \(y_i\) is the codeword and \(\ell_i\) the codeword length. It extends to sequences \(x^+ \in \mathcal A_X^+ = \mathcal A_X \cup \mathcal A_X^2 \cup \cdots\) by concatenation, \[E^+(x_{i_1}x_{i_2}\cdots x_{i_n}) = E(x_{i_1})E(x_{i_2})\cdots E(x_{i_n}).\]

For the coin, \(E : h \mapsto 0,\ t \mapsto 101\) (lengths 1 and 3) gives \(E^+(hhh) = 000\), \(E^+(ht) = 0101\), etc.

A good symbol code should be

uniquely decodable (invertible on sequences),
easy to decode,
short on average: the expected length \(L(E, X) = \sum_i p_i \ell_i\) should be minimal.


4.5.1 Unique decodability

\(E\) is uniquely decodable if \(E^+\) is injective: \(x^+ \neq x'^+ \Rightarrow E^+(x^+) \neq E^+(x'^+)\).

Distinct codewords are necessary but not sufficient.

\(h \mapsto 0,\ t \mapsto 101\) is uniquely decodable: \(0101101000101\) decodes only as \(htthhht\) (every \(1\) starts a \(101\)). But for \(\mathcal A = \{a, b, c, d\}\) with \[a \mapsto 0,\ b \mapsto 1,\ c \mapsto 00,\ d \mapsto 11,\] the string \(0011011\) can be read as \(cdad\), \(aadad\), \(aabbad\) or \(aabbabb\). All codewords are distinct, yet the code is not uniquely decodable.



4.5.2 Prefix codes
“Easy to decode” means that each codeword can be recognised as soon as its last bit arrives, without looking ahead. This requires that no codeword be a prefix of another (\(c\) is a prefix of \(d\) if \(d = ct\) for some string \(t\); e.g. \(1\) and \(10\) are prefixes of \(101\)).

A code is a prefix code (also instantaneous or self-punctuating) if no codeword is a prefix of another codeword.


\(a \mapsto 1,\ b \mapsto 101\) is uniquely decodable (each \(0\) signals a \(b\)). But on receiving \(110111\) (\(= abaa\)), after the first \(1\) we cannot yet decide between \(a\) and the beginning of \(b\); we must wait for the third digit. The culprit is that \(1\) is a prefix of \(101\). The code \(a \mapsto 0,\ b \mapsto 101\) is a prefix code and decodes instantaneously.


Every prefix code is uniquely decodable. In particular, fixed-length codes with distinct codewords are uniquely decodable.


Proof. Suppose \(E^+(x_1 \cdots x_k) = E^+(y_1 \cdots y_l)\) with \(x \neq y\). Strip the longest common initial run of symbols (\(x_i = y_i\) for \(i \leq m\)); the remaining sequences still have equal encodings, and now \(x_{m+1} \neq y_{m+1}\) (the remainders cannot both be empty since \(x \neq y\)). Both encoded strings begin with \(E(x_{m+1})\) and \(E(y_{m+1})\) respectively. If these have equal length they are equal, so two symbols share a codeword; if not, the shorter is a prefix of the longer. Either way the code is not a prefix code.

Prefix codes are binary trees. Take a probability tree in which every branching has exactly two children, \(E = E_0 \cup E_1\), and label the edges \(0\) and \(1\). Reading the labels from the root to a leaf gives a binary string; assigning these strings to the leaves gives a prefix code, because a prefix of a codeword corresponds to an internal node, which is not a leaf. Conversely every prefix code defines such a tree.

\(X \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}\) with \(p = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18)\). The tree “is it 0? / is it 1? / is it 2?” gives the prefix code \[0 \mapsto 0, \quad 1 \mapsto 10, \quad 2 \mapsto 110, \quad 3 \mapsto 111,\] with \(L = \tfrac12 \cdot 1 + \tfrac14 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot \tfrac18 \cdot 3 = 1.75\) bits \(= H(X)\). Here \(L = H\) because \(\ell_i = -\log p_i\) exactly; this is possible only when all \(p_i\) are powers of \(1/2\).


For \(X^{(3)}\) (three tosses, \(p(h) = 0.9\)), let \(M\) be the number of tails: \(p_M = (0.729, 0.243, 0.027, 0.001)\). Ask “\(M = 0\)?”, then “\(M = 1\)?”, then “\(M = 2\)?”. If \(M = 1\) or \(2\), two more binary questions identify which of the three arrangements occurred. Reading edge labels gives \[hhh \mapsto 0,\ hht \mapsto 100,\ thh \mapsto 1010,\ hth \mapsto 1011,\ htt \mapsto 1100,\ tht \mapsto 11010,\ tth \mapsto 11011,\ ttt \mapsto 111,\] with expected length \[L = 0.729 \cdot 1 + 0.081 \cdot 3 + 2(0.081) \cdot 4 + 0.009 \cdot 4 + 2(0.009) \cdot 5 + 0.001 \cdot 3 = 1.749 \text{ bits},\] much better than the 3 bits of the fixed-length code and not far from \(H(X^{(3)}) = 1.41\).



4.5.3 Kraft’s inequality
Short average length comes from giving probable outcomes short codewords. We cannot make all codewords short: unique decodability constrains the lengths.

If a binary code is uniquely decodable, its codeword lengths satisfy \[\sum_i 2^{-\ell_i} \leq 1 .\] Conversely, for any lengths satisfying this inequality there exists a prefix code with those lengths.

A code with \(\sum_i 2^{-\ell_i} = 1\) is called complete. Prefix codes read off a full binary tree are complete: replace every edge probability by \(1/2\); the leaf at depth \(\ell_i\) then gets probability \(q_i = 2^{-\ell_i}\), and these probabilities must sum to one. For the three-toss tree above, \(\sum 2^{-\ell_i} = 2^{-1} + 2\cdot 2^{-3} + 3 \cdot 2^{-4} + 2 \cdot 2^{-5} = 2^{-5}(16 + 8 + 6 + 2) = 1\).

Proof (Proof of necessity (McMillan)). Let \(S = \sum_i 2^{-\ell_i}\). Then \[S^n = \sum_{i_1, \ldots, i_n} 2^{-(\ell_{i_1} + \cdots + \ell_{i_n})},\] where \(\ell_{i_1} + \cdots + \ell_{i_n}\) is the length of the encoding of the string \(x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_n}\). With \(\ell_{\min}, \ell_{\max}\) the shortest and longest codeword lengths, group the terms by total length \(\ell\): \[S^n = \sum_{\ell = n\ell_{\min}}^{n\ell_{\max}} 2^{-\ell} |A_\ell|,\] where \(A_\ell\) is the set of length-\(n\) source strings encoded into \(\ell\) bits. Unique decodability forces \(|A_\ell| \leq 2^\ell\) (there are only \(2^\ell\) binary strings of length \(\ell\)). Hence \[S^n \leq \sum_{\ell = n\ell_{\min}}^{n\ell_{\max}} 1 \leq n\ell_{\max}.\] If \(S > 1\), the left side grows exponentially in \(n\) while the right side grows linearly — impossible for large \(n\). So \(S \leq 1\).


Proof (Proof of sufficiency). Let \(A_\ell\) now denote the number of required codewords of length \(\ell\); the inequality reads \(\sum_\ell A_\ell 2^{-\ell} \leq 1\). Assign codewords in order of increasing length, keeping the prefix property at every stage. Suppose the codewords of length up to \(\ell\) have been chosen. Each codeword of length \(\ell' \leq \ell\) is a prefix of \(2^{\ell + 1 - \ell'}\) strings of length \(\ell + 1\), which are forbidden. The number of available strings of length \(\ell + 1\) is therefore \[2^{\ell+1} - \sum_{\ell' \leq \ell} A_{\ell'}\,2^{\ell+1-\ell'},\] and we can pick \(A_{\ell+1}\) of them iff \(\sum_{\ell' \leq \ell + 1} A_{\ell'}\,2^{-\ell'} \leq 1\) — which follows from Kraft’s inequality. Starting from the shortest length (no constraints) and inducting gives a prefix code.


Remark. Kraft’s inequality is necessary for unique decodability, not sufficient: mapping every symbol to the single codeword \(0\) (with \(|\mathcal A| = 2\), \(2^{-1} + 2^{-1} = 1\)) satisfies it but is obviously not decodable. The sufficiency statement says that some prefix code with those lengths exists. A key consequence: nothing is gained by using uniquely decodable codes that are not prefix codes — prefix codes achieve every set of lengths that any uniquely decodable code can.

title: 4  Source coding: compression
section: 4.6 Source coding theorem for symbol codes
text:
4.6 Source coding theorem for symbol codes

For any uniquely decodable code, \[L(E, X) \geq H(X),\] with equality iff \(\ell_i = -\log_2 p_i\) for all \(i\). Moreover there exists a prefix code with \[H(X) \leq L(E, X) < H(X) + 1 .\]


Proof. Lower bound. Define the “implicit probabilities” of the code \(q_i = 2^{-\ell_i}/z\), with \(z = \sum_j 2^{-\ell_j} \leq 1\) by Kraft. Then \[D_{KL}(p \| q) = \sum_i p_i \log\frac{p_i}{q_i} = -H(X) + \sum_i p_i \ell_i + \log z ,\] so \[L(E, X) = H(X) + D_{KL}(p \| q) - \log z \geq H(X) + D_{KL}(p\|q) \geq H(X).\] Equality requires (1) \(z = 1\), a complete code, and (2) \(p = q\), i.e. \(p_i = 2^{-\ell_i}\).
Upper bound. Condition (2) can be met exactly only if all \(p_i\) are negative powers of 2, but the identity suggests choosing \(\ell_i \approx -\log p_i\). Take the Shannon code lengths \(\ell_i = \lceil -\log_2 p_i \rceil\). They satisfy Kraft, \[\sum_i 2^{-\lceil -\log p_i\rceil} \leq \sum_i 2^{\log p_i} = \sum_i p_i = 1,\] so a prefix code with these lengths exists, and \[L = \sum_i p_i \lceil -\log p_i \rceil < \sum_i p_i(-\log p_i + 1) = H(X) + 1 .\]

The identity \(L = H + D(p\|q) - \log z\) gives a precise meaning to the KL divergence of Chapter 2: a complete code designed for the distribution \(q\) but used on a source \(p\) wastes exactly \(D(p\|q)\) bits per symbol.

\(p = (0.4, 0.35, 0.2, 0.05)\): \(-\log p = (1.32, 1.51, 2.32, 4.32)\), so Shannon lengths are \((2, 2, 3, 5)\) and \(L = 0.8 + 0.7 + 0.6 + 0.25 = 2.35\) bits, against \(H = 1.74\) bits. The bound \(L < H + 1\) holds, but the code is far from optimal — Huffman (below) does better.


Applying the theorem to blocks \(X^{(n)}\) of \(n\) i.i.d. symbols, whose entropy is \(nH\), gives a code with \(nH \leq L_n < nH + 1\), i.e. a rate per symbol \[H(X) \leq \frac{L_n}{n} < H(X) + \frac1n .\] The overhead of at most one bit is spread over \(n\) symbols and becomes negligible.

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.7 Huffman codes
Shannon codes satisfy the bounds but are not optimal. Huffman’s algorithm constructs an optimal prefix code by building the binary tree from the leaves up.

Given probabilities \(p_1, \ldots, p_N\):

Create a node for each outcome.
Take the two least probable parentless nodes and create a parent node for them, with probability equal to their sum. Label the two edges 0 and 1.
Repeat step 2 until a single root remains. The codeword of each leaf is the string of labels from the root to the leaf.


By construction the two least probable outcomes are siblings and get codewords of equal length.

\(p = (0.4, 0.35, 0.2, 0.05)\), \(H \approx 1.74\) bits. Merges: \(0.05 + 0.2 = 0.25\); \(0.25 + 0.35 = 0.60\); \(0.60 + 0.4 = 1\). Codewords \(0, 10, 110, 111\) with lengths \((1, 2, 3, 3)\) and \(L = 0.4 + 0.7 + 0.6 + 0.15 = 1.85\) bits — \(0.5\) bits better than the Shannon code above, and only \(0.11\) above \(H\).


For \(X^{(3)}\) with \(p(h) = 0.9\), Huffman’s algorithm gives \[hhh \mapsto 0,\ hht \mapsto 100,\ hth \mapsto 101,\ thh \mapsto 110,\ htt \mapsto 11110,\ tht \mapsto 11100,\ tth \mapsto 11101,\ ttt \mapsto 11111,\] with \[L = 0.729 \cdot 1 + 3(0.081)\cdot 3 + 3(0.009)\cdot 5 + 0.001 \cdot 5 = 1.598 \text{ bits},\] better than the tree code above (1.749) and closer to \(H(X^{(3)}) = 1.41\). Per toss: \(0.53\) bits, versus \(H(X) = 0.47\).


No uniquely decodable code for the same source has smaller expected length than the Huffman code. In particular \(H(X) \leq L^{Huff} < H(X) + 1\).


Proof. Order \(p_1 \leq p_2 \leq \cdots \leq p_N\). By the Kraft–McMillan theorem we may restrict to prefix codes, and an optimal prefix code may be taken complete (otherwise some codeword could be shortened).
Step 1: in some optimal code, the two least probable symbols are siblings of maximal length. In a complete prefix code the deepest leaves come in sibling pairs. If \(\ell_1\) were not maximal, some \(x_j\) with \(p_j \geq p_1\) would sit deeper; swapping \(x_1\) and \(x_j\) changes \(L\) by \((\ell_1 - \ell_j)(p_j - p_1) \leq 0\), so it does not hurt. Likewise we can place \(x_2\) in the sibling slot of \(x_1\) without increasing \(L\). (If \(\ell_{1} > \ell_2\) in an optimal code and some \(x_3\) with \(p_3 > p_2\) had length \(\ell_1\), swapping \(x_2\) and \(x_3\) would change \(L\) by \((\ell_1 - \ell_2)(p_2 - p_3) < 0\), contradicting optimality.)
Step 2: induction on \(N\). For \(N = 2\) any code uses two codewords of length 1, which is optimal. Assume Huffman is optimal for \(N - 1\) symbols. Take an optimal tree for \((p_1, \ldots, p_N)\) in which \(x_1, x_2\) are siblings and merge them: this gives a tree for \((p_1 + p_2, p_3, \ldots, p_N)\), with \[L_{\text{opt}}(p_1, \ldots, p_N) = L(p_1 + p_2, p_3, \ldots, p_N) + p_1 + p_2,\] since the merged codeword is one bit shorter for both. The merged tree must be optimal for the reduced source (otherwise unmerging a better one would beat the optimum). The Huffman tree for \((p_1, \ldots, p_N)\) merges \(x_1, x_2\) first and then is the Huffman tree for the reduced source, which is optimal by the induction hypothesis. So both satisfy the same relation with the same reduced optimal length, and \(L^{Huff}(p_1, \ldots, p_N) = L_{\text{opt}}(p_1, \ldots, p_N)\).

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.8 Beyond symbol codes
Symbol codes waste up to one bit per symbol, which is a lot when \(H(X) \ll 1\) (e.g. the \(p = 0.99\) coin, \(H = 0.08\) bits, still needs one bit per symbol). Two remedies are used in practice:

Arithmetic coding encodes a whole sequence as a sub-interval of \([0, 1)\) of width \(P(x^{(n)})\), which needs about \(-\log P(x^{(n)})\) bits: the overhead is \(O(1)\) bits per message rather than per symbol, and it adapts naturally to probabilities that change from symbol to symbol (e.g. from a predictive model).
Universal codes (Lempel–Ziv, context-tree weighting) do not need to know \(p\) at all: they learn the statistics from the data as they go.


Lempel–Ziv coding, applied to a stationary ergodic source of entropy rate \(H_\infty\), achieves an asymptotic compression rate of \(H_\infty\) bits per symbol without any advance knowledge of the source.


Remark. gzip, bzip2 and xz are variations on Lempel–Ziv and Huffman/arithmetic coding. The theoretical guarantee that they reach the entropy limit is a consequence of the AEP for ergodic sequences (Chapter 6).

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.9 Exercises

Construct a Huffman code for a source with probabilities \((1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/16)\) and verify it achieves \(H(X)\).


Solution. \(H(X) = 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.375 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 1.875\) bits. Huffman merges \(1/16 + 1/16 = 1/8\), then \(1/8 + 1/8 = 1/4\), then \(1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2\), then \(1/2 + 1/2\). Codewords \(0, 10, 110, 1110, 1111\), lengths \((1, 2, 3, 4, 4)\), \(L = 1/2 + 1/2 + 3/8 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 1.875\) bits. Exactly \(H\) — because all probabilities are dyadic.


Show that \(\sum_i 2^{-\ell_i} = 1\) for a complete prefix code (one where every internal node of the tree has two children).


Solution. Replace every edge probability by \(1/2\). A leaf at depth \(\ell_i\) then has probability \(2^{-\ell_i}\); since the leaves of a full binary tree partition the root event, these probabilities sum to 1. A tree with a missing child has a “hole” of probability \(2^{-d}\) and gives strict inequality.


Is the code \(\{0, 01, 011, 0111\}\) uniquely decodable? Is it a prefix code? Does it satisfy Kraft?


Solution. Not a prefix code (\(0\) is a prefix of all others). It is uniquely decodable: every codeword starts with \(0\), so each \(0\) marks the start of a new codeword and the number of following \(1\)s identifies it — but decoding needs one bit of lookahead. Kraft: \(1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/16 = 15/16 \leq 1\). By Kraft–McMillan, the prefix code \(\{0, 10, 110, 1110\}\) (the reversed codewords) has the same lengths.


For the \(p = 0.9\) coin, compare the expected length per toss of the Huffman code on blocks of \(n = 1, 2, 3\) tosses with \(H(X) = 0.469\).


Solution. \(n = 1\): 1 bit/toss. \(n = 2\): probabilities \((0.81, 0.09, 0.09, 0.01)\); Huffman lengths \((1, 2, 3, 3)\), \(L_2 = 0.81 + 0.18 + 0.27 + 0.03 = 1.29\), i.e. \(0.645\) bits/toss. \(n = 3\): \(L_3 = 1.598\), i.e. \(0.533\) bits/toss. The rate approaches \(H\) as \(n\) grows, consistent with \(L_n/n < H + 1/n\).


A code designed for \(q = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18)\) (lengths \(1, 2, 3, 3\)) is used on a uniform source \(p = (\tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14)\). Compute the expected length and check it equals \(H(p) + D(p\|q)\).


Solution. \(L = \tfrac14(1 + 2 + 3 + 3) = 2.25\) bits. \(H(p) = 2\) and \(D(p\|q) = \tfrac14[\log\tfrac{1/4}{1/2} + \log 1 + 2\log\tfrac{1/4}{1/8}] = \tfrac14[-1 + 0 + 2] = 0.25\). Indeed \(2 + 0.25 = 2.25\) (the code is complete, \(z = 1\)).

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.10 Callouts






The fixed-length source-coding theorem is asymptotic: it needs \(n \sim \sigma^2/(\beta^2\delta)\). Symbol codes work with \(n = 1\) but can waste up to one bit per symbol; coding blocks of \(n\) symbols reduces this to \(1/n\).









Useful mental picture: an optimal code assigns \(\ell_i \approx -\log_2 p_i\), i.e. codeword length = surprisal. Conversely, every complete prefix code implicitly defines a probability model \(q_i = 2^{-\ell_i}\).









The most probable sequence is not typical. Typicality is about the information content \(-\tfrac1n\log P\), not about the probability being large.









Universal codes give the asymptotic compression rate. On short inputs they often expand the data due to header overhead. Don’t benchmark compressors on toy examples.
