with \(R_1 = 1 - 0.3 - 0.2 = 0.5\), \(R_2 = 1 - \tfrac12 - \tfrac13 = \tfrac16\), \(R_3 = 1 - \tfrac12 - \tfrac12 = 0\). Check stationarity row by row: \(0.5\cdot0.5 + 0.5\cdot0.3 + 0.5\cdot0.2 = 0.5\) \(\checkmark\); \(0.3\cdot0.5 + \tfrac16\cdot0.3 + 0.5\cdot 0.2 = 0.15 + 0.05 + 0.1 = 0.3\) \(\checkmark\); \(0.2\cdot0.5 + \tfrac13\cdot 0.3 + 0 = 0.2\) \(\checkmark\). Detailed balance, e.g. \(P_{21}\pi_1 = 0.3 \cdot 0.5 = 0.15 = P_{12}\pi_2 = 0.5\cdot 0.3\) \(\checkmark\).



8.5.2 Continuous state space
The same construction works in \(\mathbb R^d\). With a symmetric proposal density \(T(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x) = T(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf x')\) and acceptance \[A(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x) = \min\Bigl\{1, \frac{\pi(\mathbf x')}{\pi(\mathbf x)}\Bigr\},\] the rejection probability is \(R(\mathbf x) = \int d\mathbf x'\,T(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x)\bigl(1 - A(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x)\bigr)\) and the transition kernel is \[P(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x) = A(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x)\,T(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x) + \delta(\mathbf x' - \mathbf x)\,R(\mathbf x).\] Detailed balance \(P(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x)\pi(\mathbf x) = P(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf x')\pi(\mathbf x')\) follows exactly as in the discrete case.

From the current state \(\mathbf x\):

propose \(\mathbf x' \sim T(\cdot \mid \mathbf x)\), e.g. \(\mathbf x' = \mathbf x + \sigma\boldsymbol\xi\), \(\boldsymbol\xi \sim \mathcal N(0, I)\);
draw \(u \sim \mathcal U(0,1)\); if \(u < \pi(\mathbf x')/\pi(\mathbf x)\), move to \(\mathbf x'\); otherwise stay at \(\mathbf x\) (and record \(\mathbf x\) again as the next sample).



If \(\pi(\mathbf x) = f(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y) = f(\mathbf x, \mathbf y)/f(\mathbf y)\), then \[A(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x) = \min\Bigl\{1, \frac{f(\mathbf x', \mathbf y)}{f(\mathbf x, \mathbf y)}\Bigr\} = \min\Bigl\{1, \frac{f(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf x')f(\mathbf x')}{f(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf x)f(\mathbf x)}\Bigr\}:\] only the unnormalised posterior (likelihood × prior) is needed. The intractable marginal likelihood \(f(\mathbf y)\) cancels.

This is why Metropolis revolutionised Bayesian statistics (and, earlier, statistical physics, where the unknown constant is the partition function \(Z\)).


8.5.3 Metropolis–Hastings
With a non-symmetric proposal \(q(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x)\), detailed balance is restored by the Hastings correction: \[A(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x) = \min\Bigl\{1, \frac{\pi(\mathbf x')\,q(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf x')}{\pi(\mathbf x)\,q(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x)}\Bigr\}.\] The ratio of proposal densities compensates for the bias of proposing some moves more often than their reverses. Gibbs sampling (Chapter 8) and HMC (Chapter 11) are both special cases.

We observe \(k = 7\) heads in \(n = 10\) tosses of a coin with unknown bias \(\theta\), and use a uniform prior. The unnormalised posterior is \(\pi(\theta) \propto \theta^7(1-\theta)^3\) on \([0,1]\) (the exact answer is \(\text{Beta}(8, 4)\), with mean \(8/12 = 0.667\)). Metropolis with \(\theta' = \theta + 0.1\,\xi\): accept with probability \(\min\{1, \pi(\theta')/\pi(\theta)\}\), with \(\pi(\theta') = 0\) (always reject) if \(\theta' \notin [0,1]\). Note that rejected proposals outside the support must still be counted as a repeated sample of \(\theta\). A run of \(10^5\) steps reproduces the Beta mean and variance (\(8\cdot4/(12^2\cdot 13) \approx 0.0171\)) to about two decimal places.


Target \(\pi(x) \propto e^{-x^2/2}\), proposal \(x' = x + \sigma_p\xi\), acceptance \(\min\{1, e^{(x^2 - x'^2)/2}\}\). Tiny \(\sigma_p\): almost every move is accepted but the chain crawls (random walk with tiny steps). Huge \(\sigma_p\): proposals land in the tails and are almost all rejected; the chain sits still. The optimum is \(\sigma_p \approx 2.4\), with acceptance rate \(\approx 44\%\).
crumbs: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
text:
8.6 Convergence and correlation
The Metropolis chain is guaranteed to converge to \(\pi\). Two practical issues remain:

Convergence time: how long is the transient before equilibrium?
Autocorrelation: the samples are identically distributed but not independent, so they carry less information than an i.i.d. sample of the same size.

Both are controlled by the spectrum of the transition matrix. We work with a finite state space; the continuous case is analogous, though the operator theory is more delicate.

8.6.1 Spectrum of a reversible chain
\(\boldsymbol\pi\) is an eigenvector of \(P\) with eigenvalue 1, but \(P\) is not symmetric, so its spectrum is not obviously real. Detailed balance fixes this. Let \(\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{\pi_1}, \ldots, \sqrt{\pi_K})\) and \[V = \Lambda^{-1}P\Lambda, \qquad V_{ij} = P_{ij}\sqrt{\pi_j/\pi_i}.\] By detailed balance, \(V_{ij} = P_{ij}\pi_j/\sqrt{\pi_i\pi_j} = P_{ji}\pi_i/\sqrt{\pi_i\pi_j} = V_{ji}\): \(V\) is symmetric. Hence \(V = WDW^\top\) with \(D = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_K)\) real and \(W\) orthogonal (columns \(\mathbf w_k\)). Since \(P = \Lambda V\Lambda^{-1}\) is similar to \(V\), it has the same real eigenvalues, with

right eigenvectors \(\boldsymbol\phi_k = \Lambda\mathbf w_k\): \(P\boldsymbol\phi_k = \Lambda V\mathbf w_k = \lambda_k\boldsymbol\phi_k\);
left eigenvectors \(\boldsymbol\psi_k = \Lambda^{-1}\mathbf w_k\): \(\boldsymbol\psi_k^\top P = \mathbf w_k^\top V\Lambda^{-1} = \lambda_k\boldsymbol\psi_k^\top\);
biorthonormality \(\boldsymbol\psi_k^\top\boldsymbol\phi_l = \mathbf w_k^\top\mathbf w_l = \delta_{kl}\).

The powers of \(P\) have the spectral decomposition \[P^n = \Lambda V^n\Lambda^{-1} = \sum_k \lambda_k^n\,\boldsymbol\phi_k\boldsymbol\psi_k^\top .\]

All eigenvalues satisfy \(|\lambda_k| \leq 1\). The eigenvalue \(1\) has left eigenvector \(\mathbf 1 = (1, \ldots, 1)\) and right eigenvector \(\boldsymbol\pi\); for an ergodic chain it is simple and all others satisfy \(|\lambda_k| < 1\).


Proof. From \(P^n\boldsymbol\phi_k = \lambda_k^n\boldsymbol\phi_k\), for each component \(j\): \(|\lambda_k|^n|(\boldsymbol\phi_k)_j| \leq \sum_l (P^n)_{jl}|(\boldsymbol\phi_k)_l| \leq \gamma\sum_l (P^n)_{jl}\), with \(\gamma = \max_l|(\boldsymbol\phi_k)_l|\). Choosing \(j\) where \(|(\boldsymbol\phi_k)_j| = \gamma\) gives \(|\lambda_k|^n \leq \sum_l (P^n)_{jl} \leq K\) (entries of \(P^n\) are probabilities). A bound uniform in \(n\) forces \(|\lambda_k| \leq 1\). The left eigenvector \(\mathbf 1\) expresses \(\sum_i P_{ij} = 1\); simplicity for ergodic chains is Perron–Frobenius.

Order the eigenvalues as \(1 = \lambda_1 > |\lambda_2| \geq |\lambda_3| \geq \cdots\).


8.6.2 Convergence time
Start the chain from \(\mathbf p^{(0)}\). Since \(\boldsymbol\phi_1 = \boldsymbol\pi\) and \(\boldsymbol\psi_1 = \mathbf 1\) (so \(\boldsymbol\psi_1^\top\mathbf p^{(0)} = 1\)), \[\mathbf p^{(n)} = P^n\mathbf p^{(0)} = \boldsymbol\pi + \sum_{k \geq 2}\lambda_k^n\,\boldsymbol\phi_k\,(\boldsymbol\psi_k^\top\mathbf p^{(0)}) = \boldsymbol\pi + O(e^{-n/\tau_{\text{conv}}}),\] with \[\tau_{\text{conv}} = -\frac{1}{\log|\lambda_2|} = -\frac{1}{\log(1 - \delta\lambda)} \simeq \frac{1}{\delta\lambda}, \qquad \delta\lambda = 1 - |\lambda_2| .\] The convergence time is the inverse spectral gap: the smaller the gap, the longer the burn-in.

In the three-state Metropolis example, \(\operatorname{tr}P = 2/3\) and \(\det P = 0\), so the eigenvalues are \(1\), \(0\) and \(-1/3\): \(|\lambda_2| = 1/3\) and the chain equilibrates within a few steps (each step shrinks the deviation from \(\boldsymbol\pi\) by a factor 3). For the two-state chain of Chapter 6, \(\lambda_2 = 1 - a - b\): with \(a = b = 0.01\), \(\tau_{\text{conv}} \approx 50\) steps.



8.6.3 The step size of random-walk Metropolis
For a continuous Metropolis chain the transition operator splits as \(V = K + M\), with \[(Kf)(\mathbf x) = \int d\mathbf x'\,T(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x)A(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x)f(\mathbf x'), \qquad (Mf)(\mathbf x) = R(\mathbf x)f(\mathbf x).\] The spectrum of \(M\) is the range of the rejection probability, \([0, \max R]\), a continuum; \(K\) contributes isolated eigenvalues. Which part sets the gap depends on the proposal width \(\sigma\):

Small steps. \(T(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x) \to \delta(\mathbf x' - \mathbf x)\) as \(\sigma \to 0\), so \(Kf = f + O(\sigma^2)\): the top eigenvalues of \(K\) are \(1 - O(\sigma^2)\) and the gap closes as \(\sigma^2\). The chain is a slow random walk: covering a distance \(L\) takes \(\sim (L/\sigma)^2\) steps.
Large steps. Most proposals land in low-probability regions; \(R(\mathbf x) \to 1\), the top of the spectrum of \(M\) approaches 1, and the chain gets stuck.

In \(D\) dimensions, Taylor-expanding \(A(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x)\) around \(\mathbf x' = \mathbf x\) inside \(R(\mathbf x) = 1 - \int d^D\mathbf x'\,A(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x)\,\mathcal N(\mathbf x'; \mathbf x, \sigma^2 I)\) gives \[R(\mathbf x) = O(D\sigma^2):\] each of the \(D\) directions contributes a term of order \(\sigma^2\). To keep the rejection rate bounded away from 1 we need \(\sigma^2 \lesssim 1/D\). The optimal step size shrinks as \(\sigma \propto D^{-1/2}\), and the number of steps needed to traverse the distribution grows as \(\sim D\).

For random-walk Metropolis on a \(D\)-dimensional target with i.i.d. components, as \(D \to \infty\) the optimal proposal is \(\sigma = 2.38/\sqrt D\) (in units of the target’s standard deviation), and the corresponding acceptance rate is \(\alpha^* \approx 0.234\).

The rule of thumb “aim for 20–40% acceptance” (about 44% in one dimension) comes from this result and works surprisingly well in practice.


8.6.4 Autocorrelation and effective sample size
After burn-in, \(X_n, X_{n+1}, \ldots\) are distributed according to \(\pi\) but are autocorrelated. For any (not necessarily independent) identically distributed sample, \[\operatorname{Var}\Bigl[\frac1n\sum_i g(X_i)\Bigr] = \frac1{n^2}\Bigl[\sum_i\operatorname{Var}[g(X_i)] + \sum_i\sum_{j\neq i}\operatorname{Cov}[g(X_i), g(X_j)]\Bigr].\]

Independent samples: covariances vanish and the variance is \(\operatorname{Var}[g]/n\), the familiar \(1/\sqrt n\) error.
Perfectly correlated samples: all covariances equal \(\operatorname{Var}[g]\) and the variance is \(\operatorname{Var}[g]\) — no improvement with \(n\) at all: it is as if we had a single sample.

A stationary chain lies in between. Its covariance depends only on the lag, \(\operatorname{Cov}[g(X_i), g(X_j)] = c_{|i-j|}\), and typically decays to zero beyond some lag \(\tau\), so the covariance matrix is banded around the diagonal.

\[A_g = \frac{1}{\operatorname{Var}[g]}\sum_{j=-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}[g(X_i), g(X_{i+j})] = 1 + 2\sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{c_j}{c_0}.\]

Summing the banded covariance matrix row by row, rows away from the boundaries contribute \(c_0A_g\) each; boundary rows contribute \(O(\tau)\) in total. Hence \[\operatorname{Var}\Bigl[\frac1n\sum_i g(X_i)\Bigr] = \frac{\operatorname{Var}[g]\,A_g}{n} + O\Bigl(\frac{1}{n^2}\Bigr) = \frac{\operatorname{Var}[g]}{n_g^{\text{eff}}} + O\Bigl(\frac1{n^2}\Bigr), \qquad n^{\text{eff}}_g = \frac{n}{A_g}.\] A correlated chain of length \(n\) is worth \(n/A_g\) independent samples — the effective sample size.

Let \(X_{t+1} = \rho X_t + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\,\xi_t\) with \(\xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\) — a Markov chain with stationary \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(c_j = \rho^{|j|}\). Then \[A = 1 + 2\sum_{j\geq1}\rho^j = \frac{1 + \rho}{1 - \rho}.\] For \(\rho = 0.9\), \(A = 19\): \(10^4\) steps are worth only about 530 independent draws. For \(\rho = 0.99\), \(A = 199\).



8.6.5 Autocorrelation from the spectrum
Standardise \(h = (g - \mu_g)/\sigma_g\), so \(\mathbb E_\pi[h] = 0\), \(\operatorname{Var}[h] = 1\). At equilibrium, \(P(X_n = i, X_0 = j) = (P^n)_{ij}\pi_j\), so \[\operatorname{Cov}[h(X_n), h(X_0)] = \sum_{ij}h_ih_j\pi_j(P^n)_{ij} = \sum_{k}\lambda_k^n\sum_{ij}h_ih_j\pi_j(\boldsymbol\phi_k)_i(\boldsymbol\psi_k)_j .\] The \(k = 1\) term is \(\sum_{ij}h_ih_j\pi_i\pi_j = (\mathbb E_\pi h)^2 = 0\). Summing the geometric series \(\sum_{n \geq 1}\lambda_k^n = \lambda_k/(1 - \lambda_k)\), \[A_g = 1 + 2\sum_{n\geq1}\operatorname{Cov}[h(X_n), h(X_0)] = \sum_{k \geq 2}\frac{1 + \lambda_k}{1 - \lambda_k}\sum_{ij}h_ih_j\pi_j(\boldsymbol\phi_k)_i(\boldsymbol\psi_k)_j ,\] where we used \(1 = \operatorname{Var}[h] = \sum_{k\geq2}\sum_{ij}h_ih_j\pi_j(\boldsymbol\phi_k)_i(\boldsymbol\psi_k)_j\). In terms of the orthonormal eigenvectors of \(V\), the weights are \(a_k^2 = \bigl(\sum_i\sqrt{\pi_i}\,h_i(\mathbf w_k)_i\bigr)^2 \geq 0\) with \(\sum_{k\geq2}a_k^2 = 1\), so \[A_g = \sum_{k\geq 2}a_k^2\,\frac{1 + \lambda_k}{1 - \lambda_k}.\] The autocorrelation time is a weighted average of \((1 + \lambda_k)/(1 - \lambda_k)\): eigenvalues close to 1 (small gaps) inflate it, and the observable “feels” a slow mode only to the extent that it overlaps with it. The AR(1) result \(A = (1 + \rho)/(1 - \rho)\) is the single-mode case. (Negative eigenvalues give \(A_g < 1\): antithetic, “better than independent” samples are possible.)

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
text:
8.7 Practical MCMC

Burn-in. Discard the transient (several \(\tau_{\text{conv}}\)); check that discarding more does not change the estimate.
Trace plots of \(g(X_t)\) vs \(t\) should look like stationary noise around a constant mean.
Effective sample size: estimate \(A_g\) from the empirical autocorrelation (truncating the sum when it becomes noisy) and report \(n/A_g\), not \(n\).
Gelman–Rubin \(\hat R\): run several chains from over-dispersed starting points and compare within-chain and between-chain variances; \(\hat R \approx 1\) (in practice \(< 1.01\)) indicates convergence.
Thinning (keeping one sample every \(k\)) reduces storage but never increases the information in the chain.
crumbs: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
text:
8.8 Exercises

Prove that with a symmetric proposal the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance reduces to \(\min\{1, \pi(y)/\pi(x)\}\), and verify detailed balance for \(x \neq y\).


Solution. With \(q(y\mid x) = q(x\mid y)\) the \(q\)’s cancel in the Hastings ratio. Then \(\pi(x)q(y\mid x)\min\{1, \pi(y)/\pi(x)\} = q(y\mid x)\min\{\pi(x), \pi(y)\}\), which is symmetric in \(x \leftrightarrow y\) because \(q\) is symmetric: this is \(\pi(y)P(x \mid y)\).


Using the inverse-CDF method, give an algorithm to sample from \(f(x) = 2x\) on \([0, 1]\). Then design a rejection sampler for the same density using the uniform envelope and compute its acceptance rate.


Solution. \(F(x) = x^2\), so \(X = \sqrt U\). For rejection: \(M = \max f = 2\), \(b - a = 1\), so \(P(\text{accept}) = 1/((b-a)M) = 1/2\): draw \(Y \sim \mathcal U(0,1)\), accept if \(U_2 \leq Y\).


A Metropolis chain has \(A_g = 25\) for the observable \(g\). How long must the chain be (after burn-in) to estimate \(\mathbb E[g]\) to within \(0.01\sigma_g\) (one standard error)?


Solution. Standard error \(= \sigma_g\sqrt{A_g/n} = 0.01\sigma_g \Rightarrow n = A_g/10^{-4} = 2.5 \times 10^5\) steps, versus \(10^4\) for i.i.d. sampling.


For the two-state chain with \(P(0\to1) = a\), \(P(1\to0) = b\) and the observable \(g(x) = x\), compute \(A_g\).


Solution. Only one non-trivial eigenvalue, \(\lambda_2 = 1 - a - b\), and the centred \(g\) lies entirely along its eigenvector, so \(A_g = (1 + \lambda_2)/(1 - \lambda_2) = (2 - a - b)/(a + b)\). For \(a = b = 0.5\) (\(\lambda_2 = 0\), i.i.d.) \(A_g = 1\); for \(a = b = 0.01\), \(A_g = 99\); for \(a = b = 0.9\) (\(\lambda_2 = -0.8\), alternating) \(A_g = 1/9\).

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
text:
8.9 Callouts






Metropolis is not the fastest MCMC algorithm; it is the most general. It needs only pointwise evaluations of the unnormalised target. Specialised samplers (Gibbs, HMC) exploit more structure and do much better.









The MCMC estimator is biased by the initial transient. Always discard a burn-in. And the error bar is \(\sigma_g\sqrt{A_g/n}\), not \(\sigma_g/\sqrt n\): forgetting \(A_g\) gives wildly overconfident results.









A chain that “looks converged” may still be missing modes of a multimodal target: trace plots detect within-mode stationarity, not between-mode mixing. The spectral gap of a chain with well-separated modes is exponentially small in the barrier height.









Effective sample size per unit of computation is the right figure of merit for comparing samplers.

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and latent variables
text:
9.1 Metropolis–Hastings
Metropolis is universal but blunt: it proposes blindly and then corrects by rejection. When the target has structure — conditional distributions we can sample exactly, as in Bayesian models with conjugate priors and latent variables — a specialised algorithm, Gibbs sampling, exploits it and never rejects. This chapter derives Gibbs sampling as a special case of Metropolis–Hastings and works out in detail its most important application: inference in mixture models through latent variables, which turns out to be a stochastic cousin of K-means clustering.
Metropolis required a symmetric proposal. With a general proposal \(T(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x)\), the kernel \[P(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x) = T(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x)A(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x) + R(\mathbf x)\,\delta(\mathbf x - \mathbf x')\] satisfies detailed balance with the Hastings acceptance probability \[A(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x) = \min\Bigl\{1, \frac{\pi(\mathbf x')\,T(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf x')}{\pi(\mathbf x)\,T(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x)}\Bigr\}.\]
The ratio \(T(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf x')/T(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x)\) corrects for proposals that favour some directions. The freedom to choose \(T\) is what we now exploit.
crumbs: 9  Gibbs sampling and latent variables

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and latent variables
text:
Proof. For \(\mathbf x' \neq \mathbf x\) (the \(\delta\) term is trivially symmetric), \[\begin{aligned}
P(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x)\pi(\mathbf x) &= T(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x)\pi(\mathbf x)\min\Bigl\{1, \frac{\pi(\mathbf x')T(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf x')}{\pi(\mathbf x)T(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x)}\Bigr\} = \min\bigl\{T(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x)\pi(\mathbf x),\ T(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf x')\pi(\mathbf x')\bigr\} \\
&= T(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf x')\pi(\mathbf x')\min\Bigl\{1, \frac{T(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x)\pi(\mathbf x)}{T(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf x')\pi(\mathbf x')}\Bigr\} = P(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf x')\pi(\mathbf x').
\end{aligned}\]
crumbs: 9  Gibbs sampling and latent variables

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and latent variables
text:
9.2 The Gibbs sampling algorithm
Write \(\mathbf x = (x_1, \ldots, x_d)\) and, for each \(k\), \[\mathbf x_{<k} = (x_1, \ldots, x_{k-1}), \qquad \mathbf x_{>k} = (x_{k+1}, \ldots, x_d), \qquad \mathbf x_{-k} = (\mathbf x_{<k}, \mathbf x_{>k}).\] Gibbs sampling applies when we can sample each full conditional \(\pi(x_k \mid \mathbf x_{-k})\).

One sweep updates the coordinates in turn, always conditioning on the most recent values: \[\begin{aligned}
x_1' &\sim \pi(x_1 \mid \mathbf x_{>1}), \\
x_2' &\sim \pi(x_2 \mid x_1', \mathbf x_{>2}), \\
&\ \ \vdots \\
x_k' &\sim \pi(x_k \mid \mathbf x'_{<k}, \mathbf x_{>k}), \\
&\ \ \vdots \\
x_d' &\sim \pi(x_d \mid \mathbf x'_{<d}).
\end{aligned}\] In the random-scan variant, each step picks a coordinate \(k\) uniformly at random and resamples it.

Each update is a Metropolis–Hastings move with proposal “change only \(x_k\), drawing it from its conditional”: \[T(x_k' \mid \mathbf x) = \pi(x_k' \mid \mathbf x'_{<k}, \mathbf x_{>k}).\]

With this proposal, the Hastings acceptance probability is exactly 1.


Proof. Abbreviate \(\mathbf c = (\mathbf x'_{<k}, \mathbf x_{>k})\), the coordinates that do not change. The move is \((x_k, \mathbf c) \to (x_k', \mathbf c)\), and \[A = \min\Bigl\{1, \frac{\pi(x_k', \mathbf c)\;\pi(x_k \mid \mathbf c)}{\pi(x_k, \mathbf c)\;\pi(x_k' \mid \mathbf c)}\Bigr\}.\] Factorising \(\pi(x_k', \mathbf c) = \pi(x_k' \mid \mathbf c)\pi(\mathbf c)\) and \(\pi(x_k, \mathbf c) = \pi(x_k \mid \mathbf c)\pi(\mathbf c)\), \[A = \min\Bigl\{1, \frac{\pi(x_k' \mid \mathbf c)\pi(\mathbf c)\,\pi(x_k \mid \mathbf c)}{\pi(x_k \mid \mathbf c)\pi(\mathbf c)\,\pi(x_k' \mid \mathbf c)}\Bigr\} = 1 .\]

So every single-coordinate update leaves \(\pi\) invariant, and so does their composition (a full sweep). Note that a systematic sweep as a whole does not satisfy detailed balance (the reversed sweep updates coordinates in the opposite order), but it does leave \(\pi\) stationary, which is what matters; the random-scan version is reversible. Under mild conditions (e.g. \(\pi > 0\) everywhere) the chain is ergodic and converges to \(\pi\).

Remark. “Acceptance 1” does not mean “efficient”. Gibbs moves only along coordinate axes, with step sizes set by the conditional widths. When the target is strongly correlated, conditionals are narrow and the chain crawls.


Let \((x_1, x_2) \sim \mathcal N\Bigl(\mathbf 0, \begin{pmatrix}1 & \rho\\ \rho & 1\end{pmatrix}\Bigr)\). The full conditionals are \[x_1 \mid x_2 \sim \mathcal N(\rho x_2,\ 1 - \rho^2), \qquad x_2 \mid x_1 \sim \mathcal N(\rho x_1,\ 1 - \rho^2).\] After one sweep, \(x_1^{(t+1)} = \rho x_2^{(t)} + \ldots = \rho^2 x_1^{(t)} + \text{noise}\): the sequence \(x_1^{(t)}\) is an AR(1) process with coefficient \(\rho^2\). By Chapter 7 its integrated autocorrelation time is \[A = \frac{1 + \rho^2}{1 - \rho^2}.\] For \(\rho = 0.5\), \(A \approx 1.7\) (excellent); for \(\rho = 0.99\), \(A \approx 100\); for \(\rho = 0.999\), \(A \approx 1000\). The chain zig-zags along the narrow ridge with steps of size \(\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\) while it needs to travel distances of order 1. Reparameterising (e.g. rotating to \(u = x_1 + x_2\), \(v = x_1 - x_2\), which are independent) or blocking (updating \((x_1, x_2)\) jointly) cures the problem.

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and latent variables
text:
9.3 When Gibbs sampling helps: conjugacy
Gibbs is useful when the full conditionals belong to families we can sample directly. The paradigm is conjugacy: a prior is conjugate to a likelihood if the posterior is in the same family as the prior.








likelihood
conjugate prior
posterior




Bernoulli/Binomial(\(\theta\))
Beta\((a, b)\)
Beta\((a + k, b + n - k)\)


Categorical/Multinomial(\(\mathbf p\))
Dirichlet\((\boldsymbol\gamma)\)
Dirichlet\((\boldsymbol\gamma + \mathbf n)\)


Normal(\(\mu\)), known \(\sigma^2\)
Normal\((\mu_0, \sigma_0^2)\)
Normal (precisions add)


Normal, known \(\mu\), unknown \(\sigma^2\)
Inverse-Gamma\((\alpha, \beta)\)
Inverse-Gamma\((\alpha + n/2, \beta + \tfrac12\sum(x_i - \mu)^2)\)


Poisson(\(\lambda\))
Gamma\((\alpha, \beta)\)
Gamma\((\alpha + \sum x_i, \beta + n)\)



In a multi-parameter model, the joint posterior is rarely in a standard family, but if each parameter has a conjugate prior given the others, every full conditional is standard and Gibbs applies.

Model: \(y_i \mid \boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\beta^\top\mathbf x_i, \sigma^2)\), priors \(\boldsymbol\beta \sim \mathcal N(\mathbf 0, \tau^2 I)\) and \(\sigma^2 \sim \text{InvGamma}(\alpha, \beta)\). The full conditionals are

\(\boldsymbol\beta \mid \sigma^2, \mathbf y \sim \mathcal N(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}, \Sigma_\beta)\), with \(\Sigma_\beta = (\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X/\sigma^2 + I/\tau^2)^{-1}\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \Sigma_\beta\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y/\sigma^2\);
\(\sigma^2 \mid \boldsymbol\beta, \mathbf y \sim \text{InvGamma}\bigl(\alpha + n/2,\ \beta + \tfrac12\|\mathbf y - \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2\bigr)\).

Alternating the two conjugate draws samples the joint posterior, which is not itself a standard distribution.

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and latent variables
text:
9.4 Mixture models and latent variables

9.4.1 The mixture model
Suppose each data point \(x\) is drawn from one of \(K\) Gaussians with means \(\boldsymbol\mu = (\mu_1, \ldots, \mu_K)\) and a common, known standard deviation \(\sigma\), the \(k\)-th being chosen with probability \(p_k\): \[f(x \mid \boldsymbol\mu, \mathbf p) = \sum_{k=1}^K p_k\,(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}e^{-\frac{(x - \mu_k)^2}{2\sigma^2}}.\] For \(N\) independent points \(\mathbf x = \{x_i\}\), the likelihood and the posterior are \[f(\mathbf x \mid \boldsymbol\mu, \mathbf p) = \prod_{i=1}^N\sum_{k=1}^K p_k(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}e^{-\frac{(x_i - \mu_k)^2}{2\sigma^2}}, \qquad f(\boldsymbol\mu, \mathbf p \mid \mathbf x) = \frac{f(\mathbf x \mid \boldsymbol\mu, \mathbf p)f(\boldsymbol\mu)f(\mathbf p)}{c(\mathbf x)} .\] One could run Metropolis on this posterior, but it is unpleasant: the “sum inside the product” makes every likelihood evaluation cost \(O(NK)\), and the posterior has no convenient structure.


9.4.2 Introducing latent variables
The trick is to add variables. For each point introduce a latent label \(Z_i \in \{1, \ldots, K\}\) saying which component generated it: \[Z_i \mid \mathbf p \sim \text{Cat}(\mathbf p), \quad P(Z_i = k) = p_k; \qquad f(x_i \mid \boldsymbol\mu, Z_i) = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}e^{-\frac{(x_i - \mu_{Z_i})^2}{2\sigma^2}} .\] Summing over the labels recovers the original model, \(f(\mathbf x \mid \boldsymbol\mu, \mathbf p) = \sum_{\mathbf Z} f(\mathbf x, \mathbf Z \mid \boldsymbol\mu, \mathbf p)\). But the complete-data likelihood — given the labels — is much simpler: \[f(\mathbf x, \mathbf Z \mid \boldsymbol\mu, \mathbf p) = \prod_i p_{Z_i}(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}e^{-\frac{(x_i - \mu_{Z_i})^2}{2\sigma^2}} = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-N/2}\prod_{k=1}^K p_k^{n_k}\,e^{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i : Z_i = k}(x_i - \mu_k)^2},\] with \(n_k = \sum_i \chi(Z_i = k)\) the number of points in component \(k\). The product over points has become a product over components, each depending only on its own points. Two benefits:

the likelihood is cheap to evaluate;
with conjugate priors, every full conditional is a standard distribution, so Gibbs sampling applies.


Remark. Sampling the augmented posterior \(f(\boldsymbol\mu, \mathbf p, \mathbf Z \mid \mathbf x)\) and simply ignoring \(\mathbf Z\) in the output gives samples from the marginal \(f(\boldsymbol\mu, \mathbf p \mid \mathbf x)\). Making the space bigger makes sampling easier — a recurring theme (cf. the momentum variables of HMC in Chapter 11).



9.4.3 Priors

Means: \(\mu_k \sim \mathcal N(\mu_0, \sigma_0^2)\) independently, \(f(\boldsymbol\mu) = (2\pi\sigma_0^2)^{-K/2}\prod_k e^{-(\mu_k - \mu_0)^2/2\sigma_0^2}\). Taking \(\mu_0 = 0\), \(\sigma_0 \to \infty\) gives a flat prior.
Weights: \(\mathbf p \sim \text{Dir}(\boldsymbol\gamma)\), \(f(\mathbf p) = B(\boldsymbol\gamma)^{-1}\prod_k p_k^{\gamma_k - 1}\) on the simplex. \(\gamma_k = 1\) is uniform on the simplex.

The joint posterior is \[f(\boldsymbol\mu, \mathbf Z, \mathbf p \mid \mathbf x) \propto \prod_{k=1}^K\Bigl[e^{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i:Z_i=k}(x_i - \mu_k)^2}\;e^{-\frac{(\mu_k - \mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2}}\;p_k^{n_k + \gamma_k - 1}\Bigr].\]


9.4.4 Full conditionals
Each conditional is obtained by keeping only the factors that contain the variable of interest.
Means. For \(\mu_k\), only the \(k\)-th factor matters: \[f(\mu_k \mid \mathbf x, \mathbf Z, \mathbf p, \boldsymbol\mu_{-k}) \propto \exp\Bigl[-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i:Z_i = k}(x_i - \mu_k)^2 - \frac{(\mu_k - \mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2}\Bigr].\] The exponent is quadratic in \(\mu_k\); completing the square, \[\mu_k \mid \ldots \sim \mathcal N(\mu_k', \sigma_k'^2), \qquad \mu_k' = \frac{\mu_0/\sigma_0^2 + n_k\bar X_k/\sigma^2}{1/\sigma_0^2 + n_k/\sigma^2}, \qquad \sigma_k'^2 = \Bigl(\frac{1}{\sigma_0^2} + \frac{n_k}{\sigma^2}\Bigr)^{-1},\] with \(\bar X_k = \frac1{n_k}\sum_{i:Z_i = k}x_i\) the mean of the points currently assigned to \(k\). Precisions add, and the mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the data mean (exactly as for the Gaussian channel of Chapter 5).
Weights. Only \(\prod_k p_k^{n_k + \gamma_k - 1}\) depends on \(\mathbf p\), so \[\mathbf p \mid \ldots \sim \text{Dir}(\boldsymbol\gamma'), \qquad \boldsymbol\gamma' = \boldsymbol\gamma + \mathbf n .\] The prior parameters \(\gamma_k\) act as “pseudo-counts” added to the observed counts \(n_k\).
Labels. For \(Z_i\), only the factor involving point \(i\) matters; normalising over its \(K\) possible values, \[P(Z_i = k \mid \ldots) = \frac{p_k\,e^{-(x_i - \mu_k)^2/2\sigma^2}}{\sum_{l}p_l\,e^{-(x_i - \mu_l)^2/2\sigma^2}} \equiv p'_{ik}, \qquad Z_i \mid \ldots \sim \text{Cat}(\mathbf p'_i).\] This is Bayes’ theorem for “which component produced \(x_i\)?”, with prior \(p_k\) and likelihood \(\mathcal N(x_i; \mu_k, \sigma^2)\).

Initialise \(\mathbf Z\) (e.g. at random). Repeat:

for each \(k\): compute \(n_k\), \(\bar X_k\) and sample \(\mu_k \sim \mathcal N(\mu'_k, \sigma'^2_k)\);
sample \(\mathbf p \sim \text{Dir}(\boldsymbol\gamma + \mathbf n)\);
for each \(i\): compute \(p'_{ik}\) and sample \(Z_i \sim \text{Cat}(\mathbf p'_i)\).



Generate data from \(K = 4\) components with \(\mu_k = \{1, 3, 5, 7\}\), \(\sigma = 0.5\) and \(p_k = 0.25\). Starting from random labels, the sampled \(\mu_k\) converge to the true values within a handful of sweeps, and the agreement between true and inferred labels rises just as quickly (Allegra, Fig. 10.1). It saturates at about \(97\%\): with neighbouring means \(4\sigma\) apart, a point falls past the midpoint towards a neighbour with probability \(1 - \Phi(2) \approx 2.3\%\) per side, and such points are genuinely ambiguous — no method can classify them correctly. The posterior spread of each \(\mu_k\) is \(\approx \sigma/\sqrt{n_k}\).



9.4.5 Gibbs sampling and K-means
Soft K-means clustering alternates two steps:

assignment: each point gets a “responsibility” for each cluster, \(r_{ik} \propto e^{-(x_i - \mu_k)^2/2\sigma^2}\) (normalised over \(k\));
update: each mean moves to the responsibility-weighted average, \(\mu_k = \sum_i r_{ik}x_i\big/\sum_i r_{ik}\).

Now take the Gibbs sampler in the limit \(\sigma_0 \to \infty\) (flat prior on the means) and \(\gamma_k = \gamma \to \infty\) (weights pinned at \(p_k = 1/K\)). Then:

\(\mu_k\) is drawn from a Gaussian centred at \(\bar X_k = \sum_i\chi(Z_i = k)x_i/\sum_i\chi(Z_i = k)\) with small width \(\sigma/\sqrt{n_k}\), so \(\mu_k \approx \bar X_k\);
\(Z_i\) is drawn with \(P(Z_i = k) \propto e^{-(x_i - \mu_k)^2/2\sigma^2} = r_{ik}\).

Averaging over the random labels, \(\mathbb E[\chi(Z_i = k)] = r_{ik}\), so \(\mu_k \approx \sum_i r_{ik}x_i/\sum_i r_{ik}\): the Gibbs sampler is a stochastic version of soft K-means, and the two agree when clusters are well separated. Conversely, this reveals that K-means implicitly assumes a mixture of isotropic Gaussians with equal widths and equal weights — not at all obvious from its formulation. (The deterministic counterpart that maximises the likelihood instead of sampling is the EM algorithm.)


9.4.6 Label switching
The mixture likelihood is invariant under permutations of the component labels, so with symmetric priors the posterior has \(K!\) identical modes. A Gibbs chain typically stays in one labelling (moving between them requires relabelling all points at once — an exponentially unlikely sequence of single-site updates). For estimating label-invariant quantities this is harmless; for component-specific summaries one imposes an ordering (\(\mu_1 < \mu_2 < \cdots\)) or post-processes the samples.

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and latent variables
text:
9.5 Modern context
Gibbs sampling remains the method of choice for models with discrete latent variables — mixtures, hidden Markov models, topic models such as LDA, Ising-type models — where gradient-based methods (HMC, Chapter 11) do not apply. For continuous parameters with strong correlations, blocking, reparameterisation or Hamiltonian methods are usually preferable.
crumbs: 9  Gibbs sampling and latent variables

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and latent variables
text:
9.6 Exercises

Derive the full conditional of \(\mu_k\) in the mixture model by completing the square, and check the limits \(n_k = 0\) and \(\sigma_0 \to \infty\).


Solution. The exponent is \(-\tfrac12\bigl[\mu_k^2(n_k/\sigma^2 + 1/\sigma_0^2) - 2\mu_k(n_k\bar X_k/\sigma^2 + \mu_0/\sigma_0^2)\bigr] + \text{const}\), i.e. a Gaussian with precision \(n_k/\sigma^2 + 1/\sigma_0^2\) and mean (linear coefficient)/(precision) \(= \mu'_k\). If \(n_k = 0\) (empty cluster) the conditional is the prior \(\mathcal N(\mu_0, \sigma_0^2)\). If \(\sigma_0 \to \infty\), it is \(\mathcal N(\bar X_k, \sigma^2/n_k)\) — the frequentist sampling distribution of the mean.


Write a Gibbs sampler for the joint posterior of \((\mu, \tau)\) for data \(x_i \sim \mathcal N(\mu, 1/\tau)\) with priors \(\mu \sim \mathcal N(\mu_0, 1/\lambda_0)\) and \(\tau \sim \text{Gamma}(a, b)\).


Solution. \(\mu \mid \tau, \mathbf x \sim \mathcal N\Bigl(\frac{\lambda_0\mu_0 + \tau\sum_i x_i}{\lambda_0 + N\tau}, \frac{1}{\lambda_0 + N\tau}\Bigr)\); \(\tau \mid \mu, \mathbf x \sim \text{Gamma}\bigl(a + N/2,\ b + \tfrac12\sum_i(x_i - \mu)^2\bigr)\). Alternate the two draws.


For the bivariate Gaussian with correlation \(\rho\), how many Gibbs sweeps are needed for an effective sample size of 1000 when \(\rho = 0.95\)? How many if one first rotates to \(u = (x_1 + x_2)/\sqrt2\), \(v = (x_1 - x_2)/\sqrt 2\)?


Solution. \(A = (1 + 0.9025)/(1 - 0.9025) \approx 19.5\), so about \(19{,}500\) sweeps. After rotation \(u\) and \(v\) are independent (\(\operatorname{Var} u = 1 + \rho\), \(\operatorname{Var} v = 1 - \rho\)), the conditionals equal the marginals, and every sweep is an independent draw: 1000 sweeps.


For a two-component mixture with means \(\pm 3\) and \(\sigma = 1\), explain why the Gibbs sampler does not visit the “label-swapped” mode \((\mu_1, \mu_2) \to (\mu_2, \mu_1)\).


Solution. To swap, all points currently labelled 1 must be relabelled 2 and vice versa. Each single-site update is conditioned on the current means, under which relabelling a point costs a factor \(\approx e^{-(6)^2/2}\) in probability; the means only move once many labels have changed. The path between the two modes passes through configurations of exponentially small posterior probability, so the chain essentially never makes the transition. This is harmless for label-invariant summaries; otherwise impose \(\mu_1 < \mu_2\).
crumbs: 9  Gibbs sampling and latent variables

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and latent variables
text:
9.7 Callouts






Gibbs is simple and exact when conjugacy holds. When a conditional is not standard, replace that single update by a Metropolis step targeting the conditional (Metropolis-within-Gibbs) — still a valid sampler.









Blocking correlated variables (updating them jointly) and reparameterising to decorrelate them are the standard cures for slow Gibbs mixing.









Gibbs can fail on multimodal targets whose conditionals are unimodal: each coordinate move is local in the joint space.









The diagnostics of Chapter 7 (burn-in, autocorrelation, ESS, \(\hat R\)) apply without change. Acceptance rate 1 says nothing about how well the chain explores the target.

title: 10  A problem of high-dimensional inference
text:
10.1 The problem
This chapter works through a real research problem that ties together everything in Chapters 7–8: building a likelihood with latent variables, choosing conjugate priors, discovering that the exact posterior is a combinatorial monster, and sampling it with Metropolis and Gibbs. The problem comes from population genetics: Gaggiotti et al. (2002) studied how new colonies of grey seals are founded, and asked where the founders came from, using only the genomes of pups born in the new colony.
Grey seals live in isolated colonies; occasionally a new colony is founded by migrants from older ones. Assume the founders come from \(P\) old colonies, in unknown proportions \[\mathbf x = (x_1, \ldots, x_P), \qquad x_i \geq 0, \quad \sum_{i=1}^P x_i = 1 .\] \(\mathbf x\) is the unknown we want to infer: a point in the \((P-1)\)-dimensional simplex.
The data: \(N = 150\) pups born in the new colony (whose parents were migrants) were genotyped at \(L = 9\) loci, chosen among the most variable ones to maximise discrimination. At each locus an individual carries two variants (alleles) of the gene, one inherited from the mother (\(n = 1\)) and one from the father (\(n = 2\)), each among \(M_l\) possible alleles. Taking \(M = \max_l M_l\) (and assigning zero frequency to non-existent alleles), the data are \[y_{k,l,n} \in \{1, \ldots, M\}, \qquad k = 1..N \text{ (individual)},\ l = 1..L \text{ (locus)},\ n = 1, 2 \text{ (parent)}.\] What links \(\mathbf x\) to \(\mathbf y\) is that the allele frequencies in the old colonies are known from previous studies: \[p_m^{(i,l)} = \text{frequency of allele } m \text{ at locus } l \text{ in colony } i, \qquad \sum_m p_m^{(i,l)} = 1 .\] Different colonies have different allele frequencies, so a pup’s genotype carries (weak) information about where its parents came from; with many pups and loci, this adds up to information about \(\mathbf x\).

title: 10  A problem of high-dimensional inference
text:
10.2 Basic model
We first study a simplified model in which only the maternal alleles are observed: data \(y_{k,l} \equiv y_{k,l,1}\).

10.2.1 Likelihood
Introduce a latent variable for each pup, \[Z_k \in \{1, \ldots, P\}: \text{ the colony the mother of pup } k \text{ came from.}\] Two modelling assumptions connect the variables:

the probability of inheriting allele \(m\) at locus \(l\) from a mother of colony \(i\) is the frequency of that allele in colony \(i\): \[P(Y_{k,l} = m \mid Z_k = i) = p_m^{(i,l)};\]
the probability that a mother came from colony \(i\) is the proportion of founders from colony \(i\): \[P(Z_k = i \mid \mathbf x) = x_i .\]

Marginalising the latent variable, and using that \(Y_{k,l}\) depends on \(\mathbf x\) only through \(Z_k\) (conditional independence), \[P(Y_{k,l} = m \mid \mathbf x) = \sum_{i=1}^P P(Y_{k,l} = m \mid Z_k = i)P(Z_k = i \mid \mathbf x) = \sum_{i=1}^P x_i\,p_m^{(i,l)} .\] Assuming further that the alleles at different loci are independent given the origin (a simplification — probably not exactly true for real genomes), \[P(\mathbf Y_k = \mathbf y_k \mid Z_k = i) = \prod_{l=1}^L p^{(i,l)}_{y_{k,l}} \equiv \gamma_{ik}, \qquad P(\mathbf Y_k = \mathbf y_k \mid \mathbf x) = \sum_{i=1}^P x_i\,\gamma_{ik}.\] \(\gamma_{ik}\) is the likelihood that pup \(k\)’s maternal genotype came from colony \(i\). Assuming independent individuals, the full likelihood is \[P(\mathbf Y = \mathbf y \mid \mathbf x) = \prod_{k=1}^N\sum_{i=1}^P x_i\,\gamma_{ik} = \prod_{k=1}^N\sum_{i=1}^P x_i\prod_{l=1}^L p^{(i,l)}_{y_{k,l}} .\] This is a mixture model of exactly the type of Chapter 8: each pup is drawn from one of \(P\) “components” (colonies) with weights \(\mathbf x\), but the component distributions \(\gamma_{ik}\) are known.


10.2.2 Prior: the Dirichlet distribution
The likelihood is a polynomial in \(\mathbf x\), so the natural (conjugate) prior on the simplex is the Dirichlet distribution.

\(\mathbf x \sim \text{Dir}(\boldsymbol\alpha)\), \(\alpha_i > 0\), has density on the simplex \(\mathcal D = \{\mathbf x : x_i \geq 0, \sum_i x_i = 1\}\) \[\text{Dir}(\boldsymbol\alpha; \mathbf x) = \frac{1}{B(\boldsymbol\alpha)}\prod_{i=1}^P x_i^{\alpha_i - 1}, \qquad B(\boldsymbol\alpha) = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_1)\cdots\Gamma(\alpha_P)}{\Gamma(\alpha_1 + \cdots + \alpha_P)} .\] With \(\alpha_0 = \sum_i\alpha_i\): \(\mathbb E[x_i] = \alpha_i/\alpha_0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}[x_i] = \alpha_i(\alpha_0 - \alpha_i)/\bigl(\alpha_0^2(\alpha_0 + 1)\bigr)\). For \(P = 2\) it reduces to the Beta distribution. \(\boldsymbol\alpha = (1, \ldots, 1)\) is uniform on the simplex; large \(\alpha_0\) concentrates the mass around the mean.

The key integral, used repeatedly below, is just the normalisation: \[\int_{\mathcal D} d\mathbf x\,\prod_i x_i^{\beta_i - 1} = B(\boldsymbol\beta).\]
The posterior is \[P(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y) = \frac{1}{P(\mathbf y)}\prod_{k=1}^N\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^P x_i\gamma_{ik}\Bigr)\cdot\frac{1}{B(\boldsymbol\alpha)}\prod_{p=1}^P x_p^{\alpha_p - 1},\] with evidence \(P(\mathbf y) = \int_{\mathcal D} d\mathbf x\,(\text{numerator})\), an integral over the simplex.


10.2.3 Metropolis approach
Metropolis only needs the unnormalised posterior. A simple proposal moves \(\mathbf x\) by a small random step and then projects back onto the simplex: \[\mathbf x \;\to\; \mathbf x + \mathbf u \;\to\; b_{0,1}(\mathbf x + \mathbf u) \;\to\; \frac{b_{0,1}(\mathbf x + \mathbf u)}{\sum_i b_{0,1}(x_i + u_i)} = \mathbf x', \qquad u_i \sim \mathcal U(-\epsilon, \epsilon),\] where \(b_{0,1}(x) = \min(\max(x, 0), 1)\) clips each component into \([0, 1]\). The acceptance probability is \[A(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x) = \min\Biggl\{1, \frac{\prod_k\bigl(\sum_i x'_i\gamma_{ik}\bigr)\prod_p (x'_p)^{\alpha_p - 1}}{\prod_k\bigl(\sum_i x_i\gamma_{ik}\bigr)\prod_p x_p^{\alpha_p - 1}}\Biggr\},\] in which the evidence and \(B(\boldsymbol\alpha)\) cancel. Each evaluation costs \(O(NP)\) operations (after precomputing \(\gamma_{ik}\), which costs \(O(NPL)\) once). In practice one works with log-probabilities to avoid underflow: \(\prod_k\) of 150 small numbers is far below double-precision range.

Remark (Is this proposal symmetric?). The clip-and-renormalise map is not exactly symmetric, so strictly a Hastings correction would be needed. Cleaner alternatives: (i) parametrise by \(P - 1\) free coordinates and reject proposals that leave the simplex (a symmetric proposal on a bounded domain is fine — out-of-domain proposals have \(\pi = 0\) and are simply rejected); (ii) propose \(\mathbf x' \sim \text{Dir}(c\,\mathbf x)\) with a large concentration \(c\) and include the Hastings ratio \(\text{Dir}(c\mathbf x'; \mathbf x)/\text{Dir}(c\mathbf x; \mathbf x')\).



10.2.4 Analytic expression of the posterior
The posterior can, in principle, be written in closed form. Expand the product of sums: \[\prod_{k=1}^N\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^P x_i\gamma_{ik}\Bigr) = \sum_{i_1=1}^P\cdots\sum_{i_N=1}^P\ \prod_{k=1}^N x_{i_k}\gamma_{i_k k} = \sum_{\mathbf i}\ \prod_{k=1}^N x_{i_k}\gamma_{i_k k},\] where the multi-index \(\mathbf i = (i_1, \ldots, i_N)\) runs over all \(P^N\) assignments of pups to colonies — i.e. over all values of the latent variables \(\mathbf Z\). Let \(n_p(\mathbf i) = \sum_k\delta_{i_k p}\) count how many pups are assigned to colony \(p\). Then \(\prod_k x_{i_k} = \prod_p x_p^{n_p(\mathbf i)}\) and the numerator becomes \[\frac{1}{B(\boldsymbol\alpha)}\sum_{\mathbf i}\Bigl(\prod_k\gamma_{i_k k}\Bigr)\prod_p x_p^{n_p(\mathbf i) + \alpha_p - 1} = \sum_{\mathbf i}\xi(\mathbf i)\,\text{Dir}\bigl(\mathbf n(\mathbf i) + \boldsymbol\alpha; \mathbf x\bigr), \qquad \xi(\mathbf i) = \frac{B(\mathbf n(\mathbf i) + \boldsymbol\alpha)}{B(\boldsymbol\alpha)}\prod_{k=1}^N\gamma_{i_k k}.\] Since each Dirichlet integrates to one, the evidence is \(P(\mathbf y) = \sum_{\mathbf i}\xi(\mathbf i)\), and

\[P(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y) = \sum_{\mathbf i}\zeta(\mathbf i)\,\text{Dir}\bigl(\mathbf n(\mathbf i) + \boldsymbol\alpha; \mathbf x\bigr), \qquad \zeta(\mathbf i) = \frac{\xi(\mathbf i)}{\sum_{\mathbf j}\xi(\mathbf j)} .\] Posterior moments follow from those of the Dirichlet, e.g. \[\mathbb E[x_p \mid \mathbf y] = \sum_{\mathbf i}\zeta(\mathbf i)\,\frac{n_p(\mathbf i) + \alpha_p}{\sum_q\bigl(n_q(\mathbf i) + \alpha_q\bigr)} = \sum_{\mathbf i}\zeta(\mathbf i)\,\frac{n_p(\mathbf i) + \alpha_p}{N + \alpha_0}.\]

The interpretation is transparent: for each hypothetical assignment \(\mathbf i\) of pups to colonies, the posterior on \(\mathbf x\) would be the conjugate \(\text{Dir}(\boldsymbol\alpha + \text{counts})\); the true posterior averages these over assignments, weighted by how well each assignment explains the genotypes.

Remark (Why the analytic formula is useless). The sum has \(P^N\) terms. With \(N = 150\) and \(P = 7\) (as in the study), that is \(7^{150} \approx 10^{127}\) terms — hopeless. This is a general feature of mixture models: marginalising the latent variables analytically is exponential in \(N\). Note, by contrast, that the factorised form \(\prod_k\sum_i x_i\gamma_{ik}\) costs only \(N \cdot P\) operations, which is why Metropolis on \(\mathbf x\) is perfectly feasible.



10.2.5 A simple example
To see the structure, consider \(P = 2\) colonies, \(M = 2\) alleles and two loci, “tail length” and “fin length”, with allele 1 = long and 2 = short. The known frequencies are \[p^{(1,1)} = p^{(1,2)} = \bigl(\tfrac23, \tfrac13\bigr), \qquad p^{(2,1)} = p^{(2,2)} = \bigl(\tfrac14, \tfrac34\bigr):\] in colony 1 two thirds of the individuals have long tails (and fins), in colony 2 only a quarter. We observe two alleles \((y_1, y_2)\), one per locus, and \(\mathbf x = (x_1, 1 - x_1)\). Following Allegra’s notes, take the likelihood to be \[P(y_1, y_2 \mid \mathbf x) = \prod_{l=1}^{2}\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^2 x_i p^{(i,l)}_{y_l}\Bigr) = \sum_{i,j} x_ix_j\,p^{(i,1)}_{y_1}p^{(j,2)}_{y_2},\] i.e. each of the two alleles comes from an independently drawn founder. (This is equivalent to \(N = 2\) pups with \(L = 1\) locus each. For a single pup with two loci, the basic model would instead give \(\sum_i x_i\,p^{(i,1)}_{y_1}p^{(i,2)}_{y_2}\), linear in \(\mathbf x\), and the posterior would be a mixture of only two Beta components; see the exercises.) For the four possible observations this gives

The three components correspond to the latent configurations “both founders from colony 1” (\(\mathbf n = (2,0)\)), “one from each” (\(\mathbf n = (1,1)\), two assignments) and “both from colony 2” (\(\mathbf n = (0, 2)\)), each giving a \(\text{Dir}(\mathbf n + \boldsymbol\alpha) = \text{Beta}\) component. Observing long features shifts belief towards colony 1, short features towards colony 2, and mixed features leave the prior mean \(1/2\) almost unchanged. With two alleles the posterior remains very broad: each observation carries little information, and precision comes only from many pups.


10.2.6 Gibbs sampling approach
The smart alternative to marginalising \(\mathbf Z\) is not to marginalise it, and to sample \(\mathbf Z\) jointly with \(\mathbf x\), exactly as for the Gaussian mixture of Chapter 8. Keeping the latent variables, \[P(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf Z) = \prod_{k=1}^N\gamma_{Z_k k}, \qquad P(\mathbf Z \mid \mathbf x) = \prod_{k=1}^N x_{Z_k} = \prod_{i=1}^P x_i^{m_i(\mathbf Z)}, \quad m_i(\mathbf Z) = \sum_k\delta(Z_k = i),\] so the joint posterior is \[P(\mathbf x, \mathbf Z \mid \mathbf y) = \frac{1}{P(\mathbf y)B(\boldsymbol\alpha)}\prod_{k=1}^N\gamma_{Z_kk}\ \prod_{i=1}^P x_i^{m_i(\mathbf Z) + \alpha_i - 1}.\] The full conditionals are standard:
Proportions. Only the last factor depends on \(\mathbf x\); normalising over the simplex, \[\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y, \mathbf Z \sim \text{Dir}\bigl(\boldsymbol\alpha + \mathbf m(\mathbf Z)\bigr):\] prior pseudo-counts plus the number of mothers currently assigned to each colony.
Origins. Only the factors \(\gamma_{Z_kk}\,x_{Z_k}\) depend on \(Z_k\), so \[P(Z_k = i \mid \mathbf y, \mathbf x, \mathbf Z_{-k}) = \frac{\gamma_{ik}\,x_i}{\sum_j\gamma_{jk}\,x_j}:\] Bayes’ theorem for “which colony did this mother come from?”, with prior \(\mathbf x\) and likelihood \(\gamma_{\cdot k}\). Given \(\mathbf x\), the \(Z_k\) are conditionally independent and can all be updated at once.

Repeat:

sample \(\mathbf x \sim \text{Dir}(\boldsymbol\alpha + \mathbf m(\mathbf Z))\);
for all \(k\), sample \(Z_k \sim \text{Cat}\bigl(\gamma_{\cdot k}\odot\mathbf x / \sum_j\gamma_{jk}x_j\bigr)\).


Each sweep costs \(O(NP)\) and requires no tuning. As a bonus, the samples of \(Z_k\) give the posterior probability that each pup’s mother came from each colony — an individual-level “assignment test”.

Remark (Data augmentation). The Gibbs sampler explores the joint space of \((\mathbf x, \mathbf Z)\), of dimension \(P - 1 + N\), which is larger than the space of \(\mathbf x\) alone. Yet it is easier to sample: the \(P^N\)-term sum is never computed; instead the chain visits the relevant assignments \(\mathbf i\) with frequency \(\propto\xi(\mathbf i)\). The marginal of \(\mathbf x\) in the samples is the exact mixture-of-Dirichlets posterior.

title: 10  A problem of high-dimensional inference
text:
10.3 Refined model
The model actually used by Gaggiotti et al. is richer in three ways: both parents contribute alleles, parents tend to mate within their own origin, and the proportions \(\mathbf x\) are linked to the geography of the old colonies.

10.3.1 Two parents and assortative mating
Let \(Z_{k,n}\) be the origin of parent \(n\) of pup \(k\). As before, \[P(Y_{k,l,n} = m \mid Z_{k,n} = i) = p_m^{(i,l)}, \qquad P(\mathbf Y_{k,n} = \mathbf y_{k,n} \mid Z_{k,n} = i) = \prod_{l}p^{(i,l)}_{y_{k,l,n}} .\] If the two parents’ origins were independent, \(P(Z_{k,1} = i, Z_{k,2} = j \mid \mathbf x) = x_ix_j\), and (assuming the maternal and paternal alleles are independent given the origins) \[P(\mathbf Y = \mathbf y \mid \mathbf x) = \prod_{k=1}^N\sum_{i,j=1}^P x_ix_j\prod_{l=1}^L p^{(i,l)}_{y_{k,l,1}}p^{(j,l)}_{y_{k,l,2}} .\] But founders mate preferentially with individuals of the same origin (assortative mating). Model this with a parameter \(w \in [0,1]\): with probability \(w\) an individual mates with someone of its own origin, with probability \(1 - w\) with a random founder: \[P(Z_{k,1} = i, Z_{k,2} = j \mid \mathbf x, w) = w\,\delta_{ij}\,x_i + (1 - w)\,x_ix_j .\] Defining \(\gamma_{ijk} = \prod_l p^{(i,l)}_{y_{k,l,1}}p^{(j,l)}_{y_{k,l,2}}\), the likelihood becomes \[P(\mathbf Y = \mathbf y \mid \mathbf x, w) = \prod_{k=1}^N\Bigl[w\sum_{i=1}^P x_i\,\gamma_{iik} + (1 - w)\sum_{i,j=1}^P x_ix_j\,\gamma_{ijk}\Bigr].\] For \(w = 0\) we recover random mating; for \(w = 1\) both parents always share an origin.


10.3.2 Geography in the prior
Gaggiotti et al. further assume that the expected contribution of each old colony decays exponentially with its (known) distance \(\delta_i\) from the new colony and grows with its (known) productivity \(\pi_i\): \[\mathbb E[x_i] \propto \bigl((1 - S) + S\pi_i\bigr)e^{-R\delta_i},\] with an unknown distance decay \(R\) and productivity weight \(S\). This is built into the Dirichlet prior: \[\mathbf x \mid R, S, \alpha_0 \sim \text{Dir}(\boldsymbol\alpha), \qquad \alpha_i = \alpha_0\,\frac{\bigl((1 - S) + S\pi_i\bigr)e^{-R\delta_i}}{c}, \quad c = \sum_{i=1}^P\bigl((1 - S) + S\pi_i\bigr)e^{-R\delta_i},\] so that \(\mathbb E[x_i] = \alpha_i/\alpha_0\) has the desired form and \(\alpha_0\) controls how tightly \(\mathbf x\) follows it. The hyperparameters get uniform priors: \[\alpha_0 \sim \mathcal U(P, 100), \quad w \sim \mathcal U(0, 1), \quad S \sim \mathcal U(0, 1), \quad R \sim \mathcal U(0, 5).\] This is a hierarchical model: data ← \((\mathbf x, w)\) ← \((R, S, \alpha_0)\). The posterior is \[P(\mathbf x, w, \alpha_0, R, S \mid \mathbf y) \propto P(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf x, w)\,\text{Dir}(\boldsymbol\alpha(R, S, \alpha_0); \mathbf x)\,P(w)P(R)P(S)P(\alpha_0).\] Note that \(B(\boldsymbol\alpha)\) now depends on the hyperparameters and does not cancel in Metropolis ratios for \(R, S, \alpha_0\).
The posterior on \(R\) and \(S\) is the scientifically interesting output: do seals found colonies preferentially near their origin, and do productive colonies send more migrants?


10.3.3 Metropolis approach
Update the parameters one at a time (or in blocks) with bounded random-walk moves, \(u \sim \mathcal U(-\epsilon, \epsilon)\): \[\mathbf x \to \frac{b(\mathbf x + \mathbf u)}{\sum_i b(x_i + u_i)}, \quad w \to b_{0,1}(w + u), \quad S \to b_{0,1}(S + u), \quad R \to b_{0,5}(R + u), \quad \alpha_0 \to b_{P,100}(\alpha_0 + u),\] each accepted with the Metropolis ratio of the unnormalised posterior. (The remark on symmetry of clipped proposals applies here too.)


10.3.4 Gibbs sampling with latent variables
As in the basic model, we can keep the parental origins \(Z_{k,1}, Z_{k,2}\) as latent variables. To deal with the mixture in the mating model, introduce one more latent variable per pup, \[Q_k \in \{0, 1\}: \quad Q_k = 1 \text{ if the parents mated assortatively}, \quad P(Q_k = 1 \mid w) = w,\] with \[P(Z_{k,1}, Z_{k,2} \mid Q_k = 1, \mathbf x) = \delta_{Z_{k,1}Z_{k,2}}\,x_{Z_{k,1}}, \qquad P(Z_{k,1}, Z_{k,2} \mid Q_k = 0, \mathbf x) = x_{Z_{k,1}}x_{Z_{k,2}} .\] Summing over \(Q_k\) reproduces \(w\delta_{ij}x_i + (1-w)x_ix_j\). With a Beta prior \(w \sim \text{Beta}(\beta_1, \beta_2)\) (uniform for \(\beta_1 = \beta_2 = 1\)), the augmented posterior is \[P(\mathbf x, w, \mathbf Z, \mathbf Q \mid \mathbf y) \propto \prod_{k=1}^N\gamma_{Z_{k,1}Z_{k,2}k}\ \prod_{i=1}^P x_i^{m_i(\mathbf Z, \mathbf Q) + \alpha_i - 1}\ w^{n_q + \beta_1 - 1}(1 - w)^{N - n_q + \beta_2 - 1}\ \prod_{k : Q_k = 1}\delta_{Z_{k,1}Z_{k,2}},\] where \(n_q = \sum_k\delta(Q_k = 1)\) counts assortative matings and \[m_i(\mathbf Z, \mathbf Q) = \sum_{k=1}^N\Bigl[\delta(Q_k = 1)\,\delta(Z_{k,1} = i) + \delta(Q_k = 0)\bigl(\delta(Z_{k,1} = i) + \delta(Z_{k,2} = i)\bigr)\Bigr]\] counts the independent draws from \(\mathbf x\) that landed on colony \(i\) (an assortative pair counts once, since only one origin was drawn). The full conditionals:

Proportions: \(\mathbf x \mid \ldots \sim \text{Dir}\bigl(\boldsymbol\alpha + \mathbf m(\mathbf Z, \mathbf Q)\bigr)\).
Mating parameter: \(w \mid \ldots \sim \text{Beta}(\beta_1 + n_q,\ \beta_2 + N - n_q)\).
Parental origins, jointly for each pup: \[P(Z_{k,1} = i, Z_{k,2} = j \mid Q_k = 1, \ldots) = \frac{\gamma_{iik}\,x_i\,\delta_{ij}}{\sum_{i'}\gamma_{i'i'k}\,x_{i'}}, \qquad P(Z_{k,1} = i, Z_{k,2} = j \mid Q_k = 0, \ldots) = \frac{\gamma_{ijk}\,x_ix_j}{\sum_{i',j'}\gamma_{i'j'k}\,x_{i'}x_{j'}} .\]
Mating type, given the origins: \[P(Q_k = 1 \mid \ldots) = \frac{w\,\delta_{Z_{k,1}Z_{k,2}}\,x_{Z_{k,1}}}{w\,\delta_{Z_{k,1}Z_{k,2}}\,x_{Z_{k,1}} + (1 - w)\,x_{Z_{k,1}}x_{Z_{k,2}}}, \qquad P(Q_k = 0 \mid \ldots) = 1 - P(Q_k = 1 \mid \ldots).\] (If the parents have different origins, \(Q_k = 0\) with certainty.)


Remark (A mixing caveat). Updating \(Q_k\) given \(\mathbf Z_k\) and then \(\mathbf Z_k\) given \(Q_k\) can mix slowly: when \(Q_k = 1\) the origins are forced equal, and then \(Q_k\) can only switch if \(\mathbf Z_k\) already has equal origins. Sampling \((Q_k, Z_{k,1}, Z_{k,2})\) jointly — from the \(P + P^2\) possible configurations, with weights \(w\gamma_{iik}x_i\) and \((1-w)\gamma_{ijk}x_ix_j\) — avoids the problem at the same cost.

For the hyperparameters \(R, S, \alpha_0\) the conditionals are not standard (they enter through \(\boldsymbol\alpha\) and \(B(\boldsymbol\alpha)\)), so we use Metropolis steps for them. The result is a Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler:

Repeat:

sample \(\mathbf x \sim \text{Dir}\bigl(\boldsymbol\alpha(R, S, \alpha_0) + \mathbf m(\mathbf Z, \mathbf Q)\bigr)\);
sample \(w \sim \text{Beta}(\beta_1 + n_q, \beta_2 + N - n_q)\);
for all \(k\), sample \((Z_{k,1}, Z_{k,2})\) from their conditional;
for all \(k\), sample \(Q_k\) from its conditional;
Metropolis updates \(S \to b_{0,1}(S + u)\), \(R \to b_{0,5}(R + u)\), \(\alpha_0 \to b_{P,100}(\alpha_0 + u)\), each targeting \(\text{Dir}(\boldsymbol\alpha(R, S, \alpha_0); \mathbf x)\,P(R)P(S)P(\alpha_0)\).

title: 10  A problem of high-dimensional inference
text:
10.4 Lessons

Latent variables make likelihoods tractable. Writing down the generative story (“each pup has a mother from some colony”) gives the likelihood; keeping the story’s hidden variables gives a sampler.
Exact marginalisation is exponential. The analytic posterior is a mixture over \(P^N\) assignments; MCMC replaces the sum by a random walk through the relevant terms.
Conjugacy turns modelling choices into algorithms. Dirichlet priors for proportions and Beta priors for probabilities make every latent-variable conditional a standard distribution.
Hierarchies encode scientific hypotheses. Distance decay and productivity enter as hyperparameters whose posterior answers the scientific question; their non-conjugate updates are handled by Metropolis within Gibbs.

title: 10  A problem of high-dimensional inference
text:
10.5 Exercises

In the simple example, verify the evidence \(97/432\) for the observation (long, long) and the mixture weights \(64/97, 24/97, 9/97\). Then compute the posterior variance of \(x_1\).


Solution. \(\tfrac49\cdot\tfrac13 = \tfrac{4}{27} = \tfrac{64}{432}\), \(\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac16 = \tfrac1{18} = \tfrac{24}{432}\), \(\tfrac1{16}\cdot\tfrac13 = \tfrac1{48} = \tfrac{9}{432}\); total \(97/432\), and the weights are the three terms divided by the total. For the variance use \(\mathbb E[x_1^2] = \sum_c w_c\,\mathbb E_c[x_1^2]\) with \(\mathbb E[x^2] = a(a+1)/((a+b)(a+b+1))\): \(\text{Beta}(3,1) \to 3\cdot4/(4\cdot5) = 0.6\), \(\text{Beta}(2,2) \to 2\cdot3/(4\cdot5) = 0.3\), \(\text{Beta}(1,3) \to 2/20 = 0.1\). \(\mathbb E[x_1^2] = (64\cdot0.6 + 24\cdot0.3 + 9\cdot0.1)/97 = 46.5/97 \approx 0.479\); \(\operatorname{Var} = 0.479 - 0.642^2 \approx 0.067\) (s.d. \(\approx 0.26\)) — barely narrower than the uniform prior’s \(0.289\).


Redo the simple example for a single pup whose two loci share the same mother, \(P(y_1, y_2 \mid \mathbf x) = \sum_i x_i\,p^{(i,1)}_{y_1}p^{(i,2)}_{y_2}\), for the observation (long, long).


Solution. \(P = \tfrac49 x_1 + \tfrac1{16}x_2\). With a uniform prior, \(\int x_1 = \int x_2 = \tfrac12\), so the evidence is \(\tfrac29 + \tfrac1{32} = \tfrac{73}{288}\) and the posterior is \(\tfrac{64}{73}\text{Beta}(2,1) + \tfrac{9}{73}\text{Beta}(1,2)\), with mean \(\tfrac{64}{73}\cdot\tfrac23 + \tfrac9{73}\cdot\tfrac13 \approx 0.626\). The two components correspond to the two values of the single latent variable \(Z_1\).


Derive the full conditional \(P(Z_k = i \mid \mathbf y, \mathbf x, \mathbf Z_{-k}) \propto \gamma_{ik}x_i\) of the basic model by dividing the joint posterior by its sum over \(Z_k\).


Solution. In \(P(\mathbf x, \mathbf Z \mid \mathbf y) \propto \prod_{k'}\gamma_{Z_{k'}k'}x_{Z_{k'}}\cdot\prod_p x_p^{\alpha_p - 1}\), all factors with \(k' \neq k\) and the prior are common to numerator and denominator and cancel, leaving \(\gamma_{Z_kk}x_{Z_k}/\sum_i\gamma_{ik}x_i\).


Show that summing the augmented model over \(Q_k\) reproduces \(P(Z_{k,1} = i, Z_{k,2} = j \mid \mathbf x, w) = w\delta_{ij}x_i + (1-w)x_ix_j\), and that the likelihood reduces to the basic-model form (with both alleles from the same colony) when \(w = 1\).


Solution. \(\sum_{q}P(Q_k = q \mid w)P(i, j \mid q, \mathbf x) = w\,\delta_{ij}x_i + (1 - w)x_ix_j\). For \(w = 1\), \(P(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf x) = \prod_k\sum_i x_i\gamma_{iik}\) with \(\gamma_{iik} = \prod_l p^{(i,l)}_{y_{k,l,1}}p^{(i,l)}_{y_{k,l,2}}\): each pup is a single draw from a colony, carrying \(2L\) alleles from it — the basic model with twice as many loci.


Estimate the cost per sweep of the refined Gibbs sampler, and compare with the size of the analytic sum.


Solution. Precompute \(\gamma_{ijk}\): \(O(NP^2L)\) once. Per sweep: the \((Z_{k,1}, Z_{k,2})\) updates cost \(O(NP^2)\), the rest \(O(N + P)\). With \(N = 150\), \(P = 7\) this is \(\sim 10^4\) operations per sweep, against \(\sim (P^2)^N \approx 10^{254}\) terms in the exact marginalisation.

title: 10  A problem of high-dimensional inference
text:
10.6 Callouts






This chapter is a template for applied Bayesian work: (1) write the generative story, (2) translate it into a likelihood with latent variables, (3) choose (conjugate) priors, encoding scientific hypotheses in hyperparameters, (4) sample with Gibbs where conditionals are standard and Metropolis elsewhere.









Always test a sampler on simulated data with known \(\mathbf x\), \(w\), \(R\), \(S\) before running it on real data: if the posterior does not concentrate around the truth as \(N\) grows, there is a bug or an identifiability problem.









Products of \(N \cdot L\) probabilities underflow double precision. Work with \(\log\gamma_{ik}\) and use the log-sum-exp trick when normalising categorical conditionals: \(\log\sum_i e^{a_i} = a_{\max} + \log\sum_i e^{a_i - a_{\max}}\).
