title: 11  Variational Bayes
text:
11.1 The evidence lower bound
MCMC is asymptotically exact but can be slow, and it is hard to know when it has converged. Variational Bayes (VB) trades exactness for speed: it approximates the posterior by the closest member of a tractable family of distributions, turning inference into optimisation. The measure of closeness is — once again — the KL divergence of Chapter 2, and the objective is a lower bound on the log-evidence. This chapter derives the variational principle, the mean-field update equations, works out two examples in full (a Gaussian, and the mixture model of Chapter 8), and ends with the variational autoencoder, where the same bound trains deep generative models.
Let \(\mathbf y\) be the data and \(\mathbf z\) all unknowns (parameters and latent variables). For any distribution \(q(\mathbf z)\), \[\begin{aligned}
\log f(\mathbf y) &= \int d\mathbf z\,q(\mathbf z)\log f(\mathbf y) = \int d\mathbf z\,q(\mathbf z)\Bigl[\log\frac{f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y)}{q(\mathbf z)} + \log\frac{q(\mathbf z)\,f(\mathbf y)}{f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y)}\Bigr] \\
&= \underbrace{\int d\mathbf z\,q(\mathbf z)\log\frac{f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y)}{q(\mathbf z)}}_{\mathcal L(q)} + \underbrace{\int d\mathbf z\,q(\mathbf z)\log\frac{q(\mathbf z)}{f(\mathbf z \mid \mathbf y)}}_{D_{KL}(q \,\|\, f(\cdot \mid \mathbf y))},
\end{aligned}\] using \(f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y)/f(\mathbf y) = f(\mathbf z \mid \mathbf y)\).
The left-hand side does not depend on \(q\), so maximising the ELBO over \(q\) is the same as minimising \(D_{KL}(q\|f(\cdot\mid\mathbf y))\): we force \(q\) to be as close as possible to the posterior. Crucially, \(\mathcal L\) involves only the joint \(f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y)\) (likelihood × prior), never the intractable evidence. The VB recipe is:
Two other readings of the ELBO are useful:

title: 11  Variational Bayes
text:
\[\log f(\mathbf y) = \mathcal L(q) + D_{KL}\bigl(q(\mathbf z)\,\|\,f(\mathbf z \mid \mathbf y)\bigr), \qquad \mathcal L(q) = \mathbb E_q[\log f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y)] - \mathbb E_q[\log q(\mathbf z)].\] Since \(D_{KL} \geq 0\), \(\mathcal L(q) \leq \log f(\mathbf y)\) for every \(q\), with equality iff \(q\) is the exact posterior.



choose a family \(\mathcal Q\) of tractable distributions, and find \(q^* = \arg\max_{q\in\mathcal Q}\mathcal L(q)\).



\(\mathcal L(q) = \mathbb E_q[\log f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y)] + H[q]\): an “energy” term rewarding \(q\) for sitting where the joint is large, plus an entropy term rewarding it for spreading out — exactly a (negative) variational free energy of statistical physics, with \(\log f(\mathbf y)\) playing the role of \(-F = \log Z\).
\(\mathcal L(q) = \mathbb E_q[\log f(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf z)] - D_{KL}(q(\mathbf z)\,\|\,f_{\text{prior}}(\mathbf z))\): data fit minus a penalty for departing from the prior (used for the VAE below).


Remark (Which KL?). VB minimises \(D(q\|p)\), the “reverse” KL. Since \(D(q\|p) = \int q\log(q/p)\), it is huge wherever \(q > 0\) but \(p \approx 0\): \(q\) is pushed to avoid regions where the posterior is small. The result is mode-seeking and typically under-dispersed: for a multimodal posterior, \(q\) locks onto one mode; for a correlated posterior, \(q\) is too narrow. The “forward” KL \(D(p\|q)\) would be mass-covering instead, but it needs expectations under \(p\) — which is what we cannot compute.

title: 11  Variational Bayes
text:
11.2 The mean-field approximation
The most common choice is to assume that \(q\) factorises over groups of variables, \[q(\mathbf z) = \prod_i q_i(\mathbf z_i),\] with no assumption on the form of each factor. This is the mean-field approximation, named after the physics approximation in which each spin feels only the average field of the others.

11.2.1 Derivation of the update
Maximise \(\mathcal L\) over one factor \(q_j\), keeping the others fixed. Separating the terms that involve \(q_j\), \[\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L(q) &= \int d\mathbf z\,\prod_i q_i(\mathbf z_i)\Bigl[\log f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y) - \sum_i\log q_i(\mathbf z_i)\Bigr] \\
&= \int d\mathbf z_j\,q_j(\mathbf z_j)\Bigl[\int\prod_{i\neq j}d\mathbf z_i\,q_i(\mathbf z_i)\log f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y)\Bigr] - \int d\mathbf z_j\,q_j\log q_j + \text{const} \\
&= \int d\mathbf z_j\,q_j(\mathbf z_j)\log\tilde f(\mathbf z_j, \mathbf y) - \int d\mathbf z_j\,q_j(\mathbf z_j)\log q_j(\mathbf z_j) + \text{const},
\end{aligned}\] where “const” does not depend on \(q_j\) and we defined the distribution \(\tilde f\) by \[\log\tilde f(\mathbf z_j, \mathbf y) = \mathbb E_{i\neq j}[\log f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y)] + \text{const},\] the log-joint averaged over all other factors. Then \[\mathcal L(q) = -D_{KL}\bigl(q_j\,\|\,\tilde f\bigr) + \text{const},\] which is maximised by \(q_j = \tilde f\).

For fixed \(q_i\), \(i \neq j\), the optimal factor is \[\log q_j^*(\mathbf z_j) = \mathbb E_{i\neq j}\bigl[\log f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y)\bigr] + \text{const}, \qquad q_j^*(\mathbf z_j) = \frac{\exp\bigl(\mathbb E_{i\neq j}[\log f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y)]\bigr)}{\int d\mathbf z_j\exp\bigl(\mathbb E_{i\neq j}[\log f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y)]\bigr)} .\]

Recipe: write the log of the joint over all hidden and observed variables, keep only the terms involving \(\mathbf z_j\), take the expectation over all other factors, and recognise the resulting functional form (normalisation is usually read off at the end).
The equations for the different \(j\) are coupled — each right-hand side depends on the other factors — so they are solved iteratively: initialise all factors and cycle through them, updating each in turn (coordinate-ascent variational inference, CAVI). Each update maximises \(\mathcal L\) with respect to one factor (\(\mathcal L\) is concave in each \(q_j\) separately), so \(\mathcal L\) increases monotonically and the iteration converges — to a local maximum, which may depend on the initialisation.

Remark (VB vs Gibbs). Compare with the Gibbs sampler of Chapter 8. Gibbs updates \(\mathbf z_j\) by drawing from \(f(\mathbf z_j \mid \mathbf z_{-j}, \mathbf y) \propto \exp\log f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y)\) evaluated at the current sample of the others. Mean-field VB updates the distribution \(q_j \propto \exp\mathbb E_{-j}\log f(\mathbf z, \mathbf y)\) using the average over the others. With conjugate models the two have the same functional forms; VB replaces random draws by expectations.



11.2.2 A correlated Gaussian: the variance underestimate

Let the target be \(f(\mathbf z) = \mathcal N(\mathbf z; \boldsymbol\mu, \Lambda^{-1})\) with precision matrix \(\Lambda\), and \(q = q_1(z_1)q_2(z_2)\). Then \[\log q_1^*(z_1) = \mathbb E_{z_2}\Bigl[-\tfrac12\Lambda_{11}(z_1 - \mu_1)^2 - \Lambda_{12}(z_1 - \mu_1)(z_2 - \mu_2)\Bigr] + \text{const},\] which is quadratic in \(z_1\), so \(q_1^*\) is Gaussian — this was derived, not assumed: \[q_1^* = \mathcal N\Bigl(m_1,\ \Lambda_{11}^{-1}\Bigr), \qquad m_1 = \mu_1 - \Lambda_{11}^{-1}\Lambda_{12}(m_2 - \mu_2),\] and symmetrically for \(q_2\). The self-consistent solution is \(m_1 = \mu_1\), \(m_2 = \mu_2\): the means are exact. But the variances are \(1/\Lambda_{11}\), the conditional variances, smaller than the true marginal variances \((\Lambda^{-1})_{11}\). For unit variances and correlation \(\rho\), \(q\) has variance \(1 - \rho^2\) against the true \(1\): for \(\rho = 0.9\), the mean-field standard deviation is \(0.44\) instead of \(1\). Mean field “fits inside” the elongated posterior ellipse.

title: 11  Variational Bayes
section: 11.3 Example: one Gaussian with unknown mean and precision
text:
11.3 Example: one Gaussian with unknown mean and precision
Data \(x_i \sim \mathcal N(\mu, \tau^{-1})\), \(i = 1..n\), with \(\tau\) the precision. The likelihood is \[f(\mathbf x \mid \mu, \tau) = \Bigl(\frac{\tau}{2\pi}\Bigr)^{n/2}\exp\Bigl[-\frac\tau2\sum_i(x_i - \mu)^2\Bigr].\] The conjugate prior is normal–gamma: \[\tau \sim \text{Gamma}(a_0, b_0): f(\tau) = \frac{b_0^{a_0}}{\Gamma(a_0)}\tau^{a_0 - 1}e^{-b_0\tau}, \qquad \mu \mid \tau \sim \mathcal N\bigl(\mu_0, (\lambda_0\tau)^{-1}\bigr): f(\mu \mid \tau) = \Bigl(\frac{\lambda_0\tau}{2\pi}\Bigr)^{1/2}e^{-\frac{\lambda_0\tau}{2}(\mu - \mu_0)^2}.\] The exact posterior is again normal–gamma — but not factorised (\(\mu\) and \(\tau\) are dependent). We approximate it with \(q(\mu, \tau) = q_\mu(\mu)q_\tau(\tau)\).
Factor for \(\mu\). Keeping the terms with \(\mu\), \[\log q_\mu^*(\mu) = \mathbb E_\tau\Bigl[-\frac\tau2\sum_i(x_i - \mu)^2 - \frac{\lambda_0\tau}{2}(\mu - \mu_0)^2\Bigr] + \text{const} = -\frac{\mathbb E[\tau]}{2}\Bigl[\sum_i(x_i - \mu)^2 + \lambda_0(\mu - \mu_0)^2\Bigr] + \text{const}.\] Completing the square, \(q_\mu^* = \mathcal N(\mu', \lambda'^{-1})\) with \[\mu' = \frac{\lambda_0\mu_0 + \sum_i x_i}{\lambda_0 + n} = \frac{\lambda_0\mu_0 + n\bar x}{\lambda_0 + n}, \qquad \lambda' = (\lambda_0 + n)\,\mathbb E[\tau].\]
Factor for \(\tau\). Keeping the terms with \(\tau\) (note \(n/2\) from the likelihood, \(1/2\) from the prior on \(\mu\), \(a_0 - 1\) from the prior on \(\tau\)), \[\log q_\tau^*(\tau) = \Bigl(a_0 - 1 + \frac{n + 1}{2}\Bigr)\log\tau - \tau\Bigl(b_0 + \frac12\mathbb E_\mu\Bigl[\sum_i(x_i - \mu)^2 + \lambda_0(\mu - \mu_0)^2\Bigr]\Bigr) + \text{const},\] so \(q_\tau^* = \text{Gamma}(a', b')\) with \[a' = a_0 + \frac{n + 1}{2}, \qquad b' = b_0 + \frac12\mathbb E_\mu\Bigl[\sum_i(x_i - \mu)^2 + \lambda_0(\mu - \mu_0)^2\Bigr].\] The required moments under \(q_\mu = \mathcal N(\mu', \lambda'^{-1})\) are \(\mathbb E[\mu] = \mu'\) and \(\mathbb E[\mu^2] = \mu'^2 + \lambda'^{-1}\), giving \[\mathbb E_\mu\Bigl[\sum_i(x_i - \mu)^2 + \lambda_0(\mu - \mu_0)^2\Bigr] = \sum_i(x_i - \mu')^2 + \lambda_0(\mu' - \mu_0)^2 + \frac{n + \lambda_0}{\lambda'} ,\] and \(\mathbb E[\tau] = a'/b'\) under the Gamma.
Iteration. \(\mu'\) and \(a'\) do not change; only \(\lambda'\) and \(b'\) are coupled. Initialise \(\mathbb E[\tau]\), then alternate \[\lambda' = (\lambda_0 + n)\frac{a'}{b'}, \qquad b' = b_0 + \frac12\Bigl[\sum_i(x_i - \mu')^2 + \lambda_0(\mu' - \mu_0)^2\Bigr] + \frac{1}{2}\frac{n + \lambda_0}{\lambda'} .\]

With \(a_0 = b_0 = \lambda_0 = 0\): \(\mu' = \bar x\), \(a' = (n + 1)/2\). Substituting \(\lambda' = n a'/b'\) into the \(b'\) equation, \(b' = \tfrac12 n s^2 + \tfrac12 b'/a'\) with \(s^2 = \frac1n\sum(x_i - \bar x)^2\), whose fixed point is \(b' = \frac{n s^2 a'}{2a' - 1} = \frac{(n + 1)s^2}{2}\). Then \(\mathbb E[\tau] = a'/b' = 1/s^2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}_q[\mu] = 1/\lambda' = s^2/n\): the familiar maximum-likelihood variance estimate and the standard error of the mean. The iteration converges in a handful of steps from any starting \(\mathbb E[\tau]\), since the map \(b' \mapsto \tfrac12ns^2 + b'/(2a')\) is a contraction with factor \(1/(n + 1)\).

title: 11  Variational Bayes
text:
11.4 Example: mixture distributions
Return to the Gaussian mixture of Chapter 8 (known \(\sigma\), \(K\) components) with latent labels \(\mathbf Z\), weights \(\mathbf p \sim \text{Dir}(\boldsymbol\gamma)\) and means \(\mu_k \sim \mathcal N(\mu_{0k}, \sigma_{0k}^2)\). The joint is \[f(\mathbf x, \mathbf Z, \mathbf p, \boldsymbol\mu) = f(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf Z, \boldsymbol\mu)\,f(\mathbf Z \mid \mathbf p)\,f(\mathbf p)\,f(\boldsymbol\mu).\] Assume only that the labels decouple from the parameters, \[q(\mathbf Z, \mathbf p, \boldsymbol\mu) = q(\mathbf Z)\,q(\mathbf p, \boldsymbol\mu),\] and write \(r_{ik} \equiv q(Z_i = k) = \mathbb E_q[\chi(Z_i = k)]\) (the responsibilities).
Labels. Since \(\log f(\mathbf Z \mid \mathbf p) = \sum_{i,k}\chi(Z_i = k)\log p_k\) and \(\log f(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf Z, \boldsymbol\mu) = -\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i,k}\chi(Z_i = k)(x_i - \mu_k)^2 + \text{const}\), \[\log q^*(\mathbf Z) = \sum_{i,k}\chi(Z_i = k)\Bigl[\mathbb E[\log p_k] - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\mathbb E[(x_i - \mu_k)^2]\Bigr] + \text{const}.\] This factorises over points: \(q^*(\mathbf Z) = \prod_i\prod_k r_{ik}^{\chi(Z_i = k)}\) with \[r_{ik} = \frac{\rho_{ik}}{\sum_{k'}\rho_{ik'}}, \qquad \rho_{ik} = \exp\Bigl(\mathbb E[\log p_k] - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\mathbb E[(x_i - \mu_k)^2]\Bigr).\]
Parameters. Taking the expectation over \(\mathbf Z\) (only \(\mathbb E[\chi(Z_i = k)] = r_{ik}\) enters, by linearity), \[\log q^*(\mathbf p, \boldsymbol\mu) = \underbrace{\sum_k\Bigl(\gamma_k - 1 + \sum_i r_{ik}\Bigr)\log p_k}_{\text{depends on } \mathbf p} \ \underbrace{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i,k}r_{ik}(x_i - \mu_k)^2 - \sum_k\frac{(\mu_k - \mu_{0k})^2}{2\sigma_{0k}^2}}_{\text{depends on } \boldsymbol\mu} + \text{const}.\] The right-hand side is a sum of a term in \(\mathbf p\) and a term in \(\boldsymbol\mu\), so \(q^*(\mathbf p, \boldsymbol\mu) = q^*(\mathbf p)q^*(\boldsymbol\mu)\) factorises automatically — a result of the calculation, not an assumption. Reading off the forms, with \(N_k = \sum_i r_{ik}\) the expected number of points in cluster \(k\): \[q^*(\mathbf p) = \text{Dir}(\boldsymbol\gamma'), \quad \gamma'_k = \gamma_k + N_k; \qquad q^*(\mu_k) = \mathcal N(\mu'_k, \sigma'^2_k),\quad \mu'_k = \frac{\mu_{0k}/\sigma_{0k}^2 + \sum_i r_{ik}x_i/\sigma^2}{1/\sigma_{0k}^2 + N_k/\sigma^2},\quad \sigma'^2_k = \Bigl(\frac{1}{\sigma_{0k}^2} + \frac{N_k}{\sigma^2}\Bigr)^{-1}.\] These are exactly the Gibbs conditionals of Chapter 8 with hard counts replaced by soft counts \(N_k = \sum_i r_{ik}\).
Moments needed for \(r_{ik}\). \[\mathbb E[(x_i - \mu_k)^2] = (x_i - \mu'_k)^2 + \sigma'^2_k, \qquad \mathbb E[\log p_k] = \psi(\gamma'_k) - \psi\Bigl(\sum_j\gamma'_j\Bigr),\] where \(\psi = \Gamma'/\Gamma\) is the digamma function (the second identity is a standard property of the Dirichlet). Hence \[\rho_{ik} = \exp\Bigl[\psi(\gamma'_k) - \psi\Bigl(\sum_j\gamma'_j\Bigr) - \frac{(x_i - \mu'_k)^2}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{\sigma'^2_k}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr].\]

Iterate until \(\mathcal L\) stops increasing:

(E-like step) with \(\mu'_k, \sigma'_k, \gamma'_k\) fixed, compute \(\rho_{ik}\) and the responsibilities \(r_{ik} = \rho_{ik}/\sum_{k'}\rho_{ik'}\);
(M-like step) with \(r_{ik}\) fixed, compute \(N_k = \sum_i r_{ik}\) and \(\sum_i r_{ik}x_i\), then update \(\gamma'_k\), \(\mu'_k\), \(\sigma'_k\).


This has the structure of the EM algorithm and of soft K-means: the responsibilities are a softmax of “log-prior weight minus squared distance”, corrected by the posterior uncertainty of the parameters (\(\sigma'^2_k\) and the digamma terms). A practical bonus: with a small Dirichlet concentration \(\gamma_k < 1\), the VB solution drives the weights of superfluous components to zero, effectively selecting the number of clusters — something maximum-likelihood EM cannot do.

title: 11  Variational Bayes
text:
11.5 The variational autoencoder
Mean field is the most common choice, but VB only requires that \(q\) belong to a tractable family. Let the family be parametrised by \(\boldsymbol\theta\): \(q = q(\mathbf z \mid \boldsymbol\theta)\). Writing the joint as likelihood × prior, \[\mathcal L(q) = \int d\mathbf z\,q(\mathbf z)\log\frac{f(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf z)f_{\text{prior}}(\mathbf z)}{q(\mathbf z)} = -D_{KL}\bigl(q(\mathbf z)\,\|\,f_{\text{prior}}(\mathbf z)\bigr) + \mathbb E_{\mathbf z\sim q}\bigl[\log f(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf z)\bigr].\] Two contributions compete:

the prior term \(-D_{KL}(q\|f_{\text{prior}})\) keeps \(q\) from departing too far from the prior;
the data term \(\mathbb E_q\log f(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf z)\) pushes \(q\) to concentrate on values of \(\mathbf z\) that explain the data well.

The best approximation is \(q^* = \arg\max_{\boldsymbol\theta}\mathcal L(q(\cdot\mid\boldsymbol\theta))\), and \(\log f(\mathbf y) \geq \mathcal L(q^*)\).

11.5.1 Learning the likelihood too
Now suppose the data and the prior are given, but the likelihood is only known to belong to a family \(f(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf z, \boldsymbol\phi)\). A natural way to choose \(\boldsymbol\phi\) is to maximise the evidence \(\log f(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol\phi)\) (empirical Bayes / maximum marginal likelihood). The evidence is intractable, but the ELBO bounds it, so we maximise the bound jointly: \[\log f(\mathbf y) \geq \max_{\boldsymbol\theta, \boldsymbol\phi}\Bigl[-D_{KL}\bigl(q(\mathbf z\mid\boldsymbol\theta)\,\|\,f_{\text{prior}}(\mathbf z)\bigr) + \mathbb E_{\mathbf z\sim q}\log f(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf z, \boldsymbol\phi)\Bigr].\] Given only the prior and the data, this finds a self-consistent generative model of the data within a class of models, together with an approximate posterior.


11.5.2 Encoder and decoder
Take one latent vector \(\mathbf z_i \in \mathbb R^d\) per data point \(\mathbf y_i \in \mathbb R^D\), with \(d < D\): a low-dimensional representation of high-dimensional data. A simple and typical choice:

prior: \(f_{\text{prior}}(\mathbf z) = \mathcal N(\mathbf 0, I)\);
decoder (likelihood): \(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf z \sim \mathcal N(\mathbf d_{\boldsymbol\phi}(\mathbf z), c\,I)\) — the data point is Gaussian around a nonlinear function of its latent code;
encoder (variational posterior): \(\mathbf z \mid \mathbf y \sim q = \mathcal N\bigl(\mathbf e_{1,\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf y), \operatorname{diag}\,\mathbf e_{2,\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf y)\bigr)\) — mean and variances are functions of the data. Using one shared function of \(\mathbf y\) instead of separate parameters for each \(q(\mathbf z_i)\) is called amortised inference.

(Unless \(\mathbf d_{\boldsymbol\phi}\) is linear, the true posterior is not Gaussian; the encoder gives the best Gaussian approximation.) The KL between Gaussians is available in closed form, \[D_{KL}\bigl(\mathcal N(\mathbf m, \Sigma)\,\|\,\mathcal N(\mathbf 0, I)\bigr) = \frac12\Bigl(\mathbf m^\top\mathbf m + \operatorname{Tr}\Sigma - d - \log\det\Sigma\Bigr),\] and the data term is a reconstruction error, so (per data point, up to constants) \[-\mathcal L = \underbrace{\frac12\Bigl(\|\mathbf e_1(\mathbf y)\|^2 + \sum_j e_{2j}(\mathbf y) - d - \sum_j\log e_{2j}(\mathbf y)\Bigr)}_{\text{regulariser}} + \underbrace{\mathbb E_{\mathbf z\sim q}\frac{\|\mathbf y - \mathbf d_{\boldsymbol\phi}(\mathbf z)\|^2}{2c}}_{\text{reconstruction}} .\] \(q\) acts as a probabilistic encoder (each \(\mathbf y\) maps to a distribution over codes centred at \(\mathbf e_1(\mathbf y)\)), and \(f(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf z)\) as a probabilistic decoder. Implementing \(\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \mathbf d\) as deep neural networks, \(\boldsymbol\theta\) and \(\boldsymbol\phi\) are their weights and biases, and the loss is minimised by stochastic gradient descent with back-propagation. Without the regulariser this would be an ordinary autoencoder; the KL term forces the codes to fill the prior \(\mathcal N(0, I)\), so that sampling \(\mathbf z \sim \mathcal N(0, I)\) and decoding produces new, realistic data.


11.5.3 The reparametrisation trick
The reconstruction term is an expectation over \(\mathbf z \sim q(\cdot\mid\boldsymbol\theta)\), estimated with samples \(\mathbf z_k(\boldsymbol\theta)\): \[\mathbb E_{\mathbf z\sim q}\frac{\|\mathbf y - \mathbf d_{\boldsymbol\phi}(\mathbf z)\|^2}{2c} \approx \frac1M\sum_{k=1}^M\frac{\|\mathbf y - \mathbf d_{\boldsymbol\phi}(\mathbf z_k)\|^2}{2c}.\] But a random draw is not a differentiable function of \(\boldsymbol\theta\), so back-propagation cannot pass through it. The fix is to move the randomness outside the parameters: \[\mathbf z = \mathbf e_{1,\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf y) + \sqrt{\mathbf e_{2,\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf y)}\odot\boldsymbol\eta, \qquad \boldsymbol\eta \sim \mathcal N(\mathbf 0, I).\] Sample \(\boldsymbol\eta_k\) once, independently of \(\boldsymbol\theta\); then \[\mathbb E_{\mathbf z\sim q}\frac{\|\mathbf y - \mathbf d_{\boldsymbol\phi}(\mathbf z)\|^2}{2c} \approx \frac1M\sum_k\frac{\|\mathbf y - \mathbf d_{\boldsymbol\phi}(\mathbf e_1(\mathbf y) + \sqrt{\mathbf e_2(\mathbf y)}\odot\boldsymbol\eta_k)\|^2}{2c},\] a deterministic, differentiable function of \((\boldsymbol\theta, \boldsymbol\phi)\) to which standard back-propagation applies. In practice even \(M = 1\) sample per data point per step works, because the noise averages out over mini-batches.

title: 11  Variational Bayes
text:
11.6 Exercises

Derive the decomposition \(\mathcal L = \mathbb E_q[\log f(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf z)] - D(q\,\|\,f_{\text{prior}})\).


Solution. \(\mathcal L = \mathbb E_q[\log f(\mathbf y, \mathbf z) - \log q(\mathbf z)] = \mathbb E_q[\log f(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf z) + \log f_{\text{prior}}(\mathbf z) - \log q(\mathbf z)] = \mathbb E_q[\log f(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf z)] - D(q\,\|\,f_{\text{prior}})\).


Show that mean-field VB underestimates posterior variances for a correlated Gaussian target with covariance \(\Sigma\).


Solution. From the bivariate example, the optimal factor variance is \(1/\Lambda_{jj} = 1/(\Sigma^{-1})_{jj}\). By the Schur complement, \(1/(\Sigma^{-1})_{11} = \Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21} \leq \Sigma_{11}\), with equality iff the coordinates are uncorrelated. Mean field reports the conditional variance, which is always smaller than the marginal one.


Compute \(D_{KL}(\mathcal N(m, s^2)\,\|\,\mathcal N(0,1))\) in one dimension and check the VAE formula.


Solution. \(D = \mathbb E_q[\log q - \log p] = \mathbb E_q\bigl[-\tfrac12\log(2\pi s^2) - \tfrac{(z-m)^2}{2s^2} + \tfrac12\log 2\pi + \tfrac{z^2}{2}\bigr] = -\tfrac12\log s^2 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac12(m^2 + s^2)\), i.e. \(\tfrac12(m^2 + s^2 - 1 - \log s^2)\), matching the formula with \(d = 1\). It vanishes iff \(m = 0, s = 1\).


In the one-Gaussian example with \(a_0 = b_0 = \lambda_0 = 0\), \(n = 10\) and \(s^2 = 4\), iterate the CAVI equations starting from \(\mathbb E[\tau] = 1\) and verify the fixed point.


Solution. \(a' = 5.5\), fixed point \(b' = (n+1)s^2/2 = 22\). Start: \(\lambda' = 10\), \(b' = \tfrac12(10\cdot4) + \tfrac12\cdot10/10 = 20.5\); \(\mathbb E\tau = 0.268\), \(\lambda' = 2.68\), \(b' = 20 + 1.86 = 21.86\); \(\mathbb E\tau = 0.2516\), \(\lambda' = 2.516\), \(b' = 20 + 1.987 = 21.987\); … converging to \(b' = 22\), \(\mathbb E[\tau] = 0.25 = 1/s^2\), \(\operatorname{Var}_q\mu = 0.4 = s^2/n\).

title: 11  Variational Bayes
text:
11.7 Callouts






VB is biased by construction: the true posterior is generally not in \(\mathcal Q\). Use it when speed matters and the posterior mean is what you need; use MCMC/HMC when calibrated uncertainty matters.









Monitor \(\mathcal L\) during CAVI: it must increase at every step. A decrease always means a bug in the update equations. Run from several initialisations and keep the solution with the largest \(\mathcal L\).









Mean-field VB underestimates posterior variance and can lock onto a single mode. Richer families (full-rank Gaussians, normalising flows) reduce, but do not remove, this bias.

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.1 Hamiltonian dynamics
We now have several ways to obtain posterior estimates. Gibbs sampling and variational Bayes are very efficient, but both need strong analytical control: closed-form conditionals, typically requiring simple likelihoods and conjugate priors. When these are unavailable we can always fall back on Metropolis–Hastings, but in high dimension its random-walk proposals must be tiny to be accepted (Chapter 7), and the chain diffuses slowly. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) overcomes this by borrowing classical mechanics: it uses the gradient of the log-posterior to build distant proposals that are nevertheless accepted with probability close to 1. Like Metropolis it needs the unnormalised posterior (likelihood × prior), and in addition its derivatives with respect to the parameters.
Consider coordinates \(\mathbf x = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)\) and conjugate momenta \(\mathbf p = (p_1, \ldots, p_n)\), with Hamiltonian \[H(\mathbf x, \mathbf p) = \sum_i\frac{p_i^2}{2m_i} + U(\mathbf x),\] the sum of kinetic and potential energy. Hamilton’s equations \[\dot x_i = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i} = \frac{p_i}{m_i}, \qquad \dot p_i = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial x_i} = -\frac{\partial U}{\partial x_i}\] define a flow \(\phi_t : \mathbb R^{2n} \to \mathbb R^{2n}\), \((\mathbf x_0, \mathbf p_0) \mapsto (\mathbf x_t, \mathbf p_t)\). Three properties of this flow make it useful for Monte Carlo.

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.1.1 Energy conservation
\[\frac{dH}{dt} = \sum_i\Bigl(\frac{\partial H}{\partial x_i}\dot x_i + \frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}\dot p_i\Bigr) = \sum_i\Bigl(\frac{\partial H}{\partial x_i}\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i} - \frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial H}{\partial x_i}\Bigr) = 0 .\]


12.1.2 Volume preservation (Liouville’s theorem)

For every region \(A \subset \mathbb R^{2n}\), \(\operatorname{Vol}(\phi_t(A)) = \operatorname{Vol}(A)\); equivalently, the Jacobian determinant of the flow is \(|J_{\phi_t}| = 1\) everywhere.


Proof. Changing variables \((\mathbf x', \mathbf p') = \phi_t(\mathbf x, \mathbf p)\), \(\int_{\phi_t(A)}d\mathbf x'\,d\mathbf p' = \int_A |J_{\phi_t}|\,d\mathbf x\,d\mathbf p\), so volume preservation for all \(A\) is equivalent to \(|J_{\phi_t}| = 1\). For an infinitesimal time step, \[\phi_{\delta t}(\mathbf x, \mathbf p) = \begin{pmatrix}\mathbf x\\ \mathbf p\end{pmatrix} + \delta t\begin{pmatrix}\partial_{\mathbf p}H \\ -\partial_{\mathbf x}H\end{pmatrix} + O(\delta t^2), \qquad J_{\phi_{\delta t}} = \begin{pmatrix}1 + \delta t\,\partial_{\mathbf x}\partial_{\mathbf p}H & \delta t\,\partial^2_{\mathbf p}H \\ -\delta t\,\partial^2_{\mathbf x}H & 1 - \delta t\,\partial_{\mathbf p}\partial_{\mathbf x}H\end{pmatrix} + O(\delta t^2).\] The determinant is \(1 + \delta t\,(\partial_{\mathbf x}\partial_{\mathbf p}H - \partial_{\mathbf p}\partial_{\mathbf x}H) + O(\delta t^2) = 1 + O(\delta t^2)\): the trace of the first-order term vanishes because mixed partial derivatives commute. For finite \(t = n\,\delta t\), \(\phi_t\) is the \(n\)-fold composition, so \(|J_{\phi_t}| = (1 + O(\delta t^2))^n = 1 + O(n\,\delta t^2) = 1 + O(t^2/n) \to 1\) as \(n \to \infty\).



12.1.3 Time reversibility
The flow is invertible, and its inverse is obtained by running time backwards: \(\phi_t^{-1} = \phi_{-t}\), i.e. integrating \(\dot x_i = -p_i/m_i\), \(\dot p_i = +\partial_{x_i}U\). These are the original equations with \(\mathbf p \to -\mathbf p\). Introducing the momentum flip \(N_p(\mathbf x, \mathbf p) = (\mathbf x, -\mathbf p)\), \[\phi_t^{-1} = \phi_{-t} = N_p\circ\phi_t\circ N_p .\] To run a trajectory backwards: flip the momentum, run forwards, flip again. For every forward trajectory \((\mathbf x, \mathbf p) \to (\mathbf x', \mathbf p')\) there is a backward one \((\mathbf x', -\mathbf p') \to (\mathbf x, -\mathbf p)\).

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.2 Numerical integration of Hamilton’s equations
In practice the flow must be approximated numerically, and how matters: we need an integrator that retains volume preservation and reversibility.

12.2.1 Euler’s method
\[p_i(t + \epsilon) = p_i(t) - \epsilon\,\partial_{x_i}U(\mathbf x(t)), \qquad x_i(t + \epsilon) = x_i(t) + \epsilon\,p_i(t)/m_i .\] Its Jacobian determinant is \(\det\begin{pmatrix}1 & \epsilon/m \\ -\epsilon\,\partial^2_xU & 1\end{pmatrix} = 1 + \epsilon^2\partial_x^2U/m \neq 1\): Euler does not preserve volume. For the harmonic oscillator (\(m = 1\), \(U = x^2/2\)) each step multiplies the phase-space area by \(1 + \epsilon^2\) and the radius by \(\sqrt{1 + \epsilon^2}\): the exact circular orbit becomes an outward spiral. With \(\epsilon = 0.3\), twenty steps already inflate the radius by \((1.09)^{10} \approx 2.4\). Smaller steps (\(\epsilon = 0.01\)) delay the divergence, but over many steps (thousands) the trajectory still spirals away.


12.2.2 Modified (symplectic) Euler
Update the momentum first, then use the new momentum to update the position: \[p_i(t + \epsilon) = p_i(t) - \epsilon\,\partial_{x_i}U(\mathbf x(t)), \qquad x_i(t + \epsilon) = x_i(t) + \epsilon\,p_i(t + \epsilon)/m_i .\] This is the composition of a map that changes only momenta and a map that changes only positions, with Jacobians \[J^{(p)} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -\epsilon\,\partial^2_{\mathbf x}U & 1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad J^{(x)} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & \epsilon\,\operatorname{diag}(m^{-1}) \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix},\] both triangular with unit diagonal, hence determinant 1. The modified Euler method preserves volume exactly, and trajectories no longer diverge. But it is not reversible: flipping the momentum, running it, and flipping again does not retrace the trajectory, because the order “momentum then position” is not symmetric in time.


12.2.3 Leapfrog
The fix is to make the scheme symmetric: half a step in momentum, a full step in position, another half step in momentum.

\[\begin{aligned}
p_i(t + \tfrac\epsilon2) &= p_i(t) - \tfrac\epsilon2\,\partial_{x_i}U(\mathbf x(t)), \\
x_i(t + \epsilon) &= x_i(t) + \epsilon\,p_i(t + \tfrac\epsilon2)/m_i, \\
p_i(t + \epsilon) &= p_i(t + \tfrac\epsilon2) - \tfrac\epsilon2\,\partial_{x_i}U(\mathbf x(t + \epsilon)).
\end{aligned}\]


The leapfrog map \(\phi^{\text{lf}}_\epsilon\) is

volume-preserving: it is a composition of three shear maps (momentum, position, momentum), each with unit Jacobian determinant;
time-reversible: \((\phi^{\text{lf}}_\epsilon)^{-1} = \phi^{\text{lf}}_{-\epsilon} = N_p\circ\phi^{\text{lf}}_\epsilon\circ N_p\);
second-order accurate: the energy error is \(O(\epsilon^2)\) and, for stable step sizes, does not drift over long trajectories.



Proof (Proof of reversibility). Apply \(\phi^{\text{lf}}_{-\epsilon}\) to the endpoint \((\mathbf x(t + \epsilon), \mathbf p(t + \epsilon))\): \[\begin{aligned}
p_i' &= p_i(t + \epsilon) + \tfrac\epsilon2\partial_{x_i}U(\mathbf x(t + \epsilon)) = p_i(t + \tfrac\epsilon2), \\
x_i' &= x_i(t + \epsilon) - \epsilon\,p_i(t + \tfrac\epsilon2)/m_i = x_i(t), \\
p_i'' &= p_i(t + \tfrac\epsilon2) + \tfrac\epsilon2\partial_{x_i}U(\mathbf x(t)) = p_i(t),
\end{aligned}\] recovering the starting point exactly (each line undoes the corresponding line of the forward step, in reverse order). And running \(\phi_{-\epsilon}\) is the same as flipping \(\mathbf p\), running \(\phi_{+\epsilon}\), and flipping again.


Take \(m = 1\), \(U(x) = x^2/(2\sigma^2)\) (a Gaussian target of width \(\sigma\)). One leapfrog step is the linear map \[\begin{pmatrix}x(t + \epsilon)\\ p(t + \epsilon)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1 - \frac{\epsilon^2}{2\sigma^2} & \epsilon \\[3pt] -\frac{\epsilon}{\sigma^2} + \frac{\epsilon^3}{4\sigma^4} & 1 - \frac{\epsilon^2}{2\sigma^2}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x(t)\\ p(t)\end{pmatrix},\] with determinant \(\bigl(1 - \frac{\epsilon^2}{2\sigma^2}\bigr)^2 + \frac{\epsilon^2}{\sigma^2} - \frac{\epsilon^4}{4\sigma^4} = 1\) (volume preservation). With \(a = 1 - \epsilon^2/(2\sigma^2)\) the eigenvalues are \(\lambda_\pm = a \pm\sqrt{a^2 - 1}\), with \(\lambda_+\lambda_- = 1\).

If \(\epsilon < 2\sigma\), then \(|a| < 1\), the eigenvalues are complex conjugates with \(|\lambda_\pm| = 1\), and the trajectory is a stable (slightly distorted) ellipse.
If \(\epsilon > 2\sigma\), the eigenvalues are real with one of modulus \(> 1\): the trajectory diverges exponentially.

Rule of thumb: the step size must be smaller than the narrowest width of the target, \(\epsilon \lesssim \sigma_{\min}\).

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.3 The HMC algorithm

12.3.1 The augmented distribution
To sample \(\pi(\mathbf x)\), \(\mathbf x \in \mathbb R^n\), add \(n\) auxiliary momenta, independent of \(\mathbf x\) and of each other, \(p_i \sim \mathcal N(0, m_i)\): \[\Pi(\mathbf x, \mathbf p) = \pi(\mathbf x)\cdot\prod_i(2\pi m_i)^{-1/2}e^{-p_i^2/2m_i} .\] If we can sample \(\Pi\), the \(\mathbf x\)-components of the samples are distributed according to \(\pi\) (just discard \(\mathbf p\)). Define the potential \(U(\mathbf x) = -\log\pi(\mathbf x)\); then \[\Pi(\mathbf x, \mathbf p) = \frac{1}{Z}e^{-H(\mathbf x, \mathbf p)}, \qquad H(\mathbf x, \mathbf p) = U(\mathbf x) + \sum_i\frac{p_i^2}{2m_i},\] a Boltzmann distribution at unit temperature, with the momentum variances playing the role of masses. Below we take \(m_i = 1\), so \(H = U(\mathbf x) + \tfrac12|\mathbf p|^2\).
For Bayesian inference, \(\pi(\mathbf x) = f(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x)f_{\text{prior}}(\mathbf x)/f(\mathbf y)\); since the evidence does not depend on \(\mathbf x\) it is absorbed into \(Z\), and \[U(\mathbf x) = -\log f(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf x) - \log f_{\text{prior}}(\mathbf x).\]


12.3.2 The proposal
Each HMC iteration is a composition of two Metropolis–Hastings moves on \(\Pi\):

Momentum refresh: draw \(\mathbf p_r \sim \mathcal N(0, I)\), independently of the current \(\mathbf p\).
Hamiltonian move: evolve \((\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r)\) under the Hamiltonian flow for a time \(t\) and flip the momentum: \((\mathbf x', \mathbf p') = N_p\circ\phi_t(\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r)\).


With the exact Hamiltonian flow, both moves are accepted with probability 1.


Proof. Move 1 is a Gibbs update: it samples \(\mathbf p\) from its exact conditional \(\Pi(\mathbf p\mid\mathbf x) = \mathcal N(0, I)\). Explicitly, the proposal is \(T(\mathbf x', \mathbf p_r\mid\mathbf x, \mathbf p) = \delta(\mathbf x' - \mathbf x)(2\pi)^{-n/2}e^{-|\mathbf p_r|^2/2}\) and the Hastings ratio is \[\frac{\Pi(\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r)\,T(\mathbf x, \mathbf p\mid\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r)}{\Pi(\mathbf x, \mathbf p)\,T(\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r\mid\mathbf x, \mathbf p)} = \frac{\pi(\mathbf x)e^{-|\mathbf p_r|^2/2}\cdot e^{-|\mathbf p|^2/2}}{\pi(\mathbf x)e^{-|\mathbf p|^2/2}\cdot e^{-|\mathbf p_r|^2/2}} = 1 .\]
Move 2 is deterministic: \(T(\mathbf x', \mathbf p'\mid\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r) = \delta\bigl((\mathbf x', -\mathbf p') - \phi_t(\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r)\bigr)\). Energy conservation gives \(\Pi(\mathbf x', \mathbf p') = \Pi(\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r)\) (the flip does not change \(|\mathbf p|^2\)), so the acceptance probability reduces to \(\min\{1, T(\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r\mid\mathbf x', \mathbf p')/T(\mathbf x', \mathbf p'\mid\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r)\}\). For the reverse move, \[T(\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r\mid\mathbf x', \mathbf p') = \delta\bigl((\mathbf x, -\mathbf p_r) - \phi_t(\mathbf x', \mathbf p')\bigr) = \delta\bigl((\mathbf x', \mathbf p') - \phi_t^{-1}(\mathbf x, -\mathbf p_r)\bigr)\,|J_{\phi_t}|^{-1},\] and \(|J_{\phi_t}| = 1\) by volume preservation. By reversibility \(\phi_t^{-1}\circ N_p = N_p\circ\phi_t\), so \(\phi_t^{-1}(\mathbf x, -\mathbf p_r) = N_p\phi_t(\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r)\) and the delta function equals \(\delta\bigl((\mathbf x', -\mathbf p') - \phi_t(\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r)\bigr) = T(\mathbf x', \mathbf p'\mid\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r)\). The ratio is 1.

The proof shows exactly which properties are needed: volume preservation (no Jacobian factor), reversibility with the momentum flip (the reverse proposal exists and has the same density), and energy conservation (\(\Pi\) is unchanged). The momentum flip is required for the proof; in practice it can be skipped, because the momentum is immediately resampled at the next iteration.


12.3.3 With a numerical integrator
The exact flow is replaced by \(L = t/\epsilon\) leapfrog steps. Leapfrog is exactly volume-preserving and reversible, so the proposal densities still cancel; but energy is conserved only approximately, \(\Pi(\mathbf x', \mathbf p') \approx \Pi(\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r)\). The Metropolis correction takes care of this:

From the current state \(\mathbf x\):

draw \(\mathbf p_r \sim \mathcal N(0, I)\);
apply \(L\) leapfrog steps of size \(\epsilon\) to \((\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r)\), obtaining \((\mathbf x', \mathbf p')\) (and flip \(\mathbf p'\));
accept \(\mathbf x'\) with probability \[\min\Bigl\{1, \frac{\Pi(\mathbf x', \mathbf p')}{\Pi(\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r)}\Bigr\} = \min\bigl\{1, e^{H(\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r) - H(\mathbf x', \mathbf p')}\bigr\};\] otherwise keep \(\mathbf x\).


The acceptance probability depends only on the integration error, not on the distance travelled. With a stable step size the energy error stays small along arbitrarily long trajectories, so HMC can make large moves with high acceptance. The price is one gradient evaluation \(\nabla U(\mathbf x) = -\nabla\log f(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x) - \nabla\log f_{\text{prior}}(\mathbf x)\) per leapfrog step.

Remark (HMC as gradient descent with momentum). The update \(\mathbf p \leftarrow \mathbf p - \epsilon\nabla U\), \(\mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + \epsilon\mathbf p\) is “heavy-ball” gradient descent on \(U = -\log\pi\): the direction of motion is not just the current gradient but has inertia. HMC balances exploration (the random momentum draw, which sets the direction and energy of each trajectory) and exploitation (the deterministic flow, which follows the geometry of the posterior). Unlike gradient descent, energy conservation prevents the trajectory from simply sliding to the mode: it converts potential into kinetic energy and back, travelling along the level sets of the posterior.

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.4 Advantages of HMC
The key advantage of HMC is that it replaces the random walk of Metropolis by directed motion. A random walk with step \(\epsilon\) moves a distance \(\sim\epsilon\sqrt k\) in \(k\) steps; a Hamiltonian trajectory moves a distance \(\sim\epsilon k\).

Sample \(\mathcal N(\mathbf 0, \Sigma)\) with \[\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0.98 \\ 0.98 & 1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \text{eigenvalues } 1.98 \text{ and } 0.02 .\] The standard deviations along the principal axes are \(\sigma_1 = \sqrt{1.98} \approx 1.41\) and \(\sigma_2 = \sqrt{0.02} \approx 0.14\). Both samplers must use steps of size \(\approx\sigma_2\) to stay stable/accepted: HMC with \(\epsilon = \sigma_2\) and \(L = 20\) leapfrog steps per iteration; Metropolis with Gaussian jumps of size \(\sigma_2\).
To reach an effectively independent point we must cross the long axis, a distance \(\approx\sigma_1 \approx 10\,\sigma_2\). HMC’s momentum along the long direction is stable, so about 10 leapfrog steps suffice. Metropolis cannot move consistently in one direction: after \(k\) steps it has moved \(\sim\sigma_2\sqrt k\), so it needs \(\sim 100\) steps.
With the same budget — 20 HMC iterations (\(400\) leapfrog steps) versus \(400\) Metropolis steps — the estimated covariances are (Allegra, Fig. 13.2) \[\hat\Sigma_{\text{HMC}} = \begin{pmatrix}0.96 & 0.90 \\ 0.90 & 0.88\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \hat\Sigma_{\text{Met}} = \begin{pmatrix}0.26 & 0.26 \\ 0.26 & 0.30\end{pmatrix}.\] HMC is already close to the truth; Metropolis has explored only a small part of the long axis and badly underestimates the variances.


Take \(\Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(0.01^2, 0.02^2, \ldots, 1.00^2)\): 100 independent coordinates with widths from \(0.01\) to \(1\). Both step sizes must be of the order of the smallest width: HMC uses \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal U[0.0104, 0.0156]\) with \(L = 150\) leapfrog steps and \(1000\) iterations; Metropolis uses jumps \(\sim\mathcal U[0.0176, 0.0264]\) and \(150{,}000\) steps — the same number of gradient/likelihood evaluations. (Randomising \(\epsilon\) avoids accidental periodicities in which a trajectory returns exactly to its start.) HMC estimates the means and standard deviations of all coordinates well, including the widest ones; Metropolis gets the narrow coordinates right but grossly underestimates the spread of the wide ones, which it has barely explored.


For targets with \(d\) roughly independent components, keeping the acceptance rate fixed requires a step size \(\epsilon \propto d^{-1/2}\) for random-walk Metropolis but only \(\epsilon \propto d^{-1/4}\) for HMC. Reaching an effectively independent point (moving a distance of order the target’s width) therefore takes \(O(d)\) Metropolis steps but only \(O(d^{1/4})\) leapfrog steps. If each density or gradient evaluation costs \(O(d)\), the total cost per independent sample is \(O(d^2)\) for Metropolis versus \(O(d^{5/4})\) for HMC (Neal 2011, §5.4.4). The optimal HMC acceptance rate in this limit is about \(0.65\).

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.5 Practical considerations

Step size. Too large: leapfrog becomes unstable and acceptance collapses (“divergent transitions”). Too small: wasted gradient evaluations. Modern implementations tune \(\epsilon\) during warm-up to reach a target acceptance (\(\approx 0.65\)–\(0.8\)).
Trajectory length. Too short: HMC degenerates into a random walk. Too long: trajectories loop back (for a Gaussian, after half a period). The No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS, Hoffman & Gelman 2014) chooses \(L\) adaptively, stopping when the trajectory starts to turn back; it underlies Stan and PyMC.
Mass matrix. Using \(\mathbf p \sim \mathcal N(0, M)\) with \(M \approx \Sigma_\pi^{-1}\) (estimated during warm-up) makes all directions equally “stiff”: it is equivalent to rescaling the target to unit covariance, which removes the \(\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}\) penalty seen in the examples.
Limitations. HMC requires a differentiable log-density on a continuous space: discrete parameters need Gibbs steps (or marginalisation). Multimodality remains hard. Each step costs a gradient, which can be expensive (automatic differentiation helps).

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.6 Exercises

Show that the modified Euler map \(p \leftarrow p - \epsilon x\), \(x \leftarrow x + \epsilon p\) for the harmonic oscillator has unit Jacobian, and find the condition on \(\epsilon\) for stability.


Solution. The map is \(\begin{pmatrix}x'\\p'\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1 - \epsilon^2 & \epsilon \\ -\epsilon & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\p\end{pmatrix}\), determinant \(1 - \epsilon^2 + \epsilon^2 = 1\). Trace \(2 - \epsilon^2\): eigenvalues are complex with unit modulus iff \(|2 - \epsilon^2| < 2\), i.e. \(\epsilon < 2\) — the same stability limit as leapfrog with \(\sigma = 1\).


For a Gaussian target \(\mathcal N(\mathbf 0, \Sigma)\) show that with mass matrix \(M = \Sigma^{-1}\) the Hamiltonian dynamics reduce to independent oscillators all with the same frequency.


Solution. \(H = \tfrac12\mathbf x^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf x + \tfrac12\mathbf p^\top M^{-1}\mathbf p = \tfrac12\mathbf x^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf x + \tfrac12\mathbf p^\top\Sigma\mathbf p\). Then \(\dot{\mathbf x} = \Sigma\mathbf p\), \(\dot{\mathbf p} = -\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf x\), so \(\ddot{\mathbf x} = -\mathbf x\): every direction oscillates with unit angular frequency. With \(M = I\) instead, the mode along eigenvector \(k\) has frequency \(1/\sigma_k\), and a single step size must resolve the fastest mode while the trajectory must be long enough for the slowest: the ratio \(\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}\) is the cost of a poor mass matrix.


Write the HMC potential \(U\) and its gradient for the posterior of \(\mu\) in the model \(x_i \sim \mathcal N(\mu, 1)\), \(\mu \sim \mathcal N(0, \tau^2)\).


Solution. \(U(\mu) = \tfrac12\sum_i(x_i - \mu)^2 + \mu^2/(2\tau^2)\) + const, \(U'(\mu) = -\sum_i(x_i - \mu) + \mu/\tau^2 = (n + \tau^{-2})\mu - n\bar x\). The target is Gaussian with \(\sigma^2 = (n + \tau^{-2})^{-1}\), so stable leapfrog needs \(\epsilon < 2\sigma\).


Explain why the momentum flip is needed in the proof of detailed balance but can be omitted in practice.


Solution. Without the flip, the reverse of the proposal \((\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r) \to \phi_t(\mathbf x, \mathbf p_r)\) would require running the flow backwards, which is not the same proposal mechanism, so \(T(\text{reverse})\) would vanish and detailed balance would fail. With the flip, the proposal is an involution: applying it twice returns the start. In practice the momentum is discarded and redrawn from the symmetric \(\mathcal N(0, I)\) at the next iteration, so its sign never matters for the \(\mathbf x\)-chain.

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.7 Callouts






HMC is the default sampler for smooth posteriors over continuous parameters (Stan, PyMC, NumPyro). Use Gibbs for discrete latent variables and random-walk Metropolis only as a baseline or when gradients are unavailable.









Poor HMC mixing (low ESS, divergences) usually signals bad geometry. Reparameterise to make the posterior more isotropic, or adapt the mass matrix.









Leapfrog energy errors oscillate but do not drift for stable step sizes. This is why long trajectories remain acceptable — an integrator with energy drift (like Euler) would make acceptance decay with trajectory length.

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
13.1 Intractable likelihoods
Every method so far — Metropolis, Gibbs, variational Bayes, HMC — requires the likelihood \(f(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf x)\) to be evaluable (and HMC, its gradient). In many scientific problems it is not: the likelihood may have no closed form, or be too expensive to compute. Often, however, the model is easy to simulate: given parameters \(\mathbf x\) we can generate synthetic data \(\mathbf y \sim f(\cdot\mid\mathbf x)\). Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) performs Bayesian inference using simulations alone, by replacing the likelihood with a comparison between simulated and observed data.
Typical situations:

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
Latent dynamics. The observed data are a noisy function of a hidden stochastic process; the likelihood is a sum (or integral) over all hidden trajectories.
Implicit models. The model is a simulator — an agent-based model in ecology or epidemiology, a coalescent process in population genetics, a stochastic simulation of a physical system — with no density written down anywhere.
Intractable normalisation. The likelihood is known up to a parameter-dependent constant (e.g. a partition function), so Metropolis ratios cannot be computed.


A binary hidden state \(z_t \in \{0, 1\}\) evolves as a Markov chain that switches with probability \(x\) at each step: \[P(z_{t+1} \mid z_t) = \begin{pmatrix}1 - x & x \\ x & 1 - x\end{pmatrix}.\] We cannot see \(z_t\); we measure \(y_t\), which equals \(z_t\) with probability \(\gamma\) and is flipped with probability \(1 - \gamma\): \[p_{Y|Z}(0\mid0) = p_{Y|Z}(1\mid1) = \gamma, \qquad p_{Y|Z}(1\mid0) = p_{Y|Z}(0\mid1) = 1 - \gamma .\] We want to infer the switching rate \(x\) from an observed sequence \(y_1, \ldots, y_T\).
The likelihood is a sum over all \(2^T\) hidden paths, \[f(\mathbf y \mid x) = \sum_{z_1, \ldots, z_T}P(z_1)\prod_{t=1}^{T-1}P(z_{t+1}\mid z_t)\prod_{t=1}^T p_{Y|Z}(y_t\mid z_t),\] because the observations at different times are correlated through the hidden chain. (For this small model the sum can be organised recursively — the forward algorithm of HMMs — but for richer hidden dynamics no such shortcut exists.) Simulating data, on the other hand, is trivial: draw \(z_1\), flip it with probability \(x\) at each step, and corrupt each \(z_t\) with probability \(1 - \gamma\).

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
section: 13.2 Exact rejection ABC for discrete data
text:
13.2 Exact rejection ABC for discrete data
Suppose the data take values in a discrete set \(\mathcal D\). Consider the following scheme, repeated to produce samples \(x_1, \ldots, x_N\):


Draw \(x' \sim f_{\text{prior}}(x)\).
Simulate \(\mathbf y' \sim f(\cdot \mid x')\).
If \(\mathbf y' = \mathbf y\) (the observed data), accept: \(x_i = x'\). Otherwise go back to step 1.



The accepted values are an i.i.d. sample from the exact posterior \(f(x \mid \mathbf y)\).


Proof. The probability density of proposing \(x\) and accepting it is \[\sum_{\mathbf y' \in \mathcal D}f_{\text{prior}}(x)\,f(\mathbf y' \mid x)\,\chi(\mathbf y' = \mathbf y) = f_{\text{prior}}(x)\,f(\mathbf y \mid x) \propto f(x \mid \mathbf y).\] The likelihood is never evaluated: it is sampled, through the frequency with which \(x\) reproduces the data. The overall acceptance probability is \(\int f_{\text{prior}}(x)f(\mathbf y\mid x)\,dx = f(\mathbf y)\), the evidence.


Observed: \(k = 7\) heads in \(n = 10\) tosses. Prior \(\theta \sim \mathcal U(0,1)\). ABC: draw \(\theta'\), toss a \(\theta'\)-coin ten times, accept if the result has exactly 7 heads. (Matching the number of heads rather than the exact sequence is legitimate because \(k\) is a sufficient statistic — see below.) The accepted \(\theta\)’s are distributed as \(\text{Beta}(8, 4)\), the exact posterior. The acceptance rate is \(f(k = 7) = \int_0^1\binom{10}{7}\theta^7(1-\theta)^3\,d\theta = 1/11\). With the full sequence it would be \(1/(11\binom{10}{7}) = 1/1320\) — same posterior, 120 times slower.

Exact matching becomes hopeless as the data grow: the acceptance rate is the evidence, which decays exponentially with the size of the data set. For continuous data it is exactly zero, since \(P(\mathbf y' = \mathbf y) = 0\).

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
13.3 The ABC algorithm
Two approximations make ABC work in general: compare summary statistics instead of raw data, and accept approximate matches.

Choose a summary statistic \(\eta : \mathcal D \to \mathbb R^s\), a distance (e.g. Euclidean) and a tolerance \(\epsilon > 0\). To generate each sample:

draw \(x' \sim f_{\text{prior}}(x)\);
simulate \(\mathbf y' \sim f(\cdot\mid x')\);
if \(\|\eta(\mathbf y') - \eta(\mathbf y)\| < \epsilon\) accept \(x_i = x'\); otherwise go back to step 1.


The accepted pairs \((x, \mathbf y')\) are distributed as \[f_\epsilon(x, \mathbf y' \mid \mathbf y) = \frac{f_{\text{prior}}(x)\,f(\mathbf y'\mid x)\,\chi\bigl(\|\eta(\mathbf y') - \eta(\mathbf y)\| < \epsilon\bigr)}{\int dx\,d\mathbf y'\,f_{\text{prior}}(x)\,f(\mathbf y'\mid x)\,\chi\bigl(\|\eta(\mathbf y') - \eta(\mathbf y)\| < \epsilon\bigr)},\] so the samples of \(x\) come from the ABC posterior \[f_\epsilon(x \mid \mathbf y) = \int d\mathbf y'\,f_\epsilon(x, \mathbf y'\mid\mathbf y) \propto f_{\text{prior}}(x)\;P\bigl(\|\eta(\mathbf Y') - \eta(\mathbf y)\| < \epsilon \;\big|\; x\bigr).\] The exact likelihood \(f(\mathbf y\mid x)\) has been replaced by the probability that a simulation at \(x\) lands within \(\epsilon\) of the observed summaries. The basic intuition is that

a representative (enough) summary statistic \(\eta\) together with a small (enough) tolerance \(\epsilon\) produces a good (enough) approximation, \(f_\epsilon(x\mid\mathbf y) \approx f(x\mid\mathbf y)\).

Two sources of error must be kept in mind:

Tolerance. As \(\epsilon \to 0\), \(f_\epsilon(x\mid\mathbf y) \to f(x \mid \eta(\mathbf y))\), the posterior given the summaries. For \(\epsilon > 0\) it is broader: ABC with tolerance \(\epsilon\) is exact inference for a model in which the observed summaries are corrupted by uniform noise of size \(\epsilon\).
Insufficiency. \(f(x\mid\eta(\mathbf y))\) equals \(f(x\mid\mathbf y)\) only if \(\eta\) is sufficient; otherwise information is lost, and the ABC posterior is wider (or even biased).


13.3.1 Summary statistics and sufficiency

\(\eta(\mathbf y)\) is sufficient for \(x\) if \(f(\mathbf y \mid x)\) depends on \(\mathbf y\) only through \(\eta(\mathbf y)\) (more precisely, \(f(\mathbf y\mid x) = g(\eta(\mathbf y), x)h(\mathbf y)\) — Fisher–Neyman factorisation). Equivalently, \(f(x\mid\mathbf y) = f(x\mid\eta(\mathbf y))\) for every prior; in information-theoretic terms, \(I(X; \mathbf Y) = I(X; \eta(\mathbf Y))\) — equality in the data-processing inequality of Chapter 2.

For i.i.d. Bernoulli data the number of successes is sufficient; for i.i.d. Gaussian data with unknown mean and variance, \((\sum y_i, \sum y_i^2)\) is. For complex simulators sufficient statistics of low dimension rarely exist, and \(\eta\) is chosen by insight — moments, quantiles, autocorrelations, counts of characteristic events — or learned by regression or neural networks.
There is a trade-off: adding statistics reduces information loss but increases the dimension \(s\), and the acceptance rate of \(\|\eta' - \eta\| < \epsilon\) decays like \(\epsilon^s\) — the curse of dimensionality strikes again.

For the hidden Markov model above, natural summaries of the observed sequence are

the fraction of ones, \(\bar y\) (uninformative here: by symmetry it is \(\approx 1/2\) for any \(x\));
the number of switches \(s(\mathbf y) = \sum_t \chi(y_{t+1} \neq y_t)\), which increases with \(x\);
the lag-1 autocorrelation of \(y\).

Since the hidden state has lag-1 autocorrelation \(1 - 2x\) and each noisy observation multiplies it by \((2\gamma - 1)\), the expected switching frequency of \(y\) is \(\mathbb E[s]/(T-1) = \tfrac12\bigl(1 - (1 - 2x)(2\gamma - 1)^2\bigr)\). ABC with \(\eta = s(\mathbf y)/(T - 1)\) therefore concentrates around \(x\) values that reproduce the observed switching rate. If \(\gamma = 1/2\) the data carry no information about \(x\) and the ABC posterior correctly reproduces the prior.

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
13.4 Beyond rejection: ABC-MCMC and ABC-SMC
Plain rejection wastes most simulations on parameters drawn from the prior, far from the posterior. Two standard improvements:

From the current \(x\), propose \(x' \sim q(\cdot\mid x)\), simulate \(\mathbf y' \sim f(\cdot\mid x')\), and accept with probability \[\min\Bigl\{1, \frac{f_{\text{prior}}(x')\,q(x\mid x')}{f_{\text{prior}}(x)\,q(x'\mid x)}\Bigr\}\cdot\chi\bigl(\|\eta(\mathbf y') - \eta(\mathbf y)\| < \epsilon\bigr).\] This is Metropolis–Hastings on the augmented target \(f_\epsilon(x, \mathbf y'\mid\mathbf y)\), using the simulator as part of the proposal; the intractable likelihoods cancel. Its stationary distribution is \(f_\epsilon(x \mid \mathbf y)\).


Run a population of particles through a decreasing sequence of tolerances \(\epsilon_1 > \epsilon_2 > \cdots > \epsilon_T\). At each stage, resample particles from the previous population, perturb them, keep those whose simulations fall within the new tolerance, and reweight to correct for the perturbation. The population is gradually guided from the prior to the region of high posterior mass.


Remark (Simulation-based inference). Modern neural methods train a network on simulated pairs \((x, \mathbf y)\) to approximate the posterior \(f(x\mid\mathbf y)\) (neural posterior estimation), the likelihood, or the likelihood ratio directly. They can be seen as ABC with learned summary statistics and a learned (variational, cf. Chapter 10) posterior, and are far more simulation-efficient in high dimension.

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
13.5 Applications

Coalescent models generate gene genealogies whose likelihood involves an intractable sum over genealogies, but which are easy to simulate. ABC was developed in this field (Tavaré et al. 1997; Pritchard et al. 1999; Beaumont et al. 2002) to infer population sizes, migration rates and split times from DNA data — the same kind of question as the grey-seal problem of Chapter 9, but with demographic history included.


Stochastic compartmental and agent-based models of epidemics and of population dynamics are straightforward to simulate but have intractable likelihoods, especially with partial observation. ABC-SMC and neural simulation-based inference are routinely used to fit them to incidence time series.

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
13.6 Exercises

Show that ABC rejection with \(\epsilon = 0\) has acceptance probability zero for continuous data, and that for discrete data its acceptance probability equals the evidence \(f(\mathbf y)\).


Solution. For continuous \(\mathbf y\), \(P(\mathbf y' = \mathbf y \mid x) = 0\) for every \(x\). For discrete data, \(P(\text{accept}) = \int dx\,f_{\text{prior}}(x)P(\mathbf y' = \mathbf y\mid x) = \int dx\,f_{\text{prior}}(x)f(\mathbf y\mid x) = f(\mathbf y)\). (This even gives a — very inefficient — Monte Carlo estimator of the evidence.)


For \(\mathbf y \mid \theta \sim \mathcal N(\theta\mathbf 1, I_n)\) with prior \(\theta \sim \mathcal N(0, \tau^2)\), show that ABC with \(\eta = \bar y\) recovers the exact posterior as \(\epsilon \to 0\), and compute the ABC posterior for finite \(\epsilon\) when the uniform window is replaced by a Gaussian kernel of width \(\epsilon\).


Solution. \(\bar y\) is sufficient (\(f(\mathbf y\mid\theta) \propto e^{-n(\bar y - \theta)^2/2}\times(\text{terms without }\theta)\)), so \(f(\theta\mid\bar y) = f(\theta\mid\mathbf y)\) and the \(\epsilon \to 0\) limit is exact. With a Gaussian kernel, the ABC “likelihood” is \(P(\bar y' \approx \bar y\mid\theta) \propto \mathcal N(\bar y; \theta, 1/n + \epsilon^2)\): the ABC posterior is the exact posterior for a model with noise variance inflated from \(1/n\) to \(1/n + \epsilon^2\), i.e. \(\mathcal N\bigl(\frac{\bar y/(1/n + \epsilon^2)}{1/\tau^2 + 1/(1/n + \epsilon^2)}, (1/\tau^2 + 1/(1/n + \epsilon^2))^{-1}\bigr)\). The tolerance should be small compared to the statistical uncertainty \(1/\sqrt n\).


In the noisy HMM, why is \(\bar y\) a useless summary statistic for \(x\)? Suggest a statistic and explain how it depends on \(x\) and \(\gamma\).


Solution. The hidden chain is symmetric, so its stationary distribution is \((1/2, 1/2)\) for every \(x\), and the symmetric noise preserves this: \(\mathbb E[\bar y] = 1/2\) regardless of \(x\). The switching frequency of \(\mathbf y\) depends on \(x\): \(\mathbb E[s]/(T-1) = \tfrac12[1 - (1-2x)(2\gamma-1)^2]\). It increases with \(x\) (for \(x < 1/2\)) and its sensitivity to \(x\) is proportional to \((2\gamma - 1)^2\), vanishing for completely noisy measurements.

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
13.7 Callouts






ABC turns a simulator into an inference engine. It is the natural tool whenever the model is defined by a simulation rather than by a density.









Validate an ABC pipeline on synthetic data generated with known parameters, and check that the posterior is stable as \(\epsilon\) decreases and as summary statistics are added or removed.









ABC posteriors are approximations with two uncontrolled errors — tolerance and insufficiency. Always report \(\epsilon\), the summaries used and the acceptance rate.

title: 14  Problems
text:
Exercise 14.1 (Problem 1) Last year, a student asked me this question: “In courses from previous years, teachers often brought up the concept of information, linking it to a specific context, such as the wave function in quantum mechanics, the Lagrangian/Hamiltonian in classical mechanics, etc. As a student, I always had the impression that information was the elephant in the room: it is mentioned in various branches of physics, without ever defining was it is” Using the notion of information we have developed, try to address this question. In what sense can the wavefunction provide information about a quantum system? In what sense can the Hamiltonian provide information about a classical system.


Solution. Information is often related to enropy which can be tracked to statistical mechanics, after that you can define the entropy from the Hamiltonian or the Lagrangian as they are equivalent formulations. In the case of quantum mechanics this is different, since it is defined with the probability of an outcome which also makes sense. The first thing to do is to is to define what the entropy is.
Entropy is often introduced as a measurement of disorder so, as seen in thermodynamics, warmer systems have higher entropy and cooler systems lower entropy.
The information (or Shanon’s entropy) is defined as:
\[
H[X]=-\sum_{i}^{n}p_X(x_i)log(p_X(x_i))
\] So the less information we have (or less likelihood of something to happen), lower is the probability and higher is the entropy
